rd-school-c3-evs-e.ch24-web-of-life.title: Web of Life
rd-school-c3-evs-e.ch24-web-of-life.subtitle: Sun, air, water, soil, plants, animals and us — all holding hands

sections.md:
Imagine a mango tree in your school ground. Birds build nests in it. Squirrels run up and down. Ants march along the bark. Children sit in its shade and eat its sweet mangoes in summer. Now imagine someone cuts the tree. Where will the birds go? What will the squirrels eat? Where will you sit at lunch time?

One tree is connected to so many lives! This chapter looks back at everything we learnt this year — plants, animals, water, food, houses, travel and things around us — and asks one big question: **how is everything connected?**

The connections are like the threads of a spider's web. If one thread breaks, the whole web shakes. That is why we call it the **web of life**.

check.q: Why is it called a 'web' of life?
options: Because all living and non-living things are connected like threads
Because it is on the internet
check.why: Like threads of a web, plants, animals, people, water, air and soil are all joined, so a change in one affects the others.

sections.md:
Look around you. Some things are **living**: they grow, eat, breathe, move on their own and have young ones — a dog, a neem tree, a fish, a baby. Some things are **non-living**: a stone, a chair, a pencil, water, air.

| Living | Non-living |
|---|---|
| grass | rock |
| cow | bucket |
| butterfly | cloud |
| you! | book |

But living things **need** non-living things. A plant needs sunlight, air, water and soil. A fish needs water. We need air to breathe, water to drink, and soil to grow our food. So the non-living world is part of the web too.

> Think: Is a seed living? It looks like a little stone, but put it in wet soil and it grows! A seed is living — it is just resting.

check.q: Which of these is non-living?
check.why: A brick does not grow, breathe, eat or have young ones, so it is non-living.

sections.h: The Sun, Air, Water and Soil
sections.md:
Four great gifts keep the web of life going:

- **The Sun** gives light and warmth. Green plants use sunlight to make their own food in their leaves.
- **Air** — every living thing breathes. Plants also give out the fresh air (oxygen) that we breathe in.
- **Water** — plants, animals and people all drink water. Rain fills rivers, ponds and wells. The sun heats water, it rises as vapour, forms clouds, and falls again as rain. This goes round and round.
- **Soil** — plants grow in soil. Earthworms and tiny creatures live in it. When leaves and dead plants rot in the soil, they make it rich again.

If water gets dirty, fish die. If air is smoky, people cough. If soil is full of plastic, plants cannot grow well. Keeping these clean keeps the web strong.

check.q: Who makes food using sunlight?
check.why: Green leaves use sunlight, air and water to make food for the plant.

sections.md:
Every living thing needs food. Plants make their own. Animals cannot — they eat plants, or eat other animals that ate plants.

A **food chain** shows who eats whom:

- grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
- leaves → goat → (people drink its milk)
- grain → mouse → cat
- tiny water plants → small fish → big fish → kingfisher

Every chain **starts with a plant**, and the plant gets its energy from the Sun. Animals that eat only plants (cow, deer, rabbit) are **plant-eaters**. Animals that eat other animals (lion, tiger, eagle) are **flesh-eaters**. Some, like crows, bears and most people, eat both.

If all the frogs disappeared, there would be too many grasshoppers eating the crops, and the snakes would go hungry. Every animal has a job in the web.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='140' fill='#f0fdf4'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='34' fill='#86efac'/><text x='60' y='65'>grass</text><circle cx='180' cy='60' r='34' fill='#bef264'/><text x='180' y='65'>grasshopper</text><circle cx='300' cy='60' r='34' fill='#6ee7b7'/><text x='300' y='65'>frog</text><circle cx='420' cy='60' r='34' fill='#fcd34d'/><text x='420' y='65'>snake</text><circle cx='540' cy='60' r='34' fill='#fdba74'/><text x='540' y='65'>eagle</text></g><g stroke='#166534' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#a)'><line x1='96' y1='60' x2='142' y2='60'/><line x1='216' y1='60' x2='262' y2='60'/><line x1='336' y1='60' x2='382' y2='60'/><line x1='456' y1='60' x2='502' y2='60'/></g><defs><marker id='a' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='6' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L8 4L0 8z' fill='#166534'/></marker></defs><circle cx='60' cy='115' r='7' fill='#facc15'><animate attributeName='cx' values='60;540' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><text x='300' y='135' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='12'>food energy passes along the chain</text></svg>

keyTerms: food chain — a line showing who eats whom
plant-eater — eats only plants
flesh-eater — eats other animals

check.q: Every food chain begins with…
check.why: Only green plants can make food from sunlight, so all food chains start with them.

sections.md:
Living things do not only eat each other — they also **help** each other.

- **Bees and butterflies** drink nectar from flowers and carry pollen, so the plant can make fruits and seeds.
- **Birds and animals** eat fruits and drop the seeds far away, so new trees grow.
- **Trees** give birds a home, animals shade, and people fruits, wood, medicine and fresh air.
- **Earthworms** loosen and enrich the soil for plants.
- **Cows, goats and hens** give us milk and eggs; we feed and care for them.
- **Vultures and crows** clean up dead animals; fungi and tiny germs turn dead leaves back into soil.

People depend on everyone else: the farmer grows grain, the potter makes pots, the weaver makes cloth, the driver carries goods. We are part of the web too.

> Did you know? One out of every three spoonfuls of our food depends on bees and other pollinators.

check.q: How do bees help plants?
options: They carry pollen from flower to flower
check.why: Carrying pollen helps flowers turn into fruits and seeds.

sections.md:
This last chapter ties together the whole book. Remember:

- **Plants** — leaves of many shapes, flowers, fruits and seeds; the trees around us.
- **Animals** — what they eat, where they live, how they move and how they care for their young.
- **Water** — from rain, rivers, wells and taps; why we should not waste it.
- **Food** — from plants and animals, cooked in many ways; sharing meals.
- **Houses** — of mud, bamboo, bricks, ice or cloth, made to suit the weather.
- **Travel and communication** — bullock carts to trains, letters to mobile phones.
- **Work and things** — pots, clothes, maps and the people who make them.

Each topic connects to others. A clay pot needs soil and water; a train carries grain from farms to cities; a house of bamboo comes from a plant. Draw your own web: put yourself in the middle and draw lines to all the things you need every day.

check.q: A clay pot is connected to which part of nature?
check.why: Potters mix soil with water to shape clay, then bake it in fire.

sections.h: When the Web Breaks — and How to Mend It
sections.md:
People sometimes break threads of the web:

- cutting too many trees, so birds and animals lose their homes;
- throwing plastic and garbage into rivers;
- wasting water and electricity;
- hunting animals until very few are left.

We can mend the web:

1. Plant a tree and water it.
2. Keep a bowl of water for birds in summer.
3. Close the tap while brushing.
4. Carry a cloth bag, not plastic.
5. Put wet waste in a compost pit so it turns into soil.
6. Be kind to animals — never trouble them.

Remember the Bishnoi people of Rajasthan, who are famous for protecting khejri trees and blackbuck deer. Small actions by many people make the web strong.

check.q: Which action mends the web of life?
options: Keeping water for birds in summer
check.why: Birds struggle to find water in hot months, so a water bowl helps them survive.

story.title: The Day the Neem Tree Spoke

parts.md: Aarav lay under the old neem tree after school. "Thank you for the shade," he whispered. To his surprise a soft voice replied, "Thank you for the water you gave me yesterday." It was the tree!

"Look up," said the neem. A mynah fed her chicks in a nest. A squirrel nibbled a berry. Ants climbed the bark. "They all live with me. And my fallen leaves feed the earthworms, who feed the soil, who feeds my roots."

"What can I do?" asked Aarav. "Keep my friends safe," said the neem. Next morning Aarav put out a bowl of water and planted a neem seed in a pot. The mynah came to drink. The web had one more strong thread.

summary: Everything in nature is connected like threads of a web.
Living things grow, breathe, eat and have young; non-living things do not.
Living things need non-living things: sun, air, water and soil.
Green plants make food using sunlight.
Water moves in a cycle: vapour, clouds, rain.
A food chain shows who eats whom and always starts with a plant.
Animals are plant-eaters, flesh-eaters or eat both.
Bees, birds, earthworms and trees help each other.
People depend on nature and on each other's work.
Cutting trees, plastic and waste break the web.
Planting trees, saving water and caring for animals mend it.
practice: Write three living and three non-living things in your classroom.
What four things does a plant need to grow?
Make a food chain with four living things.
What will happen if all the frogs in a field disappear?
Write two ways in which bees and birds help plants.
How does a tree help birds, animals and people?
Draw a web with yourself in the centre and things you need around you.
Write three things you will do to protect the web of life.

rd-school-c3-evs-e.revision.title: Class 3 EVS: The Whole Book in One Read
rd-school-c3-evs-e.revision.subtitle: All 24 chapters of Looking Around — revised in one cosy afternoon

sections.md:
**Poonam's Day Out** — Poonam walks to school and spots many animals: a cow eating grass, a crow on a tree, a lizard on a wall, a frog by the pond, ants in a line, a fish in water. We sorted them: Which can fly? Which live in water? Which crawl? Which have legs — two, four, six, or none?

**The Plant Fairy** — plants are everywhere: tiny grass, climbers like money-plant and bottle gourd, bushes like rose, and tall trees like neem and banyan. Leaves come in many shapes — the long banana leaf, the round lotus leaf, the heart-shaped peepal leaf, the jagged tamarind leaflets. You can make **leaf prints** (colour and press) and **bark rubbings** (paper on bark, rub with a crayon).

Trees are old friends: some live for hundreds of years. We use plants for food, wood, medicine, shade and festivals.

check.q: A bark rubbing is made by…
options: rubbing a crayon on paper held over bark
check.why: Holding paper on the bark and rubbing a crayon copies its rough pattern.

sections.h: Water, Food and Our First School (Ch 3–6)
sections.md:
**Water O' Water** — water comes from rain, rivers, ponds, wells, hand pumps and taps. We need it to drink, cook, bathe and grow crops. Some things **float** (leaf, wood), some **sink** (stone, coin); some **dissolve** (sugar, salt), others do not (sand). Never waste water.

**Our First School** — our family is our first school. We learn to walk, talk and eat from them. Families can be big or small; members may look alike (same eyes, curly hair).

**Chhotu's House** — Chhotu made a house out of an old sheet under a table. Houses keep us safe from sun, rain and cold.

**Foods We Eat** — rice, roti, dal, idli, poha, fish, fruit. Different people eat different foods; small babies drink milk; old people eat soft food. Food comes from plants and animals and must not be wasted.

check.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
check.why: Sugar disappears into water and makes it sweet — it dissolves.

sections.md:
**Saying without Speaking** — we use faces and hands to show feelings: happy, sad, angry, surprised. Some people who cannot hear use **sign language**. Dancers show stories with mudras.

**Flying High** — birds have beaks of different shapes for different food (the parrot cracks nuts, the eagle tears meat, the woodpecker drills wood). They have feathers and hollow bones to fly, and build nests.

**It's Raining** — when it rains, people use umbrellas and raincoats, frogs croak, peacocks dance, and farmers sow seeds. Rain fills ponds and wells.

**What is Cooking** — food can be eaten raw (carrot, cucumber) or cooked by boiling, frying, steaming, roasting and baking. Cooking uses fuels like gas, wood, cow-dung cakes or electricity, and utensils of steel, clay, iron or copper. Everyone in the family can help in the kitchen.

check.q: Which bird has a strong hooked beak for tearing meat?
check.why: An eagle catches other animals, and its hooked beak tears the flesh.

sections.md:
**From Here to There** — we travel by foot, cycle, bus, train, boat, aeroplane; long ago by bullock cart and horse. Older people remember journeys very different from ours.

**Work We Do** — in a family, people do many kinds of work: cooking, cleaning, farming, office work, driving. Some work is paid and some is not, but all work matters. Boys and girls can share all jobs.

**Sharing Our Feelings** — some people have special needs (cannot see, hear or walk). We should help them, include them in games, and never tease anyone.

**The Story of Food** — growing grain: ploughing, sowing, watering, harvesting; then grinding and cooking. Eating together and sharing food is a happy custom.

**Making Pots** — potters shape wet clay on a **potter's wheel**, dry the pots and bake them in a fire. Clay pots (matka) keep water cool. Long ago people stored grain in big clay pots.

check.q: Why does a matka keep water cool?
options: Water seeps out through tiny holes and dries, cooling the pot
It is kept in the sun
check.why: Water slowly oozes through the clay and evaporates from the outside, which cools the water inside.

sections.md:
**Games We Play** — indoor games (carrom, ludo, chess) and outdoor games (kho-kho, kabaddi, gilli-danda, hide-and-seek). Games teach rules, teamwork and fair play.

**Here Comes a Letter** — the postman carries letters, parcels and money orders. A letter needs an address with a **PIN code** and a stamp. Today we also use phones and email.

**A House Like This** — houses differ: houseboats in Kashmir, igloos of ice in very cold lands, tents for people who move, houses on stilts in rainy places, mud houses in villages, tall flats in cities.

**Our Friends — Animals** — dogs, cats, cows and birds live with us. Pets need food, water, shelter, love and cleaning.

**Drop by Drop** — rainwater can be saved in tanks and ponds (water harvesting). Measure how much water your family uses in a day and find ways to save it.

check.q: Which house is made of blocks of ice?
check.why: An igloo is built from blocks of snow and ice in very cold places.

sections.h: Families, Maps, Cloth and the Web (Ch 21–24)
sections.md:
**Families Can Be Different** — some families are big (joint), some small; some children live with grandparents. Every family cares for its members in its own way.

**Left-Right** — we learnt to read a simple **map**: what is left, right, near, far, in front of and behind. Maps use symbols to show schools, roads and rivers. A map drawn from above is like a bird's view.

**A Beautiful Cloth** — sarees, turbans and dhotis are unstitched cloths worn in many ways. Fibres (cotton, wool, silk, jute) are spun into thread, woven on a loom and decorated by dyeing, tie-dye, block printing and embroidery.

**Web of Life** — sun, air, water, soil, plants, animals and people are all connected. Food chains start with plants. Helping and protecting nature keeps the web strong.

check.q: On a map, symbols are used to show…
options: places like schools, roads and rivers
check.why: Small pictures or signs on a map stand for real places so the map stays clear.

parts.md: On the last day of Class 3, Meera's teacher gave everyone a shoebox. "Fill it with one thing from each chapter," she said. Meera put in a pressed peepal leaf, a feather, a tiny clay pot and a postcard with a PIN code.
She added a scrap of bandhani cloth, a drawing of a food chain and a map of her street. Her brother added a gilli. Her grandmother added a photo of their joint family.
When she closed the box, Meera smiled. "It's the whole year — and it's all connected!" She wrote on the lid: *My Web of Life.*

summary: Animals and plants around us differ in shape, home, food and movement.
Leaves come in many shapes; trees give food, shade, wood and homes.
Water comes from many sources; some things float, sink or dissolve.
Families are our first school and can be big or small.
Food is eaten raw or cooked by boiling, frying, steaming and roasting.
Birds' beaks suit their food; feathers help them fly.
We travel and communicate in many ways — from letters to phones.
Everyone's work matters; boys and girls can share all jobs.
Potters shape clay on a wheel; matkas keep water cool.
Houses suit the weather: igloo, houseboat, tent, stilt house.
Maps use left, right, near, far and symbols.
Cloth is spun, woven and decorated in many beautiful ways.
Everything in nature is connected in a web of life.
practice: Name four animals and the places they live.
Draw three leaf shapes and name the trees.
List three things that float and three that sink.
Write four ways of cooking food with one example each.
Why do birds have different beaks?
Write your full address with PIN code.
Name three kinds of houses and the places where they are found.
How does a potter make a pot?
Draw a simple map from your house to your school.
Write one food chain and one way to protect nature.

rd-school-c3-english-a.unit1.title: Good Morning & The Magic Garden
rd-school-c3-english-a.unit1.subtitle: A sunny poem about saying hello to the world, and a garden that comes alive

sections.h: Wake up! The sun is saying hello
sections.md:
Have you ever woken up early and looked out of the window? The sky is pink and gold. A bird is singing. The air is cool. Everything feels *new*.

Unit 1 of your Class 3 English book begins with exactly this feeling. It has two parts:

1. **Good Morning** – a short, happy poem in which the speaker greets the things of the morning one by one.
2. **The Magic Garden** – a story about a garden full of flowers that a group of children love and look after, and what happens when the flowers seem to talk.

Both pieces are about the same big idea: **the world around us is alive and friendly, and we should greet it and care for it.**

In this read you will:
- understand what happens in the poem and the story,
- learn new words,
- practise speaking and writing about mornings and gardens,
- get ready for the questions your teacher may ask.

> Did you know? In many Indian homes, the first thing people say in the morning is a greeting – *Namaste*, *Suprabhat*, *Ram Ram*, *Sat Sri Akal*, *Salaam*, or simply *Good morning!* Greeting someone is a way of saying, "I see you, and I am happy you are here."

In the poem, the speaker wakes up and says *good morning* to everything they see. Think of it like this – imagine you open the door and say:

- Good morning to the **sky**, which is bright and wide.
- Good morning to the **sun**, which has come up to give light.
- Good morning to the **birds**, which are singing on the trees.
- Good morning to the **flowers**, the **bees** and every small creature that has woken up too.

The poem has a gentle, bouncy rhythm. Lines often begin the same way, with the words *Good morning*. When a poet repeats words like this, it is called **repetition**. Repetition makes a poem easy to remember and fun to say aloud.

The poem also uses **rhyming words** – words that end with the same sound, such as *sky – high*, *bee – tree*, *day – play*. Find the rhyming pairs in your book and say them aloud.

**What is the poem really saying?** That a morning is a gift. The speaker is thankful. Instead of grumbling about getting up, the speaker smiles at the world. When we are thankful, our whole day feels better.

The full poem is in your free NCERT book (link at the end) — read it aloud with actions: arms wide for the sky, a circle for the sun, flapping hands for the birds.

keyTerms: repetition – saying the same words again and again in a poem
rhyme – words ending in the same sound, like sky and high
greet – to say hello

check.q: Why does the poet keep starting lines with 'Good morning'?
options: Because the poet forgot other words
To make the poem musical and easy to remember
check.why: Repeating the same words is called repetition, and it gives a poem a happy beat that is easy to remember.

sections.md:
Now for the story. Here is a retelling in our own words.

There was a school with a lovely garden. The children of the school had planted it themselves. Every morning, before class, they watered the plants and pulled out the weeds. There were sunflowers, roses, marigolds, lilies and many more.

The flowers in the garden were happy because the children cared for them. In the story, the flowers seem to be alive like people – they feel glad, they nod in the wind, and they grow tall and bright when they are loved.

One day, the children had a holiday and nobody came to the garden for a while. The flowers felt lonely and began to droop. When the children came back and took care of them again, the garden bloomed once more. It felt like **magic** – but the real magic was the children's love and hard work.

**Why is it called 'magic'?** Nothing in the garden was really a spell. The 'magic' is that a few seeds, some water, sunlight and kindness can turn bare soil into a garden full of colour.

> Talking flowers? When a story gives feelings to plants or animals, it is called **personification**. You don't need to remember the long word yet – just notice that the flowers act a bit like children!

check.q: What was the real 'magic' in the garden?
check.why: The garden bloomed because the children watered and looked after it, so their care was the true magic.

sections.md:
The story names many flowers. Let us get to know them.

| Flower | Colour | A fun fact |
|---|---|---|
| Sunflower | yellow | turns its face towards the sun when young |
| Rose | red, pink, white | has thorns on its stem |
| Marigold | orange, yellow | used in garlands at Diwali and weddings |
| Lily | white | often grows near water |
| Lotus | pink | India's national flower |

**Word play:** Many flower names are joined words. *Sun + flower = sunflower*. *Mari + gold = marigold*. Can you think of other joined words? *Butter + fly*, *rain + bow*, *sun + shine*.

**Speaking activity:** Stand up and say, "My favourite flower is the ___ because it is ___." For example: "My favourite flower is the marigold because it is bright orange and smells nice."

check.q: Which flower is the national flower of India?
check.why: The lotus is India's national flower; it grows in ponds and is pink or white.

sections.md:
**Themes of the unit**
- **Thankfulness** – the poem teaches us to welcome each day with joy.
- **Caring for nature** – the story shows that plants need regular love and work.
- **Living things have needs** – water, sunlight, air and care.

**Model answers**

*Q: What does the speaker do in the poem 'Good Morning'?*
A: The speaker greets the sky, the sun, the birds and the flowers. The speaker is happy and thankful for a new day.

*Q: Who looked after the magic garden?*
A: The children of the school looked after the garden. They watered the plants and removed the weeds every day.

*Q: Why did the garden look sad for a while?*
A: Nobody came to care for it, so the thirsty plants drooped. When the children returned, the flowers bloomed again.

*Q: What lesson do you learn from the story?*
A: If we care for plants every day, they grow strong and beautiful. Kindness and hard work are the real magic.

check.q: Which theme do both the poem and the story share?
check.why: Both pieces show joy in nature — one by greeting it, the other by caring for it.

sections.md:
**New words from this unit**
- *bloom* – when a flower opens fully
- *droop* – to hang down, tired, like a thirsty plant
- *weed* – an unwanted plant growing in a garden
- *bright* – full of light or colour
- *dew* – tiny drops of water on grass in the morning

**Naming words (nouns):** sun, sky, bird, garden, rose, children. These are names of things, places, animals or people.

**Describing words (adjectives):** bright sun, blue sky, tall sunflower, little bird. These tell us *more* about a naming word.

**Greetings for the day**
- Good morning – till about 12 noon
- Good afternoon – from noon till about 4 pm
- Good evening – after that
- Good night – only when going to bed

**Writing task:** Write four lines about your morning. Example: *I wake up at six. I brush my teeth. I say good morning to my mother. I drink a glass of milk.*

check.q: Which greeting do we use when going to sleep?
check.why: We say 'Good night' only when someone is going to bed; for meeting people in the evening we say 'Good evening'.

sections.h: Do it yourself: grow a little garden
sections.md:
You can make your own magic garden, even on a window sill!

1. Take an old cup or a small pot with a hole at the bottom.
2. Fill it with soil.
3. Push in two or three seeds – *methi*, *mustard* or *moong* grow fast.
4. Water a little every day. Keep it in sunlight.
5. Watch: in 3–5 days tiny green shoots will peep out!

Keep a **plant diary**. Each day draw your plant and write one line: *Day 1: I planted the seeds. Day 4: I saw a green shoot!*

> Did you know? Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air. That is why a plant kept in a dark cupboard turns pale and weak.

summary: Unit 1 has a poem, 'Good Morning', and a story, 'The Magic Garden'.
In the poem the speaker greets the sky, sun, birds and flowers.
The poem uses repetition and rhyming words like sky–high.
The poem's message: be thankful for each new morning.
In the story, children plant and care for their school garden.
The flowers bloom when loved and droop when left alone.
The 'magic' is care, water and sunlight – not a spell.
Nouns name things; adjectives describe them.
Use the right greeting for the time of day.
You can grow a small garden in a cup.

glossary.d: to open into a flower
to bend or hang down
an unwanted plant
water drops on grass in the morning

practice: Name four things the speaker says good morning to.
Write three pairs of rhyming words.
Why did the flowers droop in the story?
What did the children do every morning in the garden?
Write the names of five flowers.
Write four sentences about your morning.
Fill in: We say good ___ before going to bed.
Draw your favourite flower and write two describing words for it.

rd-school-c3-english-a.unit2.title: Bird Talk & Nina and the Baby Sparrows
rd-school-c3-english-a.unit2.subtitle: What do birds say about us? And how one girl learned to be a quiet friend to a sparrow family

sections.md:
Imagine two little birds sitting on a branch outside your classroom window. They look at you and your friends. What would they say?

*"Look at them! They have no feathers!"*
*"And they can't even fly!"*

That is the fun idea behind the poem **Bird Talk**. The second part of the unit is a story, **Nina and the Baby Sparrows**, about a girl who discovers a sparrow's nest inside her house and learns how to care for wild birds without disturbing them.

The big idea of this unit: **animals and birds have their own lives, homes and feelings. We should watch them, enjoy them and protect them.**

In the poem, two birds are chatting. They think *they* are the normal ones, and that humans are rather strange. They wonder why people:

- walk on the ground instead of flying,
- live in big boxes called houses instead of cosy nests,
- have no feathers or wings.

The birds giggle at us, just as we sometimes laugh at the way birds hop and peck. The poem flips things around and makes us see ourselves through a bird's eyes. That is what makes it funny – and clever.

**What can we learn?** Everyone thinks their own way is the normal way. A bird thinks flying is normal; we think walking is normal. Both are right for their own lives. So we should not laugh at others for being different.

**Poem tricks to spot**
- The birds *speak* in the poem – so the poem is like a little conversation.
- Look for rhyming words at the ends of lines.
- Read it aloud with two friends, each taking the voice of one bird!

Read the full poem in your free NCERT book (link at the end).

check.q: What is funny about the poem 'Bird Talk'?
options: The birds are scared of cats
The birds think humans are strange
The birds are learning to fly
check.why: The poem is funny because it shows humans from a bird's point of view, and to birds we look odd without wings or feathers.

sections.h: The story: Nina and the Baby Sparrows
sections.md:
Here is the story, retold in our own words.

Nina lives with her family, including her grandmother. One day she notices two sparrows flying in and out of the house again and again, carrying bits of straw, thread and dry grass. Where are they going? Nina follows them with her eyes and finds that they are building a **nest** in a small space high up inside the room – behind a picture frame on the wall.

Soon there are tiny **eggs**, and then, one morning, Nina hears soft *cheep-cheep* sounds. Baby sparrows have hatched!

Nina is very excited. She wants to climb up and touch them. But her grandmother gently explains: if we touch the nest or the babies, the parent birds may get frightened and leave. The best way to be a friend to birds is to **watch quietly from a distance**.

So Nina does just that. She keeps the fan off when the birds are flying, does not make loud noises near the nest, and watches the mother and father sparrows bring food – tiny insects and grains – to the hungry chicks with wide-open beaks. In time, the babies grow feathers, flap their wings and finally fly out of the window into the big world.

Nina feels a little sad to see them go, but mostly proud. She helped them simply by being gentle and patient.

check.q: Why did Grandmother tell Nina not to touch the baby sparrows?
options: The parent birds might get frightened and leave
check.why: Parent birds can abandon a nest that is disturbed, so watching quietly is the kind and safe thing to do.

sections.md:
| Character | What they are like | How we know |
|---|---|---|
| **Nina** | curious, caring, learns patience | she watches the birds every day and stops herself from touching the nest |
| **Grandmother** | wise and gentle | she explains calmly why the nest must not be disturbed |
| **Parent sparrows** | busy and hard-working | they fly in and out all day with straw, then with food |
| **Baby sparrows** | tiny and hungry | they cheep loudly with wide-open beaks |

**Nina's feelings change through the story:**
1. *Curious* – who is flying in and out?
2. *Excited* – there are eggs and then babies!
3. *Impatient* – she wants to touch them.
4. *Patient* – she learns to watch from afar.
5. *Sad but proud* – the babies fly away, healthy and free.

A good story often shows a character **learning something**. Nina learns that loving something sometimes means leaving it alone.

check.q: How did Nina's feeling change by the end of the story?
check.why: Nina missed the sparrows when they flew away but was proud that she had helped them by being gentle.

sections.md:
Sparrows, like all birds, grow in stages:

1. **Nest** – the parents build it with straw, grass, feathers and thread.
2. **Eggs** – the mother lays small, speckled eggs and sits on them to keep them warm.
3. **Hatching** – after about two weeks, the chicks break out of their shells.
4. **Chicks** – they are tiny, with closed eyes and almost no feathers. They cheep for food.
5. **Fledglings** – they grow feathers and practise flapping.
6. **Flying away** – in about two more weeks they leave the nest.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.st{opacity:0;animation:show 8s infinite}@keyframes show{0%{opacity:0}10%,90%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:0}}</style><rect width='600' height='220' fill='#fffaf0'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><g class='st'><path d='M40 130 q50 40 100 0' fill='#b08850'/><text x='90' y='190'>Nest</text></g><g class='st' style='animation-delay:1s'><ellipse cx='210' cy='120' rx='18' ry='24' fill='#f1e6d0' stroke='#999'/><text x='210' y='190'>Eggs</text></g><g class='st' style='animation-delay:2s'><circle cx='320' cy='125' r='20' fill='#f8c9a0'/><path d='M335 120 l12 5 l-12 5z' fill='#f4a300'/><text x='320' y='190'>Chick</text></g><g class='st' style='animation-delay:3s'><ellipse cx='430' cy='125' rx='26' ry='18' fill='#a1887f'/><text x='430' y='190'>Fledgling</text></g><g class='st' style='animation-delay:4s'><path d='M520 120 q20 -30 40 0 q-20 -10 -40 0' fill='#6d4c41'/><text x='540' y='190'>Flies away!</text></g></g></svg>

fig.alt: Stages: nest, eggs, chick, fledgling, flying bird appear in turn.

keyTerms: nest – a bird's home
hatch – to come out of an egg
chick – a baby bird
fledgling – a young bird that is learning to fly

check.q: What does 'hatch' mean?
options: To come out of an egg
check.why: A chick hatches when it breaks its eggshell and comes out.

sections.md:
Sparrows were once seen in almost every Indian home and street. Today there are far fewer in big cities, because modern buildings have no little holes for nests and there are fewer bushes and insects.

You can help:
- Keep a shallow bowl of **water** on your balcony, especially in summer.
- Scatter a few **grains** like bajra or rice.
- Ask an adult to fix a small wooden **nest box**.
- Plant bushes and flowering plants.

> Did you know? **World Sparrow Day** is celebrated on 20 March every year. Delhi chose the house sparrow as its state bird to remind people to protect it.

**Grammar corner – action words (verbs):** fly, peck, chirp, hop, build, sing. Make sentences: *The sparrow pecks at the grain. The baby birds chirp loudly.*

**Singular and plural:** one bird → two bird**s**; one nest → many nest**s**; one egg → three egg**s**.

check.q: Which of these is an action word?
check.why: 'Chirp' tells us what a bird does, so it is an action word, or verb.

sections.md:
**Model answers**

*Q: What do the birds in 'Bird Talk' think about people?*
A: They think people are strange because people have no wings or feathers, cannot fly and live in houses instead of nests.

*Q: How did Nina find the nest?*
A: She saw two sparrows flying in and out with straw and grass, and followed them with her eyes to a space behind a picture frame.

*Q: What did Nina learn from her grandmother?*
A: She learned that we should never touch a bird's nest or babies, but watch quietly so the parents do not leave.

**Bird-watching activity:** Sit quietly near a window for ten minutes. Make a table: *Bird – Colour – What it was doing*. You may spot a crow, a myna, a pigeon, a sparrow or a parrot.

**Sounds birds make:** crows *caw*, sparrows *chirp*, pigeons *coo*, parrots *screech*, cuckoos *coo-ooh*.

check.q: Which sound does a crow make?
check.why: Crows make a harsh 'caw' sound, while pigeons coo and sparrows chirp.

summary: Unit 2 has the poem 'Bird Talk' and the story 'Nina and the Baby Sparrows'.
In the poem, two birds think humans are strange because we have no wings or feathers.
The poem shows the world from a bird's point of view.
Nina finds sparrows building a nest behind a picture frame.
The eggs hatch into hungry chicks.
Grandmother teaches Nina to watch quietly and not touch the nest.
Nina's feelings move from curious and impatient to patient and proud.
The parents feed the chicks until they can fly away.
Birds grow: egg → chick → fledgling → flying bird.
We can help sparrows with water, grains and nest boxes.
Verbs are action words; add -s to make many things.

glossary.d: home a bird builds
come out of an egg
young bird learning to fly
short sound made by a small bird

practice: What do the birds in the poem find strange about humans?
Where did the sparrows build their nest in Nina's house?
What did the sparrows use to build the nest?
Why should we not touch a bird's nest?
Describe Nina in two words and give a reason.
Write the stages of a bird's growth in order.
Write two ways you can help sparrows.
Write the plural of: egg, bird, chick, nest.
Match the bird with its sound: crow, pigeon, sparrow.
Imagine you are a sparrow. Write three lines about the girl who watched you.

rd-school-c3-english-a.unit3.title: Little by Little & The Enormous Turnip
rd-school-c3-english-a.unit3.subtitle: How a tiny acorn becomes a mighty oak – and how a tiny mouse helps pull up a giant turnip

sections.md:
Here is a riddle: *I am smaller than your thumb, but one day I can be taller than your house. What am I?*

Answer: **an acorn** – the seed of an oak tree!

Unit 3 is all about **small things becoming big** and **small helpers making a big difference**. The poem **Little by Little** follows an acorn as it slowly grows into a huge oak tree. The story **The Enormous Turnip** is a funny folk tale in which a whole chain of helpers – right down to a little mouse – work together to pull a gigantic turnip out of the ground.

Two lessons to keep in your pocket:
1. **Be patient** – growth happens slowly, a little every day.
2. **Work together** – even the smallest helper counts.

The poem tells the life of an oak tree, step by step.

- An **acorn** falls to the ground and lies hidden in the soil.
- It is dark and quiet down there, but the acorn is busy. It sends a tiny **root** downwards to drink water.
- It pushes a small **shoot** upwards towards the light.
- Day after day, year after year, *little by little*, the shoot becomes a sapling, then a young tree, then a giant **oak** with strong branches where birds can nest.

The words **little by little** keep coming back in the poem. This repetition reminds us that the tree did not grow in one day. It grew a tiny bit at a time.

**The message:** You learn the same way. You did not learn to read in one day. Every page you read, every sum you practise, is a little bit of growth. Keep going – one day you will be as strong as the oak!

Read the full poem in your free NCERT book (link at the end).

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='200' fill='#e3f4ff'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='120' fill='#8b5a2b'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='225' rx='12' ry='9' fill='#a0522d'/><path d='M300 232 v60' stroke='#f5deb3' stroke-width='3'><animate attributeName='d' values='M300 232 v0;M300 232 v70' dur='6s' fill='freeze' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><rect x='294' y='200' width='12' height='0' fill='#6d4c41'><animate attributeName='height' values='0;120' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='y' values='200;80' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><circle cx='300' cy='80' r='0' fill='#2e7d32'><animate attributeName='r' values='0;0;80' keyTimes='0;0.4;1' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><text x='300' y='310' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#fff'>acorn → root → shoot → oak</text></svg>
fig.caption: Little by little: the acorn sends a root down and a shoot up, and grows into an oak.
fig.alt: Animated acorn growing a root and trunk and a leafy crown.

keyTerms: acorn – seed of the oak tree
root – part of a plant that grows down into the soil
shoot – the first young stem that grows up
oak – a big, strong tree

check.q: What grows DOWN into the soil first from the acorn?
check.why: The root grows down first so the young plant can drink water and hold on to the soil.

sections.md:
You can see 'little by little' with your own eyes.

1. Soak a few **rajma** or **chana** seeds in water overnight.
2. Wrap them in a wet cotton cloth or put them on wet cotton in a bowl.
3. Check every morning. Keep the cotton damp.

**What you will see:** Day 2 – the seed swells and its skin cracks. Day 3 – a tiny white **root** pokes out and bends *down*. Day 4–5 – a little green **shoot** curls *up*. This is exactly what the acorn does in the poem, only faster!

Draw your seed each day in a chart. Ask: Which came first, the root or the shoot? (The root.)

> Did you know? A seed carries its own packed lunch inside – stored food that feeds the baby plant until its leaves can make food from sunlight.

check.q: In which direction does the first root grow?
check.why: Roots grow downwards to reach water and anchor the young plant.

sections.md:
Here is the tale, retold.

An old man planted turnip seeds in his garden. He watered them and waited. One turnip grew and grew until it was **enormous** – bigger than any turnip ever seen!

The old man held its leaves and pulled. *Pull! Pull!* It would not come out.

So he called the **old woman**. She held the old man, the old man held the turnip, and they pulled. Still it would not move.

The old woman called their **granddaughter**. Then the granddaughter called the **dog**. The dog called the **cat**. Each one held on to the one in front, and they all pulled together. Still the turnip stayed stuck!

At last, the cat called a tiny **mouse**. The mouse held the cat, the cat held the dog, the dog held the girl, the girl held the old woman, the old woman held the old man, and the old man held the turnip.

One, two, three – **PULL!** Out popped the enormous turnip, and everyone tumbled over in a happy heap. That evening they all shared a big pot of turnip soup.

**The joke and the lesson:** The mouse was the smallest of all, but its little bit of pulling was just enough. Every helper matters.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff8e1'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='60' fill='#8d6e63'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;12 0;0 0' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><circle cx='560' cy='190' r='8' fill='#9e9e9e'/><circle cx='520' cy='178' r='14' fill='#ff9800'/><circle cx='470' cy='170' r='20' fill='#795548'/><circle cx='405' cy='140' r='18' fill='#f48fb1'/><circle cx='345' cy='120' r='20' fill='#ce93d8'/><circle cx='285' cy='110' r='22' fill='#90caf9'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 -10;0 0' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><ellipse cx='150' cy='195' rx='70' ry='55' fill='#f3e5f5' stroke='#8e24aa' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M150 140 l-20 -60 M150 140 l0 -70 M150 140 l25 -60' stroke='#43a047' stroke-width='8'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'><text x='285' y='150'>man</text><text x='345' y='158'>woman</text><text x='405' y='175'>girl</text><text x='470' y='205'>dog</text><text x='520' y='210'>cat</text><text x='560' y='215'>mouse</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: The chain of pullers – and the smallest one makes the difference!
fig.alt: A line of characters pulling a giant turnip.

check.q: Who was the LAST helper to join the pulling?
check.why: The mouse joined last, and with its tiny help the turnip finally came out.

sections.md:
Stories like this are called **chain stories** or **cumulative tales** – each new helper is added to the list, and the whole list is repeated. That makes them great for reading aloud.

| Step | Who joins | Holds on to |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | old man | the turnip |
| 2 | old woman | the old man |
| 3 | granddaughter | the old woman |
| 4 | dog | the granddaughter |
| 5 | cat | the dog |
| 6 | mouse | the cat |

**Act it out!** Six friends can stand in a line, each holding the waist of the one in front. Shout *Pull!* together. The 'turnip' can be a cushion held by a seventh friend who 'pops out' at the end.

**India link:** Indian folk tales also love chain stories – think of the sparrow and the crow, or the story of the little ant who asks one creature after another for help.

check.q: Who did the old woman hold on to?
check.why: Each helper held the one in front, and the old woman stood right behind the old man.

sections.md:
**Characters:** the hard-working **old man** who grew the turnip; the helpful **old woman**; the eager **granddaughter**; the **dog** and **cat**, who join in even though they are animals; and the tiny **mouse**, the hero of the ending.

**Themes:** patience (both pieces), teamwork, and *never think you are too small to help*.

**Model answers**

*Q: How does an acorn become an oak?*
A: The acorn lies in the soil. It sends a root down and a shoot up. Slowly, little by little, the shoot grows into a sapling and then a tall oak tree.

*Q: Why could the old man not pull out the turnip?*
A: The turnip had grown enormous, and he was not strong enough to pull it alone.

*Q: What does the mouse teach us?*
A: Even the smallest helper can make a big difference when everyone works together.

check.q: Which idea is found in BOTH the poem and the story?
options: Big results can come from small efforts
check.why: The acorn grows by small daily steps and the mouse adds a small pull — both show small efforts adding up to something big.

sections.md:
**Opposites**
- big – small
- enormous – tiny
- old – young
- pull – push
- up – down

**Size words in order:** tiny → small → big → huge → enormous.

**Vegetables that grow under the ground:** turnip, carrot, radish (*mooli*), potato, beetroot, onion. Vegetables that grow above the ground: tomato, brinjal, peas, cauliflower.

**Writing task:** Finish the sentence in three ways.
*Little by little, I learned to ___.*
For example: *ride a cycle*, *swim*, *tie my shoelaces*.

> Did you know? Some oak trees live for more than 500 years!

check.q: What is the opposite of 'enormous'?
check.why: 'Enormous' means very big, so its opposite is 'tiny', which means very small.

summary: Unit 3: poem 'Little by Little' and story 'The Enormous Turnip'.

With the mouse's help, the turnip came out.
Message: teamwork – every helper counts, even the smallest.
Opposites: big–small, pull–push, old–young.

oak seed

rd-school-c3-english-a.unit4.title: Sea Song & A Little Fish Story
rd-school-c3-english-a.unit4.subtitle: Hear the sea inside a shell, and meet a little fish who learns that small can be special

sections.md:
Pick up a big seashell. Hold it close to your ear. Shhh… *Whoooosh.* It sounds like waves rolling on a beach, even if you are sitting in your room in Delhi, far from any sea!

Unit 4 dives into the ocean. The poem **Sea Song** is about a child who holds a shell to the ear and hears the song of the sea. The story **A Little Fish Story** is about a small fish who wishes it were big – until it discovers that being little has a surprising advantage.

Big ideas:
- The sea is wide, deep and full of life and sound.
- **Be happy with who you are.** Every size and shape has its own strengths.

In the poem, the speaker finds a shell and puts it to their ear. Inside, they seem to hear the whole sea: the waves rising and falling, the wind, the splash on the sand. The child wonders how such a big sea can fit inside such a small shell!

The poem uses **sound words** to help us hear the sea – words like *whoosh*, *splash* and *roar*. Words that sound like the noise they describe are fun to say. Try them: *buzz* (bee), *tick-tock* (clock), *drip-drop* (rain).

**What is really happening?** The shell does not hold real waves. Its curved inside catches the small sounds around you – air moving, people talking far away, even the sound of blood in your own ear – and bounces them about so they sound like a soft rushing sea. Science and poetry together!

**The feeling of the poem:** wonder. The child is amazed, dreamy and happy. When you read it, read slowly and softly, like waves.

keyTerms: shell – the hard outer covering of a sea creature
wave – water rising and falling in the sea
shore – land at the edge of the sea

check.q: Why does a shell sound like the sea?
options: Its curved shape bounces small sounds around
check.why: The curved inside of the shell catches and echoes the quiet sounds around us, which makes a soft rushing noise like waves.

sections.h: Reading the poem part by part
sections.md:
Read the poem in your NCERT book (free link at the end) and notice how it moves, part by part:

1. **Finding the shell** – the child picks up a shell, maybe on a beach or from a shelf at home. There is curiosity: *what is inside?*
2. **Listening** – the shell is held to the ear. The world goes quiet, and a soft roar begins.
3. **Imagining** – in the sound, the child pictures the whole sea: waves, wind, foam on the sand, perhaps boats and gulls.
4. **Wondering** – the child is amazed that something so tiny can 'hold' something so huge.

**Try this:** Close your eyes and listen to a shell, a cupped hand, or an empty steel tumbler held over your ear. Each makes a slightly different 'sea'. A bigger cup gives a deeper sound!

Poems like this teach us to **use our senses** – to really *listen* – and to let our imagination travel far.

check.q: What feeling fills the poem 'Sea Song'?
check.why: The child is amazed and dreamy that the big sea seems to sing inside a small shell — that feeling is wonder.

sections.h: The story: A Little Fish Story
sections.md:
Retold in our own words:

Deep in the sea lived a **little fish**. Every day it watched the big fish swim past – long, strong and grand. *"I wish I were big too,"* the little fish sighed. *"Nobody notices me. I am too small to matter."*

One day, a fishing boat came. The fishermen threw a huge **net** into the water. It swept through the sea and caught lots of fish.

The big fish were trapped – they were too large to slip through the holes of the net. But the little fish? It wriggled through a small gap and swam away free!

The little fish stopped and looked back in surprise. *"Being small saved me!"* From that day on, it never again wished to be anything other than itself. It swam happily among the corals, proud to be little.

**The message:** Don't compare yourself with others. What looks like a weakness can be a strength. A small fish can slip through a net; a small child can fit into a cosy corner during hide-and-seek!

*Tip:* read the story in the official NCERT book too, and compare it with this retelling – which details did you notice there?

check.q: How did being small help the little fish?
options: It could jump out of the boat
It slipped through the holes in the net
It hid behind a big fish
It swam faster than the boat
check.why: The net's holes were too small for big fish but big enough for the little fish to wriggle through and escape.

sections.md:
**The little fish** – at first unhappy and jealous of bigger fish; by the end, proud and content.
**The big fish** – grand and strong, but their size becomes a problem in the net.
**The fishermen** – they are simply doing their work; they are not 'bad', but their net sets up the big surprise.

**Themes:** be happy with yourself; every size has strengths; don't judge by looks.

**Model answers**

*Q: What does the child in 'Sea Song' do with the shell?*
A: The child holds the shell to the ear and seems to hear the waves and wind of the sea inside it.

*Q: Why was the little fish unhappy at first?*
A: It wanted to be big like the other fish and felt that nobody noticed it.

*Q: Why was the little fish happy at the end?*
A: Its small size let it slip through the fishing net and escape, so it learned that being small was a gift.

check.q: At the start of the story, the little fish feels…
check.why: It wishes it were big like the other fish and feels unnoticed, which shows jealousy and sadness.

sections.md:
The sea is home to amazing creatures.

| Creature | Special thing |
|---|---|
| fish | breathes through gills |
| crab | walks sideways |
| starfish | has five arms |
| octopus | has eight arms |
| whale | the biggest animal on Earth; breathes air |
| turtle | lays eggs on beaches |

**India link:** India has a long coastline – from Gujarat to West Bengal, with the Arabian Sea on the west, the Bay of Bengal on the east and the Indian Ocean to the south. Every year, Olive Ridley turtles come in thousands to Odisha's beaches to lay their eggs.

**Keep the sea clean:** plastic bags in the sea look like jellyfish to turtles, and they may swallow them. When you visit a beach, carry your wrappers and bottles back home.

> Did you know? Fish don't have eyelids – they sleep with their eyes open!

check.q: How many arms does an octopus have?
check.why: 'Octo' means eight, and an octopus has eight arms.

sections.md:
**Sound words:** whoosh (waves), splash (jumping in water), roar (big waves), swish (fish tail), drip (tap).

**Size words:** little, small, tiny, big, large, huge.

**Comparing:** small → small**er** → small**est**; big → big**ger** → big**gest**. *The shark is bigger than the fish. The whale is the biggest of all.*

**Speaking:** Tell your class about a time you visited a beach, river or lake. What did you see, hear and feel?

**Writing:** Complete: *I am happy to be me because ___.*

**Craft:** Draw a fish on paper, colour it and stick little circles of shiny paper as scales.

check.q: Fill in: The whale is the ___ animal of all.
check.why: When we compare one thing with all others, we use the '-est' form, so the whale is the biggest.

rd-school-c3-english-b.unit5.title: The Balloon Man & The Yellow Butterfly
rd-school-c3-english-b.unit5.subtitle: A rainbow of balloons at the market, and a butterfly that is happiest when it is free

sections.md:
Have you ever seen a balloon seller at a *mela*? He holds a bunch of balloons so big that it looks as if he might float up into the sky! Red, blue, green, yellow – they bob and bump and shine in the sun.

Unit 5 is full of colour and lightness. The poem **The Balloon Man** describes a balloon seller who comes to the market with his bright, bobbing balloons. The story **The Yellow Butterfly** tells of a child who chases a lovely yellow butterfly and learns something about freedom.

Big ideas:
- The world is full of beautiful colours to notice.
- Beautiful living things should be enjoyed **freely**, not trapped.

In the poem, the balloon man stands in the market place with his balloons tied on long strings. The speaker describes them:

- some are big, some are small,
- they are all colours – red, yellow, blue, green, purple,
- they tug at their strings as if they want to fly away,
- children gather round, wishing for one.

The poet makes the balloons sound almost alive – they *dance*, *bob* and *pull*. And the balloon man himself seems a cheerful, magical figure who brings joy wherever he goes.

**Words to enjoy:** *bobbing, floating, tugging, bright, string.*

**Think:** Why do balloons float? Many are filled with a gas that is lighter than air (called helium). Balloons we blow up with our breath don't float – they fall down slowly. Try it!

fig.alt: Six coloured balloons gently bobbing on strings.

keyTerms: bob – to move gently up and down
tug – to pull
string – a thin thread

check.q: Which word best describes how the balloons move?
check.why: Balloons move gently up and down in the air, which we describe as bobbing and floating.

sections.md:
The poem is by the English poet **Rose Fyleman**. Read it in your free NCERT book (link at the end) and follow its meaning stanza by stanza:

**Stanza 1 – He comes on market days.** The balloon man arrives whenever there is a market, holding a lovely big bunch of balloons. He stays in the market square the whole day, so busy and happy that he does not even seem to think about his lunch.

**Stanza 2 – The colours.** His balloons are red, purple, blue and green. On a sunny day they shine so brightly that even when carts and crowds of people come in the way, you can still spot them from far off.

**Stanza 3 – Big and small, tugging.** Some balloons are big and some are small, all tied together with string. When the wind blows, they pull and pull at the string as if they are eager to escape.

**Stanza 4 – A dream.** The speaker imagines that one day the balloons might pull so hard that they float right up into the sky – and maybe carry the balloon man away with them!

**What makes it fun:** rhyme at the ends of lines, a steady bouncy rhythm like footsteps at a fair, and a funny, magical ending that makes us smile.

check.q: Why can you see the balloons even when carts come in the way?
options: They shine brightly high above the crowd
check.why: The balloons float high on their strings and shine in the sun, so they can be seen above carts and people.

sections.md:
Retold in our own words:

One sunny morning, a little boy was playing in the garden when he saw a **yellow butterfly**. Its wings were as bright as a marigold, and it fluttered from flower to flower, drinking sweet nectar.

*"I want to catch it!"* he thought. He crept up quietly. The butterfly sat on a rose. He reached out… *flutter!* It flew away to a hibiscus. He ran after it. It flew to a sunflower, then over the hedge, then high above his head.

The boy chased it all over the garden, getting hot and tired. Finally he sat down on the grass to rest. And then – the butterfly floated down and landed softly on his knee!

He held his breath and did not move. He watched its delicate wings open and close like a tiny fan. After a moment it flew off again.

The boy smiled. He realised he did not need to *catch* the butterfly to enjoy it. If he had caught it, its wings might have been hurt. It was most beautiful when it was free.

**Message:** Love nature gently. Look, don't grab.

*Tip:* read the official chapter in the NCERT book too and spot any extra details.

check.q: When did the butterfly come and sit on the boy?
options: When he sat quietly and rested
check.why: The butterfly landed on him only when he stopped chasing and sat still, showing that gentleness works better than grabbing.

sections.md:
**The balloon man** – cheerful, hard-working, a bringer of joy.
**The boy** – eager and excited at first, tired after chasing, and finally calm and wise.
**The yellow butterfly** – light, quick and free; it cannot be caught by force.

**Themes:** colour and joy in everyday life; patience; respecting living things.

**Model answers**

*Q: When does the balloon man come?*
A: He comes on market days and stays in the market square all day with his bunch of balloons.

*Q: What do the balloons do when the wind blows?*
A: They tug and pull at their strings as if they want to fly away.

*Q: Why could the boy not catch the butterfly?*
A: Each time he came close, the butterfly flew to another flower. It was too quick for him.

*Q: What is the lesson of 'The Yellow Butterfly'?*
A: We should enjoy beautiful creatures without catching or hurting them, because they are happiest when free.

check.q: How does the boy change in the story?
options: From eager to chase, to calm and gentle
check.why: He begins by chasing the butterfly, but ends by sitting quietly and enjoying it without catching it.

sections.md:
A butterfly's life has four stages – this change is called **metamorphosis**.

1. **Egg** – laid on a leaf.
2. **Caterpillar** – hatches and eats leaves all day, growing fast.
3. **Pupa** (chrysalis) – the caterpillar wraps itself in a hard case and changes inside.
4. **Butterfly** – comes out with wings, dries them in the sun and flies away.

check.q: What does a caterpillar become inside the pupa?
check.why: Inside the pupa the caterpillar's body changes completely, and a butterfly comes out.

**Colour words:** red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet – the seven colours of the **rainbow** (remember **VIBGYOR** backwards: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).

**Things that are yellow:** banana, mango, sunflower, lemon, the sun in a drawing, haldi.

**Describing words:** *bright* balloon, *yellow* butterfly, *soft* wings, *tired* boy, *sweet* nectar.

rd-school-c3-english-b.unit6.title: Trains & The Story of the Road
rd-school-c3-english-b.unit6.subtitle: Chug along with a speeding train, then travel back in time to see how roads were born

sections.md:
*Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk… Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk… Koooo!* Have you ever travelled on a train and watched fields, rivers, villages and cows rush past the window?

Unit 6 is all about **travel**. The poem **Trains** captures the rush and rhythm of a train racing across the land. The story **The Story of the Road** is a little history lesson: how did roads begin, long, long ago, and how did they change into the smooth roads we use today?

Big ideas:
- Trains and roads connect people, places and goods.
- Things we use every day have a long history of human cleverness behind them.

The poem describes trains rushing over the land, day and night, carrying people and things from place to place. The trains go:

- **over mountains** and **over plains**,
- **over rivers**,
- carrying **passengers** and **mail**,
- through **day and darkness**, through **dusk and dawn**.

Read the poem aloud and notice its **rhythm** – it has a quick, steady beat, like the wheels going *clickety-clack, clickety-clack* on the rails. A poem's beat can make you *feel* the movement it describes.

**What trains carry:** passengers, letters and parcels, coal, food grains, fruits, cars, even milk!

**India link:** Indian Railways is one of the biggest railway networks in the world. Crores of people travel on it every day. The first passenger train in India ran in 1853 between Bombay (now Mumbai) and Thane.

check.q: Why does the poem 'Trains' have a quick, steady beat?
options: To sound like train wheels on the rails
Because it is a sad poem
check.why: The fast, regular beat copies the clickety-clack of a moving train, so we feel its speed as we read.

sections.md:
The poem is by the American poet **James S. Tippett**. Read the exact words in your free NCERT book (link at the end); here is what each of its three stanzas says.

**Stanza 1 – Where the trains go.** The poet points to trains coming over mountains, over flat plains and over rivers. The repeated word *over* makes us feel the train climbing and crossing, again and again. *Here come the trains!* — the poet is excited, as if waving from a platform.

**Stanza 2 – What they carry.** Trains carry passengers and mail. Their loads are called *precious* because they matter to people — a grandmother coming to visit, a letter from a friend, food for a city. The trains bring them in *without fail*: every day, on time, dependable.

**Stanza 3 – Never stopping.** Thousands of freight cars (goods wagons) keep rushing on, through day and darkness, through dusk and dawn. The trains work all the time — while you play, eat and even sleep.

**Poem tricks:** repetition (*over… over… over*; *carrying… carrying*; *through… through*), rhyme (*plains – trains*, *mail – fail*, *on – dawn*), and a galloping beat.

check.q: What does 'without fail' mean in the poem?
check.why: 'Without fail' means every single time, showing that trains can be trusted to deliver their loads.

sections.h: The story: The Story of the Road
sections.md:
Here is the history of roads, told simply.

**1. Paths made by feet.** Long, long ago there were no roads at all. People and animals walked through forests and over grass. When many feet walked the same way again and again, the grass wore away and a **path** appeared.

**2. Animals carry loads.** People learned to tame animals like horses, donkeys, bullocks and camels to carry heavy things. Paths had to become wider.

**3. The wheel!** Then came one of the greatest inventions ever – the **wheel**. People made carts. But carts got stuck in mud and stones, so people began to make paths **flatter** and **harder**, laying stones and pebbles.

**4. Paved roads.** Later, roads were covered with flat stones or bricks so they lasted longer. Great kings built long roads across their lands, with trees for shade and wells for water along the way.

**5. Today's roads.** Now roads are made with **tar** (a black, sticky material) or **concrete**, so cars, buses and trucks can move fast and smoothly. Big roads that join cities are called **highways**.

**India link:** The ancient road we now call the **Grand Trunk Road** runs from Bengal across north India towards Afghanistan. Rulers over many centuries, including Sher Shah Suri, improved it with rest houses and trees.

*Tip:* read the official chapter in the NCERT book too and compare it with this retelling.

check.q: How did the very first paths form?
options: Many feet walked the same way again and again
check.why: When people and animals kept walking along the same line, the grass wore away and a path formed.

sections.md: See how travel changed over time. Each step solved a problem: heavy loads → animals; slow animals → carts; muddy tracks → stone and brick; faster vehicles → tar and concrete.

*Q: When do the trains run?*

A: Carts with wheels got stuck in mud and on stones, so roads had to be made flat and hard.

*Q: What are roads made of today?*
A: Most roads today are made of tar or concrete so that vehicles can move smoothly and fast.

sections.md:
**Road safety rules**
- Always walk on the **footpath** or on the side of the road.
- Cross at the **zebra crossing**, holding an adult's hand.
- **Red** light – stop. **Yellow** – get ready. **Green** – go.
- Look **right, left, then right again** before crossing.
- Never play on the road.

**Ways to travel**
| On land | On water | In the air |
|---|---|---|
| bus, car, train, bicycle, bullock cart | boat, ship, ferry | aeroplane, helicopter |

**Sound words:** chug-chug (train), honk (car), ring-ring (bicycle bell), whoosh (aeroplane).

**Writing:** Write about a journey you made. Where did you go? How did you travel? What did you see?

> Did you know? The Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu & Kashmir is one of the highest railway bridges in the world – higher than the Eiffel Tower!

rd-school-c3-english-b.unit7.title: Puppy and I & Little Tiger, Big Tiger
rd-school-c3-english-b.unit7.subtitle: A walk where everyone is busy except one playful puppy – and a tiger cub learning the ways of the forest

sections.md:
Imagine you set out for a walk and you meet lots of people and animals. You ask each one, *"Where are you going?"* Everyone is off on some job. Then a little puppy comes along, wagging its tail – and it is going up to the hills to roll and play!

That is the poem **Puppy and I**, written by the English poet A. A. Milne (who also created Winnie-the-Pooh). The second piece, **Little Tiger, Big Tiger**, takes us into an Indian forest to meet a tiger cub and its mother.

Big ideas:
- Friendship and play are precious.
- Young animals, like children, learn from their mothers.
- Wild animals like tigers need safe forests to live in.

sections.h: 📜 Full text: Puppy and I (A. A. Milne)
sections.md:
A. A. Milne died in 1956, so this poem is free to share in India. Read it aloud!

> I met a Man as I went walking;
> We got talking,
> Man and I.
> "Where are you going to, Man?" I said
> (I said to the Man as he went by).
> "Down to the village, to get some bread.
> Will you come with me?" "No, not I."
>
> I met a Horse as I went walking;
> We got talking,
> Horse and I.
> "Where are you going to, Horse, to-day?"
> (I said to the Horse as he went by).
> "Down to the village to get some hay.
> Will you come with me?" "No, not I."
>
> I met a Woman as I went walking;
> We got talking,
> Woman and I.
> "Where are you going to, Woman, so early?"
> (I said to the Woman as she went by).
> "Down to the village to get some barley.
> Will you come with me?" "No, not I."
>
> I met some Rabbits as I went walking;
> We got talking,
> Rabbits and I.
> "Where are you going in your brown fur coats?"
> (I said to the Rabbits as they went by).
> "Down to the village to get some oats.
> Will you come with us?" "No, not I."
>
> I met a Puppy as I went walking;
> We got talking,
> Puppy and I.
> "Where are you going this nice fine day?"
> (I said to the Puppy as he went by).
> "Up in the hills to roll and play."
> "I'll come with you, Puppy," said I.

(Your NCERT book may print a slightly shorter version — check the free chapter link at the end.)

sections.h: The poem explained, stanza by stanza
sections.md:
| Stanza | Who the speaker meets | Where they are going | Does the speaker go? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a **man** | down to the village for **bread** | No |
| 2 | a **horse** | down to the village for **hay** | No |
| 3 | a **woman**, early in the morning | down to the village for **barley** | No |
| 4 | some **rabbits** in brown fur coats | down to the village for **oats** | No |
| 5 | a **puppy**, on a fine day | **up in the hills** to roll and play | **Yes!** |

**Lines 1–3 of each stanza:** the speaker is out walking, meets someone and they start chatting – *We got talking, Man and I.*
**Lines 4–5:** the speaker asks where they are going (the bracket line tells us it was said as they passed by).
**Line 6:** the answer – everyone except the puppy is going *down* to the village to fetch food.
**Line 7:** each one politely invites the speaker – *Will you come with me?* – and the speaker says *No, not I.*
**Last stanza twist:** the puppy is going *up*, not down, and not to work but to **play**. This time the speaker happily says, *I'll come with you, Puppy.*

**Why?** Fetching bread, hay, barley and oats is a chore; rolling in the hills is fun. The speaker, like any child, chooses play and a playful friend.

**Poem tricks:** a repeating pattern in every stanza; rhymes (*said – bread*, *day – hay*, *early – barley*, *coats – oats*, *day – play*); and a surprise ending that breaks the pattern.
keyTerms: errand – a small job like buying bread
hay – dried grass eaten by horses and cows
barley, oats – kinds of grain
stanza – a group of lines in a poem

check.q: Why did the speaker go with the puppy and not the others?
options: The others were going to fetch things, but the puppy was going to play
check.why: The man, horse, woman and rabbits were all going to the village to fetch food, while the puppy was going up to the hills to play — and that is what the speaker wanted.

sections.h: The story: Little Tiger, Big Tiger
sections.md:
Retold in our own words:

In a thick green forest in India lived a big **tigress** and her **cub**. The cub was small, playful and full of questions. He loved pouncing on his mother's tail, rolling in the grass and chasing butterflies.

His mother taught him everything he needed to know:
- how to **walk silently** on soft paws,
- how to **hide** in tall grass, where his stripes made him almost invisible,
- how to **swim** across a stream (tigers love water!),
- how to be patient and wait.

One day the cub wandered off alone. Everything seemed big and strange. He heard a crackle in the bushes and felt scared. Then came a deep, comforting roar – his mother had found him! She licked his face and led him home to their den. The cub learned to stay close until he was big and strong.

The story also reminds us that the forest is the tiger's home. When forests are cut down, or when people hunt tigers, the tigers have nowhere to go. Caring for forests means caring for tigers.

*Tip:* read the official chapter in the NCERT book too and compare it with this retelling.

> Did you know? The tiger is India's **national animal**. *Project Tiger* began in 1973 to protect tigers, and today India is home to most of the world's wild tigers.

check.why: A tiger's stripes look like shadows of grass stems, so it blends in and is hard to see.

A: The speaker met a man, a horse, a woman, some rabbits and a puppy.

*Q: Where were the man, horse, woman and rabbits going?*
A: They were all going down to the village – the man for bread, the horse for hay, the woman for barley and the rabbits for oats.

*Q: Why did the speaker say 'No, not I' to the others?*
A: They were going on errands to fetch food, and the speaker did not want to do chores.

*Q: Where was the puppy going?*
A: The puppy was going up in the hills to roll and play, so the speaker went with it.

*Q: What did the tigress teach her cub?*
A: She taught him to walk silently, hide in the grass, swim and be patient.

rd-school-c3-english-b.unit8.title: What's in the Mailbox? & My Silly Sister
rd-school-c3-english-b.unit8.subtitle: The thrill of a letter with your name on it, and a baby sister who does the silliest things

sections.md:
Have you ever got something in the post addressed to *you*? A birthday card from your *nani*, a postcard from a cousin in another city, a parcel with a book inside? Your heart beats a little faster as you tear open the envelope!

Unit 8 of Marigold is about **family and the people we love**. It has two pieces:

1. The poem **What's in the Mailbox?** – a child rushes to the mailbox, wondering and hoping that a letter is waiting.
2. The story **My Silly Sister** – a funny, warm tale told by an older child about a baby sister who does all sorts of silly things.

Both pieces are about the same feeling: *we belong to people, and they belong to us*. A letter from far away and a noisy baby at home are both signs of love.

**Big ideas of this unit:**
- Letters connect families and friends who live far apart.
- Waiting for something can be exciting.
- Little ones learn slowly; we should be patient and loving with them – we were little once too!
- In the exercises you will practise family words, feeling words, rhyming words, writing a letter and filling a simple address.

This read retells both pieces in our own words. For the exact poem and story, open the free official Marigold textbook from ncert.nic.in (link at the end).

sections.h: The poem: What's in the Mailbox? – stanza by stanza
sections.md:
The poem is short and bouncy, full of questions. Here is what happens, explained part by part.

**Part 1 – The wondering.** The child stands near the mailbox and asks: *What is inside today?* The child cannot see in, so imagination takes over.

**Part 2 – The guesses.** Could it be a **letter** from a friend? A **card** for a birthday? A **parcel** with a surprise gift? A **postcard** with a picture of the sea or mountains? Each guess makes the child more excited.

**Part 3 – The worry.** Maybe there is *nothing at all*! Maybe the mail is only for grown-ups – bills and papers. The child feels a little nervous.

**Part 4 – The joy.** The child opens the mailbox and finds something with **their own name** written on it. It is a wonderful feeling to know that someone, somewhere, thought of you.

**What does the poem mean?** The fun of the poem lies in **waiting and hoping**. It also shows that a simple letter can make someone's whole day.

**Poem tools to notice:**
- **Questions** – the poet asks many questions, so we feel the child's curiosity.
- **Rhyme** – line endings sound alike, which makes the poem easy to remember and sing.
- **Repetition** – the title question comes back again and again like a chorus.

Today many people send messages on phones. But a handwritten letter is special: you can keep it in a box, read it again and again, and see the writer's own handwriting.

check.q: What makes the child in the poem so happy at the end?
options: There is a bill for Father
There is something with the child's own name on it
check.why: The child's joy comes from finding mail addressed to them, which shows that someone cared enough to write.

sections.md:
Let us follow a letter from Riya in Lucknow to her Nani in Chennai.

1. Riya writes the letter and folds it into an **envelope**.
2. She writes the **address** clearly: name, house number, street, city, state and the six-digit **PIN code**.
3. She sticks a **stamp** on the top right corner. The stamp shows the postage has been paid.
4. She drops it in the red **post box**.
5. A **postman** collects letters from the box and takes them to the **post office**.
6. Letters are **sorted** by PIN code and sent by van, train or aeroplane.
7. At the Chennai post office they are sorted again, and a postman **delivers** the letter to Nani's door.

**Writing an address:**

> Smt. Kamala Iyer
> 12, Temple Street, Mylapore
> Chennai, Tamil Nadu – 600004

> Did you know? India has one of the largest postal networks in the world, with well over 1.5 lakh post offices – including a floating post office on a houseboat on Dal Lake in Srinagar!

sections.h: The story: My Silly Sister – scene by scene
sections.md:
Retold in our own words:

**Scene 1 – Meet the sister.** The narrator, an older child, tells us about the baby of the family. Oh, she is *silly*! She cannot talk properly yet – she just babbles *ba-ba-ga-ga*.

**Scene 2 – Mealtime mess.** At mealtimes food ends up everywhere – on her face, her frock, the floor, and sometimes on the narrator! She bangs her spoon and laughs.

**Scene 3 – Everything in the mouth.** She grabs things and puts them in her mouth: toys, spoons, even the narrator's crayons. The narrator has to hide favourite things.

**Scene 4 – Noisy nights.** When she wants something she cries loudly, sometimes in the middle of the night, and wakes everyone up.

**Scene 5 – The question.** The narrator, annoyed, asks Mother, *"Why is she so silly?"*

**Scene 6 – Mother's surprise.** Mother smiles and says the narrator was *just the same* as a baby! Babies are still learning everything – talking, eating, walking. It takes time.

**Scene 7 – A new way of seeing.** The narrator thinks about this and begins to help: showing the baby how to clap, playing peek-a-boo, laughing when she giggles. The silly sister is not so annoying any more – she is fun!

**Message:** Be patient and kind with younger brothers, sisters and cousins. Everyone grows up step by step.

check.q: What did Mother tell the narrator about the baby?
options: That the baby was very naughty
That the narrator was just the same as a baby
That the baby would go away
That the baby could already talk
check.why: Mother reminded the narrator that all babies, including the narrator once, are still learning, which helped the narrator become patient.

sections.md:
| Character | What they are like | How we know |
|---|---|---|
| Narrator | older, a little impatient at first, then caring | gets annoyed, then helps the baby |
| Baby sister | tiny, curious, noisy, happy | babbles, makes a mess, giggles |
| Mother | calm, wise, loving | explains gently instead of scolding |

**How the narrator's feelings change:** annoyed → puzzled → surprised → understanding → loving.

Think about it: is the baby really *silly*, or just *little*? The word "silly" in the title is said with love, the way we tease people we care about.

check.q: How did the narrator feel at the END of the story?
check.why: After Mother's explanation, the narrator understands the baby and starts enjoying playing with her.

sections.md:
Babies learn things in a rough order (every baby is different, so ages vary):

- **Smiling** – in the first few months.
- **Sitting up** – around half a year.
- **Crawling** – a little later.
- **First words** like *ma*, *pa* – around one year.
- **Walking** – around one year or a bit after.

So when your little sister makes a mess, remember – she is just on her learning journey!

**Activity:** Ask your parents what your first word was and when you took your first step. Write it down and share it in class.
