sections.md:
**Family words:** mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother (dadi/nani), grandfather (dada/nana), aunt, uncle, cousin.

**Feeling words:** happy, excited, annoyed, surprised, proud, sleepy.

**Rhyming words:** box – socks – fox; card – hard – yard; letter – better; name – game – same.

**Opposites:** big – small, noisy – quiet, open – shut, early – late.

**Write a short letter** to a grandparent:

> Dear Nani,
> How are you? I am fine. My baby sister is learning to walk now. I miss you. Please come for Diwali.
> With love,
> Riya

**Parts of a letter:** greeting (*Dear Nani*), body (your news), ending (*With love*), your name.

**Speaking activity:** Tell the class one funny thing a baby you know does.

check.q: Which part of a letter is 'Dear Nani'?
check.why: A letter begins with a greeting such as 'Dear Nani' that names the person we are writing to.

summary: Unit 8: poem 'What's in the Mailbox?' and story 'My Silly Sister'.
In the poem a child excitedly wonders what is in the mailbox.
The child guesses a letter, card, parcel or postcard – or nothing.
The joy is finding something with one's own name on it.
A letter needs an envelope, an address with PIN code and a stamp.
The postman collects, sorts and delivers letters.
In the story, the narrator thinks the baby sister is silly.
The baby babbles, makes a mess and puts things in her mouth.
Mother says the narrator was the same as a baby.
The narrator learns to be patient and plays with the baby.
Babies learn step by step: smile, sit, crawl, talk, walk.
A letter has a greeting, body, ending and name.

glossary.d: a box where letters are put
baby sounds that are not yet words
a packet sent by post
a person who delivers letters
a little angry

practice: What did the child hope to find in the mailbox?
Write the steps for sending a letter.
Write your own home address with PIN code.
Write three silly things the baby sister did.
Why was the narrator annoyed?
What did Mother say?
How did the narrator change at the end?
Write five family words and three rhyming pairs.
Write a short letter to a friend.

rd-school-c3-english-c.unit10.title: How Creatures Move & The Ship of the Desert
rd-school-c3-english-c.unit10.subtitle: Hop, slither, swim, fly – and meet the camel, the hero of the hot sands

sections.md:
Watch a garden for five minutes. A sparrow **hops**. A snail **creeps**. A butterfly **flutters**. A dog **runs**. A frog **leaps**. A fish in the pond **swims**. Every creature moves in its own special way!

Unit 10 of Marigold is about **animals and how they live**. It has two pieces:

1. The poem **How Creatures Move** – a lively list of animals and the ways they get around, with a fun question at the end.
2. The lesson **The Ship of the Desert** – all about the **camel**, the animal that can cross hot, dry deserts where few others survive.

**Big ideas of this unit:**
- Each animal's body suits the way it moves and the place it lives.
- Movement words are **action words (verbs)**.
- The camel is perfectly built for the desert and is a great helper to desert people.
- In the exercises you will match animals to movements, learn describing words, practise opposites, and talk and write about animals.

This read explains both pieces in our own words. For the exact poem and lesson, open the free official Marigold book (link at the end).

sections.h: The poem: How Creatures Move – part by part
sections.md:
The poem goes from creature to creature like a parade.

**Part 1 – Creatures of air and water.** The poet tells us that birds use their wings to **fly** and fish use their fins and tails to **swim**. The lines feel light and quick, like flying.

**Part 2 – Creatures of the ground.** Some animals have no legs at all – the snake **slithers** and the worm **wriggles**. Some have very strong legs – the frog **leaps**, the kangaroo **jumps**, the horse **gallops**. Some are slow – the snail **creeps**.

**Part 3 – The question.** At the end the poet turns to us: if every creature has its own way of moving, how do *you* move? And the happy answer is that children can do almost all of them – walk, run, skip, hop, jump, climb, swim, and even dance!

| Creature | How it moves |
|---|---|
| birds | fly |
| fish | swim |
| snakes | slither / glide |
| frogs | hop and leap |
| horses | gallop / trot |
| worms | wriggle / crawl |
| kangaroos | jump |
| we (people) | walk, run, skip, dance! |

**Why read it aloud?** The poem's rhythm copies the movements. Act each one out as you read: flap your arms to *fly*, wiggle to *slither*, bounce to *hop*.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='140' fill='#bbdefb'/><rect y='140' width='600' height='70' fill='#a5d6a7'/><rect y='210' width='600' height='70' fill='#4fc3f7'/><path d='M0 0 q10 -10 20 0 q10 -10 20 0' stroke='#333' stroke-width='3' fill='none'><animateMotion path='M0 60 L600 40' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><g><animateMotion path='M0 175 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0 q40 -50 80 0' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='0' rx='14' ry='10' fill='#2e7d32'/><circle cx='8' cy='-8' r='3' fill='#fff'/></g><path d='M0 0 q15 -10 30 0 t30 0 t30 0' stroke='#795548' stroke-width='6' fill='none'><animateMotion path='M600 195 L0 195' dur='9s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><g><animateMotion path='M600 245 L-40 245' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='0' rx='20' ry='9' fill='#ff7043'/><path d='M18 0 l14 -9 v18z' fill='#ff7043'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#0d47a1'><text x='10' y='20'>fly</text><text x='10' y='160'>hop</text><text x='520' y='160'>slither</text><text x='10' y='270'>swim</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: A bird flies, a frog hops, a snake slithers and a fish swims.
fig.alt: Animated bird, hopping frog, sliding snake and swimming fish.

keyTerms: slither – to slide along the ground, like a snake
gallop – to run fast, like a horse
wriggle – to twist and turn
creep – to move very slowly and quietly

check.q: How does a snake move?
check.why: A snake has no legs, so it slides its long body along the ground, which we call slithering.

sections.md:
Why can a fish swim but not walk? Because each body is built for its job.

- **Wings and feathers** – light and wide, to push against air (birds, and insects like bees with thin wings).
- **Fins and a tail** – to push against water; a smooth, pointed body slips through easily (fish).
- **Strong back legs** – to spring up high (frog, kangaroo, grasshopper).
- **Long, bendy body with scales** – to push against the ground in curves (snake).
- **Hooves** – hard feet for running on hard ground (horse, deer).
- **A slimy foot** – the snail glides on a thin layer of slime.

Some animals move in more than one way. A duck walks, swims *and* flies! A frog hops on land and swims in a pond.

> Did you know? The cheetah is the fastest land animal, and a peregrine falcon diving through the air is faster still!

check.q: Which animal can walk, swim AND fly?
check.why: A duck has legs for walking, webbed feet for swimming and wings for flying.

sections.md:
Why do we call the camel the **ship of the desert**? Because, just as a ship carries people and goods across the sea, a camel carries them across the great 'sea' of sand!

In India, camels are found mostly in **Rajasthan** and **Gujarat**, in and around the **Thar Desert**. They pull carts, carry loads, give milk and help farmers plough fields. Their hair can be made into rugs and ropes. At the famous **Pushkar fair** in Rajasthan, thousands of camels are decorated and traded.

**How is a camel built for the desert?**
- **Hump:** stores **fat**, not water! The camel's body can use this fat for energy when food is scarce. When a camel goes hungry for long, the hump becomes small and floppy.
- **Drinking:** a thirsty camel can drink a very large amount of water at once, and then go for many days without drinking.
- **Long eyelashes** and **closable nostrils** keep out blowing sand.
- **Wide, padded feet** spread out so they don't sink into soft sand.
- **Thick lips** let it eat thorny desert plants.
- **Long legs** keep its body away from the hot ground.
- **Kneeling:** a camel folds its legs and sits down so people can climb on and load it; tough pads on its knees protect it.

So the camel can walk for long distances in heat and sandstorms, carrying heavy loads. No wonder desert people value it so much!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='d' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#ffe0b2'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#ffb74d'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='url(#d)'/><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='30' fill='#ffeb3b'><animate attributeName='r' values='28;34;28' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><path d='M0 240 q150 -40 300 0 t300 0 V300 H0Z' fill='#f9a825'/><g fill='#a1662f'><ellipse cx='280' cy='170' rx='80' ry='35'/><ellipse cx='275' cy='130' rx='38' ry='30'/><path d='M350 160 Q390 120 400 90 L420 90 L420 105 L405 110 Q395 150 365 180Z'/><rect x='220' y='190' width='12' height='60'/><rect x='250' y='190' width='12' height='60'/><rect x='305' y='190' width='12' height='60'/><rect x='330' y='190' width='12' height='60'/></g><circle cx='412' cy='96' r='3' fill='#000'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='#3e2723'><text x='230' y='92'>hump (fat)</text><text x='430' y='90'>long lashes</text><text x='170' y='270'>wide padded feet</text><text x='360' y='230'>long legs</text></g></svg>

fig.alt: Labelled camel in a desert with a pulsing sun.

check.q: What is stored in a camel's hump?
check.why: A camel's hump stores fat, which its body can use for energy when food is hard to find.

sections.md:
**Desert facts**
- A desert gets very little rain.
- Days are very hot; nights can be cold.
- Strong winds blow sand into **dunes** – hills of sand that slowly move.
- Plants like **cactus** store water in thick stems and have spines instead of leaves.
- Other desert animals: desert fox, lizards, snakes, the great Indian bustard.
- People in the Thar wear loose, light clothes and turbans to keep off the sun, and store rainwater carefully.

**Comparing animals**

| Animal | Lives in | Special body part |
|---|---|---|
| camel | desert | hump, padded feet |
| fish | water | fins, gills |
| bird | trees/air | wings, feathers |
| frog | water and land | strong back legs |

> Did you know? Some camels have **two humps**. These Bactrian camels live in the cold deserts of Central Asia, and a small number are found in Ladakh, India!

check.q: Why is the camel called the 'ship of the desert'?
options: It carries people and goods across the sand like a ship across the sea
It is shaped like a boat
check.why: Just as ships carry loads across the sea, camels carry loads across the wide desert.

sections.md:
**Action words (verbs):** fly, swim, hop, crawl, creep, gallop, slither, wriggle, leap, run, skip.

**Describing words:** a *tall* camel, a *hot* desert, *soft* sand, a *thorny* bush, *long* eyelashes.

**Opposites:** hot – cold, fast – slow, wet – dry, tall – short, heavy – light.

**Fill in:** A horse ____ (gallops). A worm ____ (wriggles). A fish ____ (swims).

**Animal sounds:** a camel grunts, a horse neighs, a frog croaks, a snake hisses.

**Speaking:** Pretend you are a camel. Tell the class about your day in the desert – where you walked, what you carried, what you ate.

**Writing:** Write four sentences about an animal you like: where it lives, how it moves, what it eats, why you like it.

check.q: Which is the opposite of 'wet'?
check.why: Deserts are dry because they get very little rain, the opposite of wet places.

story.title: Raju the Camel Saves the Day

parts.md: In a village near Jaisalmer lived a camel called Raju and a girl called Meera. Every morning Raju carried water pots from the well, three kilometres away, while Meera walked beside him singing. Raju walked slowly but never stopped, his wide feet going *puff, puff* in the sand.

One afternoon the sky turned orange and a sandstorm came roaring. Meera covered her face with her dupatta. Raju simply closed his nostrils and blinked his long lashes, and the sand could not hurt his eyes. He knelt down, and Meera sheltered beside his big warm body until the wind died away.

When the storm was over, all the paths were covered in new dunes. But Raju knew the way home. He carried Meera and the water safely back. That evening the whole village thanked him with a bundle of fresh leaves. "You really are the ship of the desert," laughed Meera.

summary: Unit 10: poem 'How Creatures Move' and lesson 'The Ship of the Desert'.
Animals move in different ways: fly, swim, slither, hop, gallop, crawl, creep.
The poem ends by asking how we move – children can move in many ways.
Movement words are verbs.
Body parts like wings, fins and strong legs suit each movement.
The camel is called the ship of the desert.
In India camels live mainly in Rajasthan and Gujarat (Thar Desert).
The hump stores fat, not water.
Long lashes and closable nostrils keep out sand.
Wide padded feet stop camels sinking in sand.
Camels give milk, carry loads, pull carts and help in farming.
Deserts are dry, hot by day and cool at night.

glossary.d: a very dry place with little rain
the raised lump on a camel's back
to run fast like a horse
a desert plant that stores water
a hill of sand made by wind

practice: How do birds, fish and snakes move?
Name four ways children can move.
Why can a frog jump so high?
Why is the camel called the ship of the desert?
What does a camel's hump store?
How do a camel's feet and eyelashes help it?
How do camels help people?
Write three facts about deserts.
Write the opposites of hot, fast and heavy.
Draw a camel and label three parts.

rd-school-c3-english-c.unit9.title: Don't Tell & He is My Brother
rd-school-c3-english-c.unit9.subtitle: A secret that is hard to keep, and a load that feels light because it is carried with love

sections.md:
*Psst! Come close. I have a secret… but don't tell anyone!*

We all love secrets. They make us feel special and a little bit giggly. But secrets can also be hard to keep, and some secrets should not be kept at all.

Unit 9 of Marigold is about **feelings between people who care for each other**. It has two pieces:

1. The poem **Don't Tell** – a playful poem in which a child shares a little secret and begs the listener not to tell.
2. The story **He is My Brother** – a moving tale about a child who carries a younger brother a long way, and does not feel the weight at all, because of love.

**Big ideas of this unit:**
- Some secrets are fun (a surprise party!), but if a secret makes you feel scared or unsafe, **always tell a trusted grown-up**.
- Love makes hard things feel easy.
- Families look after each other – older children help younger ones.
- In the exercises you will practise opposites, 'is' and 'are', helping words and speaking about your family.

This read retells both pieces in our own words. For the exact poem and story, open the free official Marigold book (link at the end).

sections.h: The poem: Don't Tell – part by part
sections.md:
**Part 1 – The whisper begins.** The child leans close and says there is something to share – but it must stay a secret. We can almost feel the child's breath in our ear.

**Part 2 – The cheeky secret.** The child has done something small and naughty – the sort of thing every child does, like sneaking a sweet before dinner or peeking at a hidden present. Nothing terrible, just a little mischief.

**Part 3 – The worry.** What if a grown-up finds out? The child keeps begging, *"Don't tell!"* again and again, sounding more and more worried and giggly at the same time.

**Part 4 – The fun ending.** The poem ends with the secret still a secret – between the child and us, the readers. We feel like trusted friends.

**What does the poem show?** Children love to share secrets with friends; it makes them feel close. The poem is funny because the secret is so small but the child treats it as very big!

**Poem tools:**
- **Repetition** – the words *don't tell* come back like a chorus.
- **Whispering voice** – read it softly with a finger on your lips.
- **Rhyme** – line endings sound alike, making it bouncy.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#ede7f6'/><circle cx='200' cy='140' r='60' fill='#ffcc80'/><circle cx='180' cy='125' r='6' fill='#000'/><circle cx='220' cy='125' r='6' fill='#000'/><rect x='196' y='145' width='8' height='40' rx='4' fill='#f57c00'/><ellipse cx='200' cy='165' rx='14' ry='5' fill='#c62828'/><circle cx='400' cy='140' r='60' fill='#ffe0b2'/><circle cx='380' cy='125' r='6' fill='#000'/><circle cx='420' cy='125' r='6' fill='#000'/><ellipse cx='400' cy='165' rx='12' ry='9' fill='#6d4c41'/><g font-family='sans-serif' fill='#4527a0'><text x='270' y='70' font-size='18'>psst…<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='280' y='105' font-size='22'>don't tell!<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;1;0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Shh… a whispered secret.
fig.alt: Two faces, one with a finger on lips, with whispered words appearing.

keyTerms: secret – something kept hidden from others
whisper – to speak very softly
trust – to believe someone will keep you safe

check.q: Which words keep coming back in the poem?
check.why: The child repeats 'don't tell' again and again, which is the repetition that makes the poem fun.

sections.md:
| Good secrets (surprises) | Secrets to share with an adult |
|---|---|
| a birthday surprise for Papa | someone hurting you |
| a gift you made for Ma | someone asking you to keep a scary secret |
| a surprise party for a friend | something that makes you feel bad inside |

A good secret is one that will make someone happy when it comes out – and it comes out soon! A worried secret makes your tummy feel tight and your heart feel heavy.

If you ever have a worried secret, tell your parent, teacher or another grown-up you trust. **That is never 'telling tales' – that is being brave.** In India, children can also call **1098**, the free Childline number, any time.

**Your safety circle:** draw your hand, and on each finger write the name of one grown-up you can talk to.

check.q: What should you do if a secret makes you feel scared?
check.why: Scary secrets should always be shared with a grown-up you trust, because they can help keep you safe.

sections.h: The story: He is My Brother – scene by scene
sections.md:
Retold in our own words:

**Scene 1 – The long path.** High in the hills, a girl had to cross a steep, rocky path to reach the village on the other side. On her back she carried her little brother, who was too small to walk that far.

**Scene 2 – The hard climb.** The path went up and up. The sun was hot. Pebbles rolled under her feet. Other travellers puffed and panted under their own loads of wood and grain.

**Scene 3 – The kind man's question.** A man walking beside her looked at the little girl with the boy tied on her back and said gently, *"That is a heavy load for such a small child. Aren't you tired?"*

**Scene 4 – The answer.** The girl looked up in surprise and smiled. *"He isn't heavy,"* she said. *"He is my brother."*

**Scene 5 – Understanding.** The man was quiet for a long time. He understood. The girl did not think of her brother as a *load* at all. She loved him, so carrying him felt like a joy, not a burden. The two of them went on up the hill together.

**What does it mean?** When we do something for someone we love – carrying a sibling, helping a grandparent climb stairs, sharing our lunch with a friend – it does not feel like hard work. Love makes it light.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#e3f2fd'/><path d='M0 280 L250 120 L380 40 L600 200 V280Z' fill='#a5d6a7'/><path d='M40 270 Q200 200 280 140 T400 60' stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='10' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='8 6'/><g><animateMotion path='M40 255 Q200 185 280 125 T400 45' dur='8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><circle cx='0' cy='-30' r='10' fill='#ffcc80'/><rect x='-7' y='-20' width='14' height='26' rx='5' fill='#e91e63'/><circle cx='-12' cy='-34' r='7' fill='#ffe0b2'/><rect x='-18' y='-28' width='10' height='16' rx='4' fill='#42a5f5'/></g><text x='450' y='250' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#1b5e20'>"He isn't heavy…"</text></svg>
fig.caption: A girl climbs the hill path carrying her little brother.
fig.alt: A small figure carrying a smaller one moves up a winding hill path.

check.q: Why did the girl say her brother was not heavy?
options: She loved him, so carrying him felt easy
check.why: The girl's love for her brother made the task feel light, so she did not think of him as a heavy load.

sections.md:
| Character | What they are like |
|---|---|
| The girl | loving, strong-hearted, cheerful, responsible |
| Little brother | small, trusting, safe on his sister's back |
| The kind man | caring, thoughtful – he learns something |

**Values in the story:** love, care for family, responsibility, cheerfulness in hard work.

**Link the two pieces:** The poem and the story are both about people who are close. In the poem, a child trusts a friend with a secret. In the story, a little boy trusts his sister to carry him safely. **Trust** is the thread that joins them.

> Did you know? The idea 'he isn't heavy, he's my brother' is so loved that it has appeared in stories, posters and songs around the world.

check.q: Which word joins both the poem and the story?
check.why: In both pieces someone trusts a person close to them – a friend with a secret, a brother with his sister.

sections.md:
**Opposites:** heavy – light; up – down; tired – fresh; tell – hide; whisper – shout; near – far.

**Helping words at home:** *May I help you?* *Let me carry that.* *Thank you for helping me.*

**Sentences with 'is' and 'are'**
- He **is** my brother. (one person)
- They **are** my brothers. (more than one)
- The bag **is** heavy. The bags **are** heavy.

**Family tree activity:** Draw a tree. Put yourself on the trunk, your parents on the branches above, and brothers, sisters or cousins on the side branches.

**Speaking:** Tell your class about a time you helped someone in your family. How did you feel?

**Writing:** Complete: *I love my ___ because ___.*

check.q: Fill in: They ___ my sisters.
check.why: We use 'are' with more than one person, so 'They are my sisters' is correct.

summary: Unit 9: poem 'Don't Tell' and story 'He is My Brother'.
In the poem, a child whispers a small, cheeky secret and says 'don't tell!'.
The poem uses repetition, rhyme and a whispering voice.
Surprise secrets are fine; scary secrets must be told to a trusted adult.
Childline 1098 is a free helpline for children in India.
In the story, a girl carries her little brother up a steep hill path.
A kind man asks if the load is heavy.
She replies that he isn't heavy – he is her brother.
Message: love makes hard work feel light.
Trust links the poem and the story.
Use 'is' for one, 'are' for many.
Opposites: heavy–light, whisper–shout.

glossary.d: a heavy load
rising sharply, hard to climb
to speak very softly
a person on a journey
small naughty behaviour

practice: What does the child in the poem keep saying?
What kind of secret did the child have?
Give one example of a good secret and one you must tell an adult.
Where was the girl going in the story?
Whom was she carrying?
What did the man ask her?
What did her answer mean?
Write the opposites of heavy, up, whisper.
Use 'is' and 'are' in two sentences each.
Write about a time you helped a family member.

rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch1-where-to-look-f.title: Where to Look From
rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch1-where-to-look-f.subtitle: The same thing looks different from the top, the front and the side

sections.h: A Bird, an Ant and a Glass
sections.md:
Put a steel glass on the table. Now pretend you are a **bird** flying above it. What do you see? Just a **circle** — the round mouth of the glass. Now pretend you are an **ant** standing on the table next to it. What do you see? A tall shape, like a **rectangle** that is a little wider at the top.

It is the same glass! It only *looks* different because you are looking from a different place. This chapter is all about **where you look from**:

- **Top view** — looking down from above, like a bird or a fan on the ceiling.
- **Front view** — looking straight at the front, like standing in front of a shop.
- **Side view** — looking from the left or right side.

Mathematicians, architects and engineers draw objects from all three views so that builders know exactly what to make.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#f0f9ff'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle'><path d='M110 70 L190 70 L180 200 L120 200 Z' fill='#cbd5e1' stroke='#475569' stroke-width='3'/><ellipse cx='150' cy='70' rx='40' ry='10' fill='#e2e8f0' stroke='#475569' stroke-width='3'/><text x='150' y='235'>the glass</text><circle cx='330' cy='130' r='50' fill='#e2e8f0' stroke='#475569' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='330' cy='130' r='32' fill='none' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='330' y='235'>top view: circle</text><path d='M470 70 L550 70 L540 200 L480 200 Z' fill='#cbd5e1' stroke='#475569' stroke-width='3'/><text x='510' y='235'>side view</text></g><g><path d='M310 20 l10 -8 l10 8 l10 -8 l10 8' stroke='#0f172a' stroke-width='3' fill='none'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 6;0 0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g></svg>
fig.caption: A bird above sees a circle; from the side the glass looks like a tall shape.
fig.alt: A glass with its round top view and tall side view

keyTerms: top view — what you see from above
front view — what you see from the front
side view — what you see from the side

check.q: What does the top view of a round steel glass look like?
check.why: From above, you only see the round mouth of the glass, which is a circle.

sections.h: Top Views of Things at Home
sections.md:
Let us guess the top view of things around us:

| Object | Top view looks like |
|---|---|
| ball | circle |
| matchbox or brick | rectangle |
| dice (cube) | square |
| ice-cream cone (point down) | circle |
| bucket | circle (big ring) |
| cup with handle | circle with a small bump |
| table | rectangle (you cannot see the legs!) |
| chair | square seat with a back edge |

Notice: from the top, you often **cannot see** parts hidden below, like the legs of a table. From the top, a cone and a ball both look like circles, so the top view alone does not always tell you what the object is.

**Activity:** Stand on a stool (carefully!) and look down at things placed on the floor — a water bottle, a book, a plate, a kettle. Draw what you see.

check.q: From the top, the legs of a table…
check.why: The table top covers the legs, so from above you only see the rectangle of the top.

sections.md:
Now look at things from the **front** and the **side**.

- A **bus** from the front shows the big windscreen and two headlights; from the side you see a long row of windows and the wheels.
- An **elephant** from the front shows its trunk, two tusks and big ears; from the side you see its long body, four legs and tail.
- A **cup with a handle**: from one side you see the handle; from the other side the handle is hidden behind the cup.
- A **house** from the front shows the door; from the side you may see only a wall and a window.

Try this game in pairs: one child holds a toy and turns it slowly. The other child says "front!", "side!", "top!" and draws each view. Swap.

check.q: From which view can you see all the windows along a bus?
check.why: The windows of a bus run along its sides, so the side view shows them all.

sections.md:
In the book, a family is sitting around a table and one picture is taken from each side. We must match the picture with the person who took it.

Think like a detective:

- If a photo shows a **girl's face** and the **back of a boy's head**, the photographer was standing behind the boy.
- If you see the **jug on the left** and the **plate on the right**, turn around and the jug will be on the right!

Similarly, a picture of **a road from a high building** looks very different from a picture of the same road taken by someone walking on it. From the top, cars look like small rectangles and people look like dots with heads.

> Did you know? Pilots and drone cameras see cities in top view. Google-style satellite maps are giant top views of the Earth.

check.q: If a photo shows the back of Rahul's head, where was the camera?
check.why: You can only see the back of a head when you are behind the person.

sections.h: From a Top View to a Map
sections.md:
A **map** is a top view of a place, drawn small and simple.

Imagine you are a bird above your classroom. You see desks (small rectangles), the teacher's table (a bigger rectangle), the door (a gap in the wall), the blackboard (a thick line) and the windows. Draw them on paper — you have made a **map of your classroom**!

On maps we use:

- **symbols**: a small tree for a park, a cross for a hospital, a blue line for a river;
- **directions**: left, right, near, far, next to;
- **paths**: roads drawn as lines.

In the book, Neha's school map shows the school, a park, a tank and roads. Questions ask: *Which is nearer to the school — the park or the tank? Which road would you take to go from the gate to the playground?*

**Activity:** Draw a map of the route from your home to school. Mark three landmarks — a temple, a shop, a big tree.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fefce8'/><rect x='40' y='40' width='520' height='220' fill='#fff' stroke='#78350f' stroke-width='4'/><rect x='60' y='55' width='200' height='14' fill='#1f2937'/><text x='160' y='90' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>blackboard</text><rect x='420' y='60' width='110' height='50' fill='#fcd34d' stroke='#92400e'/><text x='475' y='90' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>teacher</text><g fill='#93c5fd' stroke='#1e3a8a'><rect x='80' y='130' width='70' height='34'/><rect x='190' y='130' width='70' height='34'/><rect x='300' y='130' width='70' height='34'/><rect x='80' y='195' width='70' height='34'/><rect x='190' y='195' width='70' height='34'/><rect x='300' y='195' width='70' height='34'/></g><rect x='500' y='250' width='50' height='12' fill='#fefce8'/><text x='525' y='285' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'>door</text><circle cx='525' cy='240' r='8' fill='#ef4444'><animateMotion path='M0 0 L-90 -40 L-240 -40' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></svg>
fig.caption: A classroom drawn from the top becomes a map. The red dot walks from the door to a desk.
fig.alt: Top-view map of a classroom with desks, blackboard, teacher's table and door

check.q: A map is a kind of…
check.why: Maps show places as seen from above, so they are top views drawn small.

sections.h: Big and Small: Drawing to Size
sections.md:
When we draw a map, everything becomes smaller but must keep the **same shape** and the **same order**. A big hall should still look bigger than a small room on the map. If the park is next to the school in real life, it must be next to it on your map.

Compare: from close up, a coin looks big; from far away the same coin looks tiny. Things that are far away look smaller. That is why mountains look small from a train window, and why a plane in the sky looks like a toy.

**Try:** Draw your bedroom from the top. Use a big rectangle for the bed, a small square for a stool, and a long thin rectangle for a cupboard against the wall.

check.q: Why does a plane in the sky look small?
check.why: Things that are far from us look smaller even though their real size does not change.

parts.md: On Makar Sankranti, Kittu the kite flew high above the town. Down below, houses looked like matchboxes, the pond looked like a blue coin and the cricket ground was a green rectangle.

"What do you see?" shouted Chinku the ant from the grass. "Squares and circles!" said Kittu. "No!" said Chinku, "I see a GIANT wall and a huge round tree trunk!" They were both looking at the same school.
When Kittu came down, Riya drew Kittu's top view on paper. "This is a map!" she laughed. Now everyone in the street could find the pond, the temple and the ground.

summary: Things look different from the top, front and side.
A top view is what a bird above would see.
The top view of a ball, glass or bucket is a circle; of a brick, a rectangle; of a dice, a square.
Hidden parts, like table legs, may not show in the top view.
Different objects can have the same top view.
The front and side views show different details of the same thing.
Left and right swap when you look from the opposite side.
A map is a simple top view of a place drawn smaller.
Maps use symbols, directions and paths.
Things far away look smaller.
practice: Draw the top view of a cup, a book and a ball.
Name two objects whose top view is a circle.
Draw an elephant from the front and from the side.
What can you see of a table from the top? What is hidden?
Draw a map of your classroom and mark the door and blackboard.
Draw a map from your house to the nearest shop with two landmarks.
Why does a tree look small from far away?
Your friend sits opposite you. Your water bottle is on your right. Where is it for your friend?

rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch2-fun-with-number.title: Fun with Numbers
rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch2-fun-with-number.subtitle: Hundreds, tens and ones — numbers up to 999 and beyond

sections.md:
How many people fit in your school bus? About 40. How many in a cinema hall? Maybe 300. How many in a big cricket stadium? Tens of thousands! Numbers help us tell **how many**.

In this chapter we play with big numbers up to **999** and a little beyond. We guess, count, compare and write them.

**Guessing game:** Look at a jar of toffees. Guess: 10? 50? 200? Then count them in groups of 10. Your guess becomes better with practice. Grown-ups guess too — a shopkeeper guesses how many kilograms of rice are left in a sack, a farmer guesses how many mangoes are on a tree.

Which is more: the number of hairs on your head or the number of students in your school? (Your hair wins — you have about one lakh hairs!)

check.q: Which is the best guess for the number of students in one Class 3 section?
check.why: A class usually has a few tens of students, so about 35 is sensible.

sections.md:
Counting one by one is slow. So we make **bundles**:

- 10 ones make **1 ten** (like 10 sticks tied together).
- 10 tens make **1 hundred** (10 bundles tied into one big bundle).

So 100 = 10 tens = 100 ones.

Skip counting helps: 10, 20, 30 … 100 and 100, 200, 300 … 900. In the book we count things like matchsticks, beads and notes — ₹100 notes, ₹10 notes and ₹1 coins are just like hundreds, tens and ones!

| Notes | Value |
|---|---|
| 3 notes of ₹100 | ₹300 |
| 4 notes of ₹10 | ₹40 |
| 5 coins of ₹1 | ₹5 |
| Total | **₹345** |

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='220' fill='#fff7ed'/><g fill='#f59e0b'><rect x='40' y='40' width='100' height='100' rx='4'/><rect x='160' y='40' width='100' height='100' rx='4'/><rect x='280' y='40' width='100' height='100' rx='4'/></g><g fill='#0ea5e9'><rect x='410' y='40' width='10' height='100'/><rect x='426' y='40' width='10' height='100'/><rect x='442' y='40' width='10' height='100'/><rect x='458' y='40' width='10' height='100'/></g><g fill='#22c55e'><rect x='500' y='120' width='10' height='10'/><rect x='516' y='120' width='10' height='10'/><rect x='532' y='120' width='10' height='10'/><rect x='548' y='120' width='10' height='10'/><rect x='564' y='120' width='10' height='10'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0.2;1' dur='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'><text x='210' y='175'>3 hundreds</text><text x='440' y='175'>4 tens</text><text x='540' y='175'>5 ones</text><text x='300' y='210' font-size='22' fill='#9a3412'>= 345</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Three hundred-blocks, four ten-rods and five ones make 345.
fig.alt: Base ten blocks showing 345

keyTerms: ones, tens, hundreds — the places of a number
place value — what a digit is worth because of its place

check.q: How many tens make one hundred?
check.why: Ten bundles of ten each give 100.

sections.md:
In **345**, each digit has a **place**:

| Hundreds | Tens | Ones |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 5 |

The 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, the 5 means 5. So 345 = 300 + 40 + 5. This is called the **expanded form**.

We write it in words as **three hundred forty-five**.

Watch out for **zero**: 405 has 4 hundreds, **0 tens** and 5 ones — four hundred five. 450 is four hundred fifty. The zero holds the place empty so the number does not change.

More examples:

- 607 = 600 + 0 + 7 → six hundred seven
- 290 = 200 + 90 + 0 → two hundred ninety
- 999 = 900 + 90 + 9 → nine hundred ninety-nine — the **greatest 3-digit number**
- 100 is the **smallest 3-digit number**.

check.q: What is the value of 7 in 573?
check.why: 7 is in the tens place, so it stands for 7 tens = 70.

sections.md:
Which is bigger, 438 or 483? Compare from the **left**:

1. Hundreds: 4 and 4 — same.
2. Tens: 3 and 8 — 8 is bigger.
3. So **483 > 438**.

We use **>** (greater than), **<** (less than) and **=** (equal). Remember: the open mouth of the sign faces the bigger number, like a hungry crocodile!

**Ordering:** Arrange 512, 125, 251, 215 from smallest to biggest: 125, 215, 251, 512.

**Making numbers:** With digits 3, 7, 1, the biggest number is 731 and the smallest is 137. Can you make all six numbers? (137, 173, 317, 371, 713, 731.)

check.q: Which is true?
check.why: Both have 6 hundreds, but 690 has 9 tens while 609 has 0 tens, so 609 is smaller.

sections.h: The Number Line, Before and After
sections.md:
Numbers live on a **number line**, in order. The number just **after** is 1 more; the number just **before** is 1 less.

- Before 400 comes 399; after 399 comes 400.
- After 509 comes 510.
- 10 more than 285 is 295; 100 more than 285 is 385.

Numbers **between** 197 and 203 are 198, 199, 200, 201, 202.

**Fun patterns:** Count by 100s from 50: 50, 150, 250, 350… Count backwards by 10s from 300: 300, 290, 280…

**Beyond 999:** after 999 comes **1000**, one thousand — 10 hundreds. It is the smallest 4-digit number.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='140' fill='#f0fdf4'/><line x1='30' y1='80' x2='570' y2='80' stroke='#14532d' stroke-width='3'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><g stroke='#14532d' stroke-width='2'><line x1='60' y1='72' x2='60' y2='88'/><line x1='150' y1='72' x2='150' y2='88'/><line x1='240' y1='72' x2='240' y2='88'/><line x1='330' y1='72' x2='330' y2='88'/><line x1='420' y1='72' x2='420' y2='88'/><line x1='510' y1='72' x2='510' y2='88'/></g><text x='60' y='110'>396</text><text x='150' y='110'>397</text><text x='240' y='110'>398</text><text x='330' y='110'>399</text><text x='420' y='110'>400</text><text x='510' y='110'>401</text></g><circle cx='60' cy='55' r='12' fill='#f97316'><animate attributeName='cx' values='60;150;240;330;420;510' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite' calcMode='discrete'/></circle><text x='300' y='30' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'>hop +1 each time</text></svg>
fig.caption: Hopping along the number line from 396 to 401.
fig.alt: Number line from 396 to 401 with a hopping dot

check.q: What comes just after 699?
check.why: 699 + 1 = 700 because 9 ones and 9 tens both roll over.

sections.md:
The chapter ends with games:

- **Who has more?** Two children draw digit cards and each makes the biggest number. Bigger number wins a point.
- **Snake and ladder of numbers:** jump +10 on ladders, −10 on snakes.
- **Guess my number:** "It has 2 hundreds, it is between 240 and 250, and its ones digit is 6." (246!)
- **Tambola:** call out numbers and mark them.

> Did you know? Our way of writing numbers with ten digits and a zero was developed in ancient India and travelled to the rest of the world through Arab traders.

check.q: I have 8 hundreds, 0 tens and 3 ones. Who am I?
check.why: 8 hundreds + 0 tens + 3 ones = 803.

workedExamples.q: Write 568 in expanded form and in words.
Riya has 2 notes of ₹100, 7 notes of ₹10 and 4 coins of ₹1. How much money?
Arrange 702, 270, 720, 207 from biggest to smallest.
Make the biggest and smallest 3-digit numbers from 5, 0, 9 (use each once).
steps: Smallest: zero cannot be first, so 5 first, then 0, then 9

parts.md: Dadaji's orchard had so many mangoes that Tara and Kabir argued: "A thousand!" "No, a hundred!" Dadaji laughed and gave them baskets that each held exactly ten mangoes.
They filled basket after basket. When ten baskets were full, they put them in a crate — one hundred mangoes. By evening they had 4 crates, 6 baskets and 3 loose mangoes.
"Four hundred sixty-three!" shouted Tara. "We were both wrong," grinned Kabir. Dadaji wrote 463 in chalk on the barn door, proud of his two mathematicians.

summary: 10 ones make a ten; 10 tens make a hundred; 10 hundreds make a thousand.
Each digit's value depends on its place: hundreds, tens or ones.
Expanded form: 345 = 300 + 40 + 5.
Zero keeps a place empty, as in 405.
100 is the smallest and 999 the greatest 3-digit number.
Compare numbers from the left-most digit.
Use > , < and = to compare.
On a number line, 'after' is one more and 'before' is one less.
₹100, ₹10 and ₹1 work like hundreds, tens and ones.
Good guesses (estimates) improve with practice.
practice: Write in words: 406, 760, 919.
Write in numbers: two hundred thirty-eight; five hundred five.
Write the expanded form of 872.
What is 10 more and 100 more than 467?
Write the numbers between 596 and 602.
Make the biggest and smallest numbers using 4, 1, 8.
How much money: 6 notes of ₹100, 3 notes of ₹10, 9 coins of ₹1?

rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch3-give-and-take.title: Give and Take
rd-school-c3-maths-a.ch3-give-and-take.subtitle: Adding and taking away — with carrying, borrowing and clever shortcuts

sections.h: Every Day We Give and Take
sections.md:
At the vegetable market, Amma gives the seller ₹100 and takes back change. In a cricket match, the team's score goes up with every run. When you share 20 laddoos with your cousins, the plate gets emptier. All this is **addition** (giving more, putting together) and **subtraction** (taking away, finding the difference).

Words that mean **add**: altogether, in all, total, more, plus, sum.
Words that mean **subtract**: left, remaining, fewer, how many more, difference, minus.

This chapter is about adding and subtracting numbers up to 999: first in your head, then on paper, and finally in word stories.

check.q: 'How many are left?' usually means you should…
check.why: 'Left' means something was taken away, so we subtract.

sections.h: Mental Maths: Adding Tens and Hundreds
sections.md:
Some sums are easy in your head:

- 30 + 40 = 70 (3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens)
- 300 + 400 = 700 (3 hundreds + 4 hundreds)
- 56 + 10 = 66 (tens digit goes up by 1)
- 56 + 20 = 76
- 245 + 100 = 345

**Making ten** is a great trick: 8 + 5 → 8 + 2 + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13. And 48 + 7 → 48 + 2 + 5 = 50 + 5 = 55.

**Adding by breaking:** 36 + 23 = (30 + 20) + (6 + 3) = 50 + 9 = 59.

On a number line, adding means **jumping forward** and subtracting means **jumping back**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='160' fill='#eff6ff'/><line x1='30' y1='110' x2='570' y2='110' stroke='#1e3a8a' stroke-width='3'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><text x='60' y='135'>36</text><text x='260' y='135'>46</text><text x='460' y='135'>56</text><text x='540' y='135'>59</text></g><g fill='none' stroke='#f97316' stroke-width='3'><path d='M60 105 Q160 30 260 105'/><path d='M260 105 Q360 30 460 105'/><path d='M460 105 Q500 70 540 105'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#9a3412' text-anchor='middle'><text x='160' y='50'>+10</text><text x='360' y='50'>+10</text><text x='500' y='70'>+3</text></g><circle r='9' fill='#22c55e'><animateMotion path='M60 105 Q160 30 260 105 Q360 30 460 105 Q500 70 540 105' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></svg>
fig.caption: 36 + 23: jump +10, +10, then +3 to land on 59.
fig.alt: Number line jumps from 36 to 59

check.q: What is 450 + 300?
check.why: 4 hundreds + 3 hundreds = 7 hundreds, and the 50 stays: 750.

sections.md:
For bigger numbers, write them one below the other — **ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds**.

Add 267 + 158:

| | H | T | O |
|---|---|---|---|
| carry | 1 | 1 | |
| | 2 | 6 | 7 |
| + | 1 | 5 | 8 |
| = | 4 | 2 | 5 |

1. Ones: 7 + 8 = 15. Write 5, **carry 1 ten**.
2. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12. Write 2, **carry 1 hundred**.
3. Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

Answer: **425**. Carrying works because 10 ones make a ten and 10 tens make a hundred — just like swapping ten ₹1 coins for a ₹10 note.

**Check by estimating:** 267 is about 270, 158 is about 160; 270 + 160 = 430. Our 425 is close, so it is sensible.

check.q: In 46 + 38, what do you carry after adding the ones?
check.why: 6 + 8 = 14 ones = 1 ten and 4 ones, so 1 ten is carried.

sections.md:
Subtract 432 − 178:

1. Ones: 2 − 8? Not possible. **Borrow** 1 ten from the tens: tens become 2, ones become 12. 12 − 8 = 4.
2. Tens: 2 − 7? Not possible. Borrow 1 hundred: hundreds become 3, tens become 12. 12 − 7 = 5.
3. Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2.

Answer: **254**.

**Check by adding back:** 254 + 178 = 432 ✔. Subtraction and addition are opposite: if 254 + 178 = 432, then 432 − 178 = 254 and 432 − 254 = 178.

**Zeros in the middle:** 503 − 127. The tens has 0, so first borrow 1 hundred → 4 hundreds and 10 tens, then borrow 1 ten → 9 tens and 13 ones. 13 − 7 = 6; 9 − 2 = 7; 4 − 1 = 3 → **376**.

check.why: Borrow: 12 − 7 = 5 ones, then 4 − 2 = 2 tens, so 25.

sections.md:
The book has stories from a fair, a shop and a school. Read carefully, find the numbers and decide: add or subtract?

- *A train has 345 passengers. At a station 128 get off and 76 get on.* First 345 − 128 = 217, then 217 + 76 = 293 passengers.
- *Raju has ₹500. He buys a cricket bat for ₹285.* 500 − 285 = ₹215 left.
- *In a school there are 238 girls and 249 boys.* Total = 487 children. How many more boys? 249 − 238 = 11.

**Make your own story:** Take a sum like 120 + 35 and write a story: *"A bakery made 120 buns in the morning and 35 in the evening…"* Swap stories with a friend and solve.

check.q: A box has 150 pencils; 64 are given away. How many are left?
check.why: 150 − 64: borrow to get 10 − 4 = 6 ones and 14 − 6 = 8 tens, giving 86.

sections.md:
**Magic triangle:** Put 1 to 6 on the corners and sides of a triangle so each side adds up to the same number (try 9 or 10!).

**Missing digits:** 4_6 + 2_3 = 739 → tens: _ + _ must give 3 tens. Try: 446 + 293 = 739 ✔ (6+3 = 9; 4+9 = 13, carry 1; 4+2+1 = 7).

**Patterns:** 100 − 1 = 99, 200 − 1 = 199, 300 − 1 = 299… What comes next?

**Ten more, ten less:** start at 555 and keep subtracting 10: 545, 535, 525… Only the tens digit changes.

> Did you know? Shopkeepers often count change by adding up: for ₹100 given for a ₹68 item they say "68… 70 (2) … 100 (30)" — that's ₹32 change, and it's subtraction done by adding!

check.q: A ₹73 item is paid with ₹100. Change is…

workedExamples.q: Subtract 600 − 248.
Meena scored 128 runs in a season and Sunil scored 95. How many more runs did Meena score?
A library had 475 books, got 168 new ones and lent out 210. How many are on the shelves?

parts.md: Chotu set up a balloon stall at the Diwali mela with 250 balloons. By lunchtime he had sold 137. "How many left?" asked his sister. Chotu borrowed and wrote: 250 − 137 = 113.
Uncle brought 90 more balloons. 113 + 90 = 203. In the evening children rushed in and Chotu sold 185 more. 203 − 185 = 18 balloons left.
"Sold altogether?" 137 + 185 = 322 balloons! Chotu tied the last 18 into a giant bunch and gave them to the little children for free. Give and take — that was the best sum of the day.

summary: Addition puts together; subtraction takes away or finds the difference.
Learn the key words: total, altogether, left, how many more.
Add tens and hundreds in your head; use 'making ten'.
On paper, line up ones, tens and hundreds.
Carry when a column adds to 10 or more.
Borrow when the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit.
With zeros, borrow from the next non-zero place.
Check subtraction by adding back.
Estimate first to see if the answer is sensible.
Read word problems slowly and choose the right operation.
practice: Subtract: 700 − 365 and 524 − 279.
Find the missing number: 245 + __ = 500.
A bus had 56 people; 19 got off and 23 got on. How many now?
Ravi has ₹350 and spends ₹178. How much is left?
Estimate 312 + 489 by rounding to tens, then find the exact answer.
Write a word story for 430 − 215 and solve it.
Fill digits: 3_7 + 1_5 = 512.

rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch4-long-and-short.title: Long and Short
rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch4-long-and-short.subtitle: From hand-spans to centimetres and metres — how we measure length

sections.md:
Long ago, a king wanted a new kurta. The tailor measured the king's arm with his **hand-spans** — 4 spans. Then he went home and cut the cloth using his apprentice's hand — but the apprentice had small hands, and the kurta sleeve came out too short! Why?

Because **hand-spans are not the same for everyone**. A child's span is smaller than a grown-up's. That is why people invented **standard units** like the **centimetre** and the **metre**, which are the same everywhere in the world.

In this chapter we measure with our body first, then with a ruler, and learn to **guess** lengths well.

check.q: Why did the sleeve come out short?
options: The apprentice's hand-span was smaller than the tailor's
check.why: Different people's spans are different, so the same 'number of spans' gives different lengths.

sections.md:
Before rulers, people measured with their body:

- **Hand-span** — from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, hand stretched out.
- **Finger width** — to measure small things like a pencil or eraser.
- **Foot** — walking heel-to-toe.
- **Pace / step** — measuring a room or a playground.
- **Arm length (cubit / haath)** — from elbow to the fingertip; shopkeepers in old markets measured cloth this way.

**Activity:** Measure your desk in hand-spans. Ask your friend and teacher to do the same. Record:

| Who | Desk length |
|---|---|
| Me | 6 spans |
| Friend | 7 spans |
| Teacher | 4½ spans |

Same desk, different answers! The person with the biggest span gets the smallest number.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='220' fill='#fff7ed'/><rect x='40' y='120' width='520' height='30' fill='#a16207' rx='4'/><text x='300' y='190' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>desk</text><g fill='#fdba74' stroke='#9a3412' stroke-width='2'><path d='M40 115 L60 70 L80 60 L100 70 L120 115 Z'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;80 0;160 0;240 0;320 0;400 0' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite' calcMode='discrete'/></path></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#7c2d12'><text x='60' y='40'>one span … two spans … three …</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Measuring a desk span by span.
fig.alt: A hand stepping along a desk

keyTerms: hand-span — stretched hand from thumb tip to little finger tip
standard unit — a unit that is the same for everyone

check.q: Who will get the smallest number of spans for the same table?
options: A person with a large hand
check.why: Bigger spans cover more length each time, so fewer of them are needed.

sections.md:
A **ruler** (scale) shows **centimetres**, written **cm**. 1 cm is about the width of your little finger nail.

**How to use a ruler correctly:**

1. Put the **0** mark exactly at one end of the object (not the edge of the ruler!).
2. Keep the ruler straight along the object.
3. Read the number at the other end.

Some lengths: an eraser is about 4 cm, a pencil about 15–18 cm, a matchbox about 5 cm, your school notebook about 25 cm long.

If the ruler is broken and starts at 3, you can still measure: if the object ends at 10, the length is 10 − 3 = **7 cm**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 180' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='180' fill='#f8fafc'/><rect x='40' y='90' width='520' height='50' fill='#fde68a' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='2'/><g stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='2'><line x1='60' y1='90' x2='60' y2='115'/><line x1='110' y1='90' x2='110' y2='115'/><line x1='160' y1='90' x2='160' y2='115'/><line x1='210' y1='90' x2='210' y2='115'/><line x1='260' y1='90' x2='260' y2='115'/><line x1='310' y1='90' x2='310' y2='115'/><line x1='360' y1='90' x2='360' y2='115'/><line x1='410' y1='90' x2='410' y2='115'/><line x1='460' y1='90' x2='460' y2='115'/><line x1='510' y1='90' x2='510' y2='115'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'><text x='60' y='132'>0</text><text x='110' y='132'>1</text><text x='160' y='132'>2</text><text x='210' y='132'>3</text><text x='260' y='132'>4</text><text x='310' y='132'>5</text><text x='360' y='132'>6</text><text x='410' y='132'>7</text><text x='460' y='132'>8</text><text x='510' y='132'>9</text></g><rect x='60' y='55' width='0' height='26' fill='#3b82f6' rx='4'><animate attributeName='width' values='0;250;250' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><text x='190' y='40' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle'>eraser grows to 5 cm</text></svg>
fig.caption: Start at 0 and read the number at the other end: 5 cm.
fig.alt: Ruler with a blue bar growing from 0 to 5

check.q: A stick starts at 2 cm and ends at 9 cm on a ruler. Its length is…
check.why: Length = end − start = 9 − 2 = 7 cm.

sections.md:
Centimetres are too small for a room or a road. For long things we use the **metre (m)**.

**1 metre = 100 centimetres.**

A metre is roughly the length from your nose to the tip of your stretched arm in a grown-up, or about the height of a Class 3 child up to the shoulder. Tailors use a soft **measuring tape**, carpenters use a folding rule, and builders use a long steel tape.

What would you measure in cm and what in m?

| cm | m |
|---|---|
| pencil | classroom |
| book | cricket pitch (about 20 m) |
| shoe | saree (about 5–6 m) |
| finger | height of a building |

Even longer distances, like Delhi to Agra, are measured in **kilometres** — you will learn these later.

check.q: How many centimetres make 1 metre?
check.why: A metre is defined as 100 centimetres.

sections.md:
Good mathematicians **estimate** first. Guess, then measure, and see how close you were.

| Thing | My guess | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| my pencil | 15 cm | 14 cm |
| blackboard | 2 m | 3 m |
| my jump | 1 m | 90 cm |

**Long jump activity:** Each child jumps from a line; mark where the heels land and measure with a tape. Who jumped farthest?

**Height chart:** Stick a long paper strip on the wall and mark everyone's height. Who is tallest? Who is shortest? Arrange in order.

**Thread puzzle:** Use a thread to measure a curved line (like a snake drawn on paper). Lay the thread along the curve, then straighten it on a ruler.

check.q: How can you measure a curved line?
options: Lay a thread along it, then measure the thread straight
check.why: A thread bends to follow the curve and then can be straightened along a ruler.

sections.md:
Comparing words:

- **long / longer / longest** for things lying down (snakes, ropes, trains).
- **tall / taller / tallest** for things standing (trees, buildings, people).
- **short / shorter / shortest**; also **wide** and **narrow**, **thick** and **thin**.

The giraffe is the **tallest** animal; a blue whale is the **longest**. The Statue of Unity in Gujarat is about 182 m tall — one of the tallest statues in the world.

> Did you know? The cricket pitch is 22 yards long, about 20 m — an old British unit still used today!

check.q: For a tree we say it is…
check.why: Things standing upright are compared by how tall they are.

workedExamples.q: A ribbon is 75 cm. Another is 48 cm. How much longer is the first?
Three pencils of 12 cm each are placed end to end. Total length?
Is 1 m more or less than 85 cm? By how much?

parts.md: Ishaan and Zoya each planted a sunflower. After a month, both said, "Mine is taller!" They measured in hand-spans: Ishaan's was 5 spans and Zoya's was 6. Zoya cheered.
But Ishaan's hands were bigger! Didi brought a measuring tape. Ishaan's sunflower was 95 cm; Zoya's was 90 cm.
"So spans can trick us," laughed Zoya. They made a height chart on the wall and measured every Sunday. By the end of summer both sunflowers had crossed 1 metre.

summary: Body measures (span, foot, pace, arm) differ from person to person.
Standard units are the same for everyone.
Small lengths are measured in centimetres (cm).
Long lengths are measured in metres (m); 1 m = 100 cm.
Place 0 of the ruler at one end of the object.
With a broken ruler, length = end reading − start reading.
Tailors use measuring tapes; builders use long tapes.
Estimate first, then measure to check.
Curved lines can be measured with a thread.
Use long, tall, short, wide and narrow to compare.
practice: Measure your notebook in hand-spans and in cm.
Why do two people get different span counts for the same table?
Which unit (cm or m) would you use for a door, a crayon, a road?
Draw a line 8 cm long.
A rope is 1 m. 35 cm is cut. How much is left?
Write three things longer than 1 metre in your house.
Measure a curved line with a thread and record it.
Arrange five friends from shortest to tallest.

rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch5-shapes-and-desi.title: Shapes and Designs
rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch5-shapes-and-desi.subtitle: Corners, sides, tangrams, tiles and rangoli — the maths of beautiful patterns

sections.md:
Look at a railway station: the clock is a **circle**, the tickets are **rectangles**, the signal boards may be **triangles**, the floor tiles are **squares** or **hexagons**. Shapes are hiding everywhere!

In this chapter we play with flat shapes. We count their **sides** and **corners**, sort them, fold them, cut them, fit them together, and use them to make **designs** like rangoli, tiles and borders.

**Find out:** Make a list of 10 things in your home and write their shapes — the roti (circle), the door (rectangle), a samosa (triangle-ish!), a carrom board (square).

check.q: The face of a wall clock is usually a…
check.why: A round clock face is a circle — it has no corners and no straight sides.

sections.md:
A flat shape made of straight lines has **sides** (the straight edges) and **corners** (where two sides meet).

| Shape | Sides | Corners |
|---|---|---|
| triangle | 3 | 3 |
| square | 4 (all equal) | 4 |
| rectangle | 4 (opposite ones equal) | 4 |
| pentagon | 5 | 5 |
| hexagon | 6 | 6 |
| circle | 0 straight sides | 0 |

Notice: for these shapes the number of sides **equals** the number of corners!

Some lines are **straight** and some are **curved**. A circle is made of one curved line. A shape like the moon on Eid (crescent) has two curved lines and two pointed corners.

**Corner game:** Blindfold a friend, give them a cut-out shape and ask them to count the corners by touch and guess the shape.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='200' fill='#faf5ff'/><g stroke='#581c87' stroke-width='3'><polygon points='70,150 120,50 170,150' fill='#f0abfc'/><rect x='210' y='60' width='90' height='90' fill='#a5b4fc'/><polygon points='390,50 440,85 420,150 360,150 340,85' fill='#86efac'/><polygon points='510,50 550,73 550,127 510,150 470,127 470,73' fill='#fcd34d'/></g><g fill='#dc2626'><circle cx='120' cy='50' r='6'><animate attributeName='r' values='4;9;4' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='70' cy='150' r='6'><animate attributeName='r' values='4;9;4' dur='1.2s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='170' cy='150' r='6'><animate attributeName='r' values='4;9;4' dur='1.2s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><text x='120' y='185'>triangle 3</text><text x='255' y='185'>square 4</text><text x='390' y='185'>pentagon 5</text><text x='510' y='185'>hexagon 6</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Count the corners: 3, 4, 5, 6. The triangle's corners blink.
fig.alt: Triangle, square, pentagon and hexagon with corner counts

keyTerms: side — a straight edge of a shape
corner — a point where two sides meet
curved line — a line that bends

check.q: How many corners does a hexagon have?
check.why: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners.

sections.h: Making Shapes by Folding and Cutting
sections.md:
Take a square sheet of paper.

- Fold it corner to corner → you get **two triangles**.
- Fold it edge to edge → you get **two rectangles**.
- Fold it twice corner to corner → **four small triangles**.

Cut a long rectangle into squares: a 2 × 6 strip gives three 2 × 2 squares.

**Matchstick shapes:** With 3 matchsticks make a triangle. With 4, a square. With 5 sticks, can you make two triangles that share a side? (Yes — a diamond shape with a stick down the middle.)

**Dot-paper drawing:** Join dots to draw shapes of different sizes. How many squares can you find in a 3 × 3 dot grid? (4 small ones + 1 big = 5.)

check.q: Folding a square paper along its diagonal (corner to corner) gives…
check.why: The diagonal cuts the square into two equal triangles.

sections.md:
A **tangram** is an old puzzle from China. A square is cut into **7 pieces** called **tans**:

- 2 large triangles,
- 1 medium triangle,
- 2 small triangles,
- 1 square,
- 1 parallelogram (a slanted rectangle).

Using all 7 pieces, without overlapping, you can make a cat, a boat, a running man, a house, a fish… thousands of figures!

**Try:** Use the two small triangles to make a square. Use them again to make a bigger triangle. Use the medium triangle and the two small ones to make a rectangle.

Tangrams teach that the **same pieces can make different shapes**, while the total space they cover (their area) stays the same.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#f0fdfa'/><g stroke='#134e4a' stroke-width='2' transform='translate(60 20)'><polygon points='0,0 200,0 100,100' fill='#f87171'/><polygon points='0,0 100,100 0,200' fill='#60a5fa'/><polygon points='200,0 200,100 150,50' fill='#fbbf24'/><polygon points='100,100 150,50 200,100 150,150' fill='#34d399'/><polygon points='150,150 200,100 200,200' fill='#a78bfa'/><polygon points='0,200 100,100 150,150 50,200' fill='#f472b6'/><polygon points='50,200 200,200 150,150 100,200' fill='#fb923c'/></g><g transform='translate(380 60)'><polygon points='0,100 100,0 100,100' fill='#f87171' stroke='#134e4a' stroke-width='2'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' values='0 50 50;360 50 50' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></polygon></g><text x='160' y='250' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'>7 tans make one square</text><text x='430' y='250' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'>turn a piece to fit</text></svg>
fig.caption: The seven tangram pieces fit into one square.
fig.alt: Seven coloured tangram pieces forming a square

check.q: How many pieces are in a tangram?
check.why: A tangram has 7 pieces: 5 triangles, 1 square and 1 parallelogram.

sections.md:
Look at floors, walls and footpaths. Tiles **fit together without gaps** — this is called **tiling**.

- **Squares** and **rectangles** tile easily (brick walls!).
- **Triangles** fit together point-up, point-down.
- **Hexagons** tile beautifully — that is how bees build honeycombs.
- **Circles cannot tile**: gaps always remain between them.

**Patterns** repeat: red-blue-red-blue; big-small-big-small; a shape turning a little each time. Find the rule, then continue the pattern.

Sarees, durries and temple walls have **border patterns** that repeat along a line, made by stamping one block again and again.

check.q: Which shape cannot cover a floor without gaps?
check.why: Round edges never fit snugly, so gaps are left between circles.

sections.md:
On Diwali, Pongal and Onam, families draw **rangoli**, **kolam** or **pookalam** at the doorstep. Many start with a grid of dots and loop lines around them. They often look the same on both sides of a middle line — this is **symmetry** (you will learn more in Class 4 and 5).

**Make an ink-blot butterfly:** put drops of paint on one half of a paper, fold it, press, open. Both halves match!

**Draw a kolam:** make a 3 × 3 grid of dots and draw curves around them without lifting your chalk.

> Did you know? Some kolam drawings follow such clever rules that computer scientists study them!

check.q: In an ink-blot butterfly, the two halves…
check.why: Folding presses the same paint pattern onto both halves, so they match like a mirror.

parts.md: Grandpa was laying a new floor on the verandah. He gave Anaya a box of tiles — squares, triangles, hexagons and round ones. "Make a floor with no holes," he said.
The squares fitted perfectly. The hexagons made a honeycomb. But the round tiles left little star-shaped gaps everywhere. "Where will the ants live?" giggled Anaya.
In the end she mixed squares and triangles into a pattern and drew a kolam in the centre. Grandpa clapped. "An engineer and an artist!"

summary: Shapes are everywhere around us.
Triangle 3, square 4, rectangle 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6 sides and corners.
A circle has no corners and no straight sides.
Lines can be straight or curved.
Folding a square gives triangles or rectangles.
A tangram has 7 pieces that make many figures.
Tiling means fitting shapes with no gaps.
Squares, rectangles, triangles and hexagons tile; circles do not.
Patterns repeat by a rule.
Rangoli and kolam often show matching halves (symmetry).
practice: Draw a triangle, a square and a hexagon and write their sides and corners.
Name three things shaped like a rectangle.
How many triangles do you get by folding a square along both diagonals?
Name the seven tangram pieces.
Make an animal with tangram pieces and draw it.
Why can't circles tile a floor?
Continue the pattern: ▲ ■ ▲ ■ ▲ __ __
Draw a simple kolam using a 3 × 3 dot grid.

rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch6-fun-with-give-a.title: Fun with Give and Take
rd-school-c3-maths-b.ch6-fun-with-give-a.subtitle: Adding and subtracting with games, money, number grids and clever tricks

sections.md:
In *Give and Take* we learnt to add and subtract on paper. Now we **play** with these skills. This chapter is full of games, puzzles and shopping stories — and lots of quick mental maths.

Imagine your class runs a school fair. You sell lemonade for ₹15 a glass and popcorn for ₹20 a packet. A friend buys one of each and pays ₹50. How much change? 15 + 20 = 35, and 50 − 35 = **₹15**. Every stall at the fair is a give-and-take puzzle!

check.q: One lemonade (₹15) and one popcorn (₹20) are paid for with ₹50. Change?
check.why: Cost is 15 + 20 = ₹35; change is 50 − 35 = ₹15.

sections.md:
**Adding 9:** add 10, then take away 1. 46 + 9 = 56 − 1 = 55.
**Adding 99:** add 100, then take 1. 234 + 99 = 333.
**Subtracting 9:** take 10, add 1. 72 − 9 = 62 + 1 = 63.
**Doubling:** 25 + 25 = 50, 35 + 35 = 70, 125 + 125 = 250.
**Near doubles:** 25 + 26 = double 25 + 1 = 51.
**Counting on:** to find 300 − 285, count up from 285 → 290 (5) → 300 (10) = 15.

**Adding three numbers:** look for pairs that make 10 or 100 first. 37 + 25 + 63 → 37 + 63 = 100, plus 25 = 125.

check.q: What is 58 + 9 using the trick?

sections.md:
Remember the steps:

**Adding 356 + 278**

1. Ones: 6 + 8 = 14 → write 4, carry 1.
2. Tens: 5 + 7 + 1 = 13 → write 3, carry 1.
3. Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

Answer **634**.

**Subtracting 634 − 278**

1. Ones: 4 − 8? Borrow → 14 − 8 = 6.
2. Tens: now 2; 2 − 7? Borrow → 12 − 7 = 5.
3. Hundreds: now 5; 5 − 2 = 3.

Answer **356** — back where we started! Adding and subtracting undo each other.

Always **estimate**: 356 ≈ 360, 278 ≈ 280, 360 + 280 = 640. Our 634 is close ✔.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='200' fill='#fefce8'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='22' text-anchor='middle'><rect x='60' y='70' width='120' height='60' rx='10' fill='#93c5fd'/><text x='120' y='108'>356</text><rect x='420' y='70' width='120' height='60' rx='10' fill='#86efac'/><text x='480' y='108'>634</text></g><g fill='none' stroke-width='4'><path d='M180 85 Q300 10 420 85' stroke='#f97316'/><path d='M420 115 Q300 190 180 115' stroke='#a855f7'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'><text x='300' y='40' fill='#c2410c'>+ 278</text><text x='300' y='180' fill='#7e22ce'>− 278</text></g><circle r='8' fill='#f97316'><animateMotion path='M180 85 Q300 10 420 85' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle r='8' fill='#a855f7'><animateMotion path='M420 115 Q300 190 180 115' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></svg>
fig.caption: Add 278 to go forward; subtract 278 to come back.
fig.alt: Two boxes 356 and 634 linked by +278 and −278 arrows

check.why: Subtraction undoes addition, so we get back 412.

sections.md:
Money is the best place to practise. Prices in a stationery shop:

| Item | Price |
|---|---|
| notebook | ₹35 |
| pencil box | ₹120 |
| crayons | ₹65 |
| geometry box | ₹185 |

- Notebook + crayons = 35 + 65 = **₹100**.
- Pencil box + geometry box = 120 + 185 = **₹305**.
- With ₹500, buy the geometry box: change = 500 − 185 = **₹315**.
- Which costs more, the pencil box or the crayons, and by how much? 120 − 65 = **₹55**.

**Play shop:** make paper notes of ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100 and coins of ₹1, ₹2, ₹5. One child is the shopkeeper, others are buyers. Count change carefully!

check.q: What is the cost of 2 notebooks at ₹35 each?

sections.md:
**Hundred grid:** in a 1–100 grid, moving one box **right** adds 1, moving one box **down** adds 10. From 34, go down 2 and right 3: 34 → 44 → 54 → 55 → 56 → 57.

**Magic square:** numbers 1 to 9 in a 3 × 3 grid so every row, column and diagonal adds to **15**:

| 2 | 7 | 6 |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 5 | 1 |
| 4 | 3 | 8 |

Check: 2 + 7 + 6 = 15, 9 + 5 + 1 = 15, 2 + 5 + 8 = 15 ✔.

**Number pyramids:** each brick is the sum of the two below it. Bottom 3, 5, 4 → middle 8, 9 → top 17.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 230' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='230' fill='#f0fdf4'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='22' text-anchor='middle' stroke='#14532d' stroke-width='2'><rect x='180' y='150' width='80' height='50' fill='#bbf7d0'/><rect x='260' y='150' width='80' height='50' fill='#bbf7d0'/><rect x='340' y='150' width='80' height='50' fill='#bbf7d0'/><rect x='220' y='100' width='80' height='50' fill='#fde68a'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='300' y='100' width='80' height='50' fill='#fde68a'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='260' y='50' width='80' height='50' fill='#fca5a5'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='22' text-anchor='middle'><text x='220' y='183'>3</text><text x='300' y='183'>5</text><text x='380' y='183'>4</text><text x='260' y='133'>8</text><text x='340' y='133'>9</text><text x='300' y='83'>17</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Number pyramid: each brick is the sum of the two beneath it.
fig.alt: Pyramid of bricks 3,5,4 then 8,9 then 17

check.q: In a hundred grid, moving one box down from 47 lands on…
check.why: Each row in a hundred grid is 10 more than the one above.

sections.md:
- **Race to 100:** two players take turns adding any number from 1 to 10. Whoever says 100 wins. (Secret: try to say 89!)
- **Dice difference:** roll two dice, make a 2-digit number each, and subtract. The bigger difference scores.
- **Snakes and subtraction:** each square tells you to add or subtract a number.
- **Bus game:** a bus starts with 40 passengers; cards say "8 get on", "15 get off". Who can keep track?
- **Estimation jar:** guess how many beans, then count in tens.

The more you play, the faster your mental maths becomes.

> Did you know? Many vegetable sellers who never went to school calculate bills in their heads faster than a calculator — through years of practice!

check.q: A bus has 40 people. 15 get off and 8 get on. How many now?

sections.h: Making and Solving Your Own Stories
sections.md:
A good word problem has numbers, a question, and words that tell you the operation.

*"Our class collected 245 old newspapers in week one and 178 in week two. We need 500 for the recycling prize. How many more?"*

Step 1: 245 + 178 = 423 collected.
Step 2: 500 − 423 = 77 more needed.

Now write your own two-step story about a cricket match, a train journey or a Diwali sweet shop, and swap it with a friend.

check.q: 245 + 178 equals…

workedExamples.q: Find 499 + 236 quickly.
A shopkeeper had 350 eggs. He sold 128 on Monday and 97 on Tuesday. How many are left?
Fill the missing number: 573 − __ = 288.

parts.md: Neel's mother ran a tiffin shop near the railway station. One Saturday she let Neel handle the cash box. A passenger bought dosa for ₹45 and paid ₹100. Neel counted up: 45 → 50 (₹5) → 100 (₹50). "₹55 change, sir!"
Then a whole group from the train arrived: 6 idlis at ₹10 each, 3 vadas at ₹15 each. Neel added 60 + 45 = ₹105. They paid ₹200. "₹95 change!"
At closing time the box had ₹1,250. They had started with ₹300, so they earned ₹950 that day. "You're my lucky accountant," said Amma, and gave Neel the last crispy dosa.

summary: Mental tricks: +9 is +10−1; +99 is +100−1.
Find pairs making 10 or 100 when adding three numbers.
Count up to find a difference or change.
Carry and borrow carefully in 3-digit sums.
Addition and subtraction undo each other.
Estimate to check your answer.
Money problems use the same addition and subtraction.
In a hundred grid, right adds 1 and down adds 10.
Magic squares and number pyramids are fun sum puzzles.
Two-step stories need two operations in the right order.
practice: Work out mentally: 67 + 9, 145 + 99, 83 − 9.
You have ₹200 and buy items of ₹65 and ₹78. How much is left?
Make a number pyramid with bottom row 6, 2, 7.
In a hundred grid, what number is 3 down and 2 right of 21?
Write and solve a two-step story about a cricket match.
Check that every row of the magic square 2-7-6 / 9-5-1 / 4-3-8 adds to 15.

rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch3-a-day-with-nandu.title: A Day with Nandu
rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch3-a-day-with-nandu.subtitle: Spend one whole day inside an elephant family — who leads, what they eat, and why they love mud

sections.md:
Imagine you wake up in a forest at dawn. The grass is wet. Somewhere close by, a branch cracks — *snap!* — and a huge grey shape walks out of the trees. Then another. Then a tiny one, wobbling between their legs. That tiny one is **Nandu**, a baby elephant about three months old.

Nandu does not live alone. He lives in a **herd** — a big family group. In this read we will follow Nandu for one whole day and find out:

- who is in an elephant herd and who is the boss,
- what elephants eat and how much,
- how elephants keep cool and clean,
- how they sleep, and
- what happens when young male elephants grow up.

A baby elephant is already heavy when it is born — heavier than most grown-up people! Even so, Nandu needs his mother and his aunts all the time. He drinks his mother's milk and stays close to her side.

> **Did you know?** An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together. It can smell, breathe, drink, pick up a single peanut, or pull down a whole branch.

sections.h: The herd: a family of mothers, aunts and children
sections.md:
Nandu's herd has about **ten to twelve elephants**. Look carefully and you will notice something interesting: almost all the grown-ups are **females** — his mother, his grandmother, his aunts and older sisters and cousins. The young ones in the herd are both boys and girls.

Who leads the herd? The **oldest female elephant**. She is often Nandu's grandmother. She has lived for many years, so she remembers:

- where the water holes are in the hot summer,
- which paths are safe,
- where the best food grows in each season.

When she starts walking, everyone follows. When she senses danger, she rumbles a warning and the whole herd gathers the babies into the middle, with the big elephants standing around them like a wall.

In many human families too, grandparents guide everybody with their experience. Elephants show us that the wisdom of elders matters.

> **Think:** Who is the eldest member of your family? What do they know that nobody else knows?
