fig.alt: Three adult elephants and a baby walking in a line

check.q: Who leads an elephant herd?
check.why: The oldest female leads because she has the most experience and remembers where food, water and safe paths are.

sections.h: Breakfast, lunch and dinner — all day long!
sections.md:
What does a herd do most of the day? **Eat!** Elephants are **herbivores** — they eat only plants: grass, leaves, twigs, bark, bamboo, fruits like wood apple and jackfruit, and sugarcane if they find a field.

An adult elephant eats around **100 kilograms of leaves and twigs in a day**. That is like eating about 400 plates of rice every day! And it drinks a lot of water too.

Why so much? Plants do not give much energy per mouthful, and an elephant's body is enormous. So elephants spend most of their waking hours — morning, afternoon, even part of the night — pulling, chewing and walking to the next patch of food.

Nandu is still learning. He tries to copy the grown-ups with his little trunk, but mostly he drinks milk. Slowly he will learn which plants are tasty and which are not.

| Elephant fact | Roughly |
|---|---|
| Food per day (adult) | about 100 kg of leaves and twigs |
| Sleep per day | only 2–4 hours |
| Herd size | about 10–12 |
| Age when males leave | about 14–15 years |

check.q: Elephants are herbivores. This means they eat —
check.why: Herbivores like elephants eat only plant food such as grass, leaves, twigs and fruits.

sections.md:
In the afternoon the sun becomes hot. Nandu's herd walks to a muddy pool. What fun! The elephants splash, roll and throw mud and water over their backs with their trunks. Nandu slips and slides and comes up looking like a chocolate bar.

This is not just play. An elephant's skin can get hurt by strong sun, and insects bite it. A coat of **mud**:

- keeps the body **cool** in the heat,
- acts like **sunscreen**,
- protects the skin from **insects**.

Elephants also love water. They drink by sucking water into the trunk and then squirting it into the mouth. They can take a shower by spraying water over themselves. Many elephants are good swimmers and can cross rivers, holding their trunks up like a snorkel.

> **Did you know?** Elephants flap their big ears like fans. Blood flowing through the thin ears cools down, which helps cool the whole body.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff3c4'/><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='35' fill='#ffb300'><animate attributeName='r' values='33;38;33' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><ellipse cx='300' cy='255' rx='260' ry='35' fill='#7a5230'/><ellipse cx='280' cy='190' rx='90' ry='60' fill='#8a8f98'/><circle cx='370' cy='160' r='42' fill='#8a8f98'/><path d='M395 175 Q430 120 410 70' stroke='#8a8f98' stroke-width='18' fill='none' stroke-linecap='round'/><g fill='#6b4422'><circle cx='410' cy='60' r='7'><animate attributeName='cy' values='60;20;140;200' dur='1.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='cx' values='410;380;320;290' dur='1.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='405' cy='65' r='5'><animate attributeName='cy' values='65;30;150;205' dur='1.6s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='cx' values='405;360;300;260' dur='1.6s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='412' cy='62' r='6'><animate attributeName='cy' values='62;25;145;200' dur='1.6s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='cx' values='412;390;340;310' dur='1.6s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><text x='30' y='40' font-size='18' fill='#5a3a10'>Mud = coolness + sunscreen + no insect bites</text></svg>
fig.caption: An elephant sprays mud over its back with its trunk to stay cool and protected.
fig.alt: Elephant spraying mud drops from its trunk under the hot sun

keyTerms: Herd — a family group of animals living together
Herbivore — an animal that eats only plants
Trunk — the elephant's long nose and upper lip

sections.md:
Elephants are always 'chatting'. They trumpet loudly when excited or angry, and they make deep **rumbling** sounds — some so low that we humans cannot hear them, yet other elephants far away can! They also touch each other with their trunks to say 'I am here' or 'Are you OK?'.

And sleep? Surprise — elephants sleep only about **two to four hours** a day. Adults often sleep **standing up**, leaning slightly. Babies like Nandu sometimes lie down on their side, while the grown-ups keep watch.

Compare this with you: children your age need about 9–11 hours of sleep! Elephants need so many hours for eating that there is little time left for sleeping.

check.q: About how many hours does an elephant sleep in a day?
check.why: Elephants spend most of the day eating and moving, so they sleep only about two to four hours.

sections.md:
What will happen to Nandu when he grows up? Male elephants stay with the herd until they are about **14 or 15 years old**. Then they leave. Some live alone; others join small groups of other young males. Female elephants usually stay in their family herd for their whole lives, helping raise the babies that are born later.

So one day, Nandu will say goodbye to his grandmother and mother and walk off into the forest on his own path. He will remember the paths and water holes his family taught him.

Elephants need very large forests to roam. When forests are cut, elephants lose their homes and food, and may wander into farms and villages. People and elephants then both get hurt. Protecting forests and elephant **corridors** (forest paths connecting one forest to another) helps everyone. The elephant is India's **National Heritage Animal**.

check.q: At about what age do male elephants leave the herd?
check.why: Young male elephants leave their family herd at about 14 to 15 years and live alone or with other males.

sections.h: Elephants and you: compare and think
sections.md:
Let us compare an elephant family with a human family.

- In both, babies need care from grown-ups for many years.
- In both, elders share what they know.
- In elephant herds, the females stay together; in human families, it differs from family to family.

Next time you see an elephant at a temple, a zoo or on television, look for these things: its trunk, its flapping ears, its thick skin with wrinkles, its tusks (only some elephants have big tusks — in Asian elephants, mostly males).

Sadly, some people kill elephants for their **ivory tusks**. This is against the law in India. Elephants are protected so that babies like Nandu can grow up safe.

parts.md: The sun peeped over the hills. Nandu opened one eye. His mother was already pulling down a bamboo shoot, crunch, crunch. 'Wake up, little one,' rumbled Grandmother Dadi Haathi. 'We walk to the river today.' Nandu yawned, stretched his tiny trunk, and tripped over it. His cousin Chhoti giggled.

All morning the herd walked and munched. Nandu tried to pull a leaf like his aunt, but the branch sprang back and tickled his nose. *Aaachoo!* Grandmother stopped suddenly and lifted her trunk to sniff. 'Tiger smell,' she rumbled softly. At once the big elephants made a circle, with Nandu and Chhoti in the middle. After a while the smell faded and the herd moved on, calmer but watchful.

By afternoon the sun was blazing. Then — the river! The elephants rushed in with joyful trumpets. Mother sprayed cool water on Nandu. Chhoti rolled in the mud and Nandu rolled too, until only his eyes shone. 'Mud keeps away the biting flies,' said Mother. That night, under the stars, Nandu slept curled against her legs while Grandmother stood watch. It had been the best day ever.

summary: Elephants live in family groups called herds of about 10–12 members.
Adults in a herd are mostly females; young ones are both male and female.
The oldest female leads the herd because she has the most experience.
Elephants are herbivores: they eat grass, leaves, twigs, bark and fruit.
An adult elephant eats about 100 kg of leaves and twigs a day.
They spend most of the day eating.
Mud baths keep elephants cool, protect skin from sun and insects.
Elephants sleep only 2–4 hours a day, often standing.
Male elephants leave the herd at about 14–15 years.
The trunk is a nose and upper lip joined; it is used to smell, drink, lift and touch.
Forests and elephant corridors must be protected so elephants keep their homes.

glossary.d: A group of animals that live and move together
An animal that eats only plants
The hard material of elephant tusks
A strip of forest connecting two forests so animals can move

rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch4-the-story-of-amri.title: The Story of Amrita
rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch4-the-story-of-amri.subtitle: A village in the desert that loved its trees more than anything — and what we can learn from it

sections.h: A green village in a sandy land
sections.md:
Picture the Thar desert in Rajasthan: hot sand, strong winds, very little rain. Now picture a village in the middle of it that is *green* — full of **khejri trees**, with deer called blackbuck and chinkara walking fearlessly near the houses. Strange? This is the village of **Khejadli** near Jodhpur, about 300 years ago.

The people of Khejadli belonged to the **Bishnoi** community. Their elders, following the teachings of Guru Jambheshwar, had given them rules for life. Two of the most important were:

- **Do not cut green trees.**
- **Do not harm animals.**

They took only dry, fallen wood for cooking. They shared water and grain with animals. And because of this care, their village stayed cooler, greener and full of life even in the desert.

> **Think:** Is there an old tree near your home or school? Who planted it? How old do you think it is?

Amrita Devi, a woman of the village, used to say that trees and people are friends who help each other. Let us see how true that is. Trees give us:

| What trees give | Examples |
|---|---|
| Food | fruits, nuts, the khejri's beans (sangri) |
| Shade and coolness | a resting place in the hot sun |
| Fodder | leaves for goats, camels and cows |
| Medicine | neem, amla, tulsi plants |
| Wood | for fuel, furniture, houses (from dry or planted trees) |
| Clean air | trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen |
| Homes | for birds, squirrels, insects |

Tree roots hold the soil so that wind and rain do not blow or wash it away. In a desert, this is very important — without trees the sand spreads and fields turn barren.

> **Did you know?** The khejri is the state tree of Rajasthan. Its roots go very deep to find water, so it stays green even in drought.

check.q: How do tree roots help in a desert?
options: They hold the soil so wind cannot blow it away
They drink all the water so nothing else grows
check.why: Roots bind the soil together, so wind and rain cannot carry it away and fields stay fertile.

sections.md:
Before we hear Amrita's story, let us look around our own homes. Almost everything we use on a normal day has come from a plant in some way.

**Activity — the plant hunt:** Walk around your house with a notebook. Write down every thing that comes from a plant. Here is a start:

- **In the kitchen:** rice, wheat flour, dal, vegetables, fruits, sugar (from sugarcane), tea leaves, spices like jeera and haldi, cooking oil (from mustard, groundnut or coconut).
- **In the cupboard:** cotton clothes, a jute bag, a wooden comb.
- **In the study corner:** pencils, notebooks and books (paper is made from wood pulp), a wooden table.
- **In the bathroom:** a neem twig some grandparents use as a toothbrush, coconut oil for hair.
- **In the medicine box:** many medicines are made from plant parts; at home, people use tulsi and ginger for coughs.

Now think the other way round: which things in your house do *not* come from plants? A steel plate, a plastic bucket, a glass bottle... but even here, the wooden handle of a steel pan is from a tree!

> **Talk about it:** If all the trees near you disappeared, which three things would you miss first? Why?

check.q: Which of these does NOT come directly from a plant?
check.why: Steel is made from iron ore dug out of the ground, while cotton, oil and paper all come from plants.

sections.h: The day the king's men came
sections.md:
One day, the Maharaja of Jodhpur needed a lot of wood for building a new palace. His men were told: *go to Khejadli — it has plenty of trees.* They arrived with axes.

When **Amrita Devi** saw them ready to cut the khejri trees, she ran out and hugged a tree. She told them they would have to cut her first. Her three daughters did the same. Then villagers from Khejadli and nearby villages came, one after another, each hugging a tree to protect it.

The king's men did not stop. Sadly, many people lost their lives that day — the story tells that **363 people** gave their lives to protect the trees. This is a sad and serious part of history, and people remember them with great respect.

When the Maharaja heard what had happened, he was deeply sorry. He came to the village and ordered that **no green tree would ever be cut and no animal hunted** in Bishnoi villages. That rule was followed for a very long time.

> **Think:** Amrita Devi chose to stand up for something she believed was right, even though it was dangerous. What gives a person that kind of courage?

check.q: Why did the Maharaja's men come to Khejadli?
options: To collect wood for the king's new palace
check.why: The king needed wood for building a palace, so his men came to cut the village's khejri trees.

sections.md:
Amrita Devi's courage was not forgotten. The Government of India gives the **Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award** to people who do brave work to protect animals and nature. Every year, people gather at Khejadli to remember the 363 tree-savers.

Many years later, in the 1970s, villagers in the Himalayan hills (in today's Uttarakhand) also hugged trees to stop them being cut. This was called the **Chipko movement** — 'chipko' means 'to stick' or 'to hug'. Ordinary people, especially women, again showed that forests belong to the people who live with them.

Even today the Bishnoi people are known for protecting blackbuck and chinkara. In their villages the deer roam safely.

items.what: Amrita Devi and the villagers of Khejadli protect their khejri trees
The Maharaja orders no green tree be cut in Bishnoi villages
Chipko movement: villagers in the Himalayas hug trees to save forests
Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award honours nature protectors

fig.caption: How the idea of protecting trees has travelled through time.

check.q: What does the word 'chipko' mean?
check.why: In the Chipko movement people hugged (stuck to) trees so they could not be cut.

sections.md:
The Bishnoi are not the only people in India who look after trees as a group. In many parts of the country there are **sacred groves** — patches of forest that a village protects for its local god or goddess. Nobody cuts trees there; often even dry leaves are left on the ground. Such groves are called *devrai* in Maharashtra, *kavu* in Kerala and *orans* in Rajasthan. Because they have been protected for hundreds of years, they are full of old trees, birds, medicinal plants and springs of water.

Many families also have a tree they feel close to — a peepal at the village square where elders sit, a neem in the courtyard, a mango tree planted when a grandparent was born.

**Activity — know your trees:**
1. Find three trees near your home or school. Draw each leaf and write the tree's name (ask an adult if you do not know).
2. Hug the trunk. Can your arms reach around it? How many children are needed to circle the biggest one? A thick trunk usually means an old tree.
3. Ask an elder how long the tree has been there, and who looks after it.
4. Look carefully: which birds, insects or squirrels live on it?
keyTerms: Sacred grove — a forest patch protected by a community for religious or cultural reasons
Trunk — the thick main stem of a tree

check.q: What is a sacred grove?
options: A forest patch protected by a village for generations
check.why: Villagers protect sacred groves for their deity, so the trees and animals there stay safe for a very long time.

sections.md:
The Bishnoi rule said: *do not harm animals*. Why is that so important?

All living things are connected. Birds eat insects and spread seeds. Deer eat grass and are food for wild cats. Bees help flowers make fruits. If one living thing disappears, others suffer too.

Around you, you can help animals by:

- keeping a bowl of water for birds in summer,
- not throwing stones at dogs, cats or birds,
- not disturbing nests,
- not buying things made from wild animals.

Some animals, like the **blackbuck**, **tiger** and **Great Indian Bustard**, are in danger because their homes are being destroyed. Laws in India now protect them.
keyTerms: Bishnoi — a community in Rajasthan known for protecting trees and animals
Khejri — a desert tree, state tree of Rajasthan
Chipko — a movement where people hugged trees to save them

sections.md:
You do not need to be a hero in a story to protect nature. Small things matter:

1. **Plant a tree** on your birthday and look after it.
2. **Use both sides of paper** — paper comes from trees.
3. **Save water** for plants and animals.
4. **Say no to waste** — reuse bags and bottles.
5. **Talk** — tell your family the story of Amrita Devi.

Ask the elders in your family: *Do you remember a big tree that was cut near our home? What happened to the birds that lived in it?* You will be surprised by their stories.

> **Did you know?** A single big tree can be home to dozens of kinds of insects, birds and small animals — it is like a whole apartment building!

check.q: Which of these helps save trees?
options: Using only one side of paper
Using both sides of paper and recycling
check.why: Paper is made from trees, so using less and recycling it means fewer trees are cut.

parts.md: In a corner of Khejadli stands an old khejri tree. If trees could talk, this one would tell you about a girl who used to sit in its shade, sharing her rotis with a baby deer. The girl grew up, and her children grew up, and the tree grew taller every monsoon.

'One hot morning,' the tree would say, 'I heard the clink of axes. A woman ran to me and wrapped her arms around my trunk. Her heart was beating fast, but her voice was steady. Others came, and soon every tree had a friend holding it.' The tree would go quiet for a moment, remembering the sadness of that day.

'But after that day,' the tree would whisper, 'no axe came again. Children planted my seeds. The deer came back. Even now, when the wind blows through my leaves, I am saying thank you.' Next time you sit under a tree, listen. Perhaps it is saying thank you to you too.

summary: Khejadli is a Bishnoi village near Jodhpur in Rajasthan.
Bishnoi people follow rules to not cut green trees and not harm animals.
Trees give food, fodder, shade, medicine, wood, clean air and homes for animals.
Tree roots hold soil and stop it from blowing or washing away.
Many things in our homes — food, cloth, paper, furniture — come from plants.
About 300 years ago, the king's men came to cut trees for a palace.
Amrita Devi and her daughters hugged trees to protect them.
Many villagers — 363 people — gave their lives to protect the trees.
The king then ordered that no green trees be cut in Bishnoi villages.
The Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award honours those who protect wildlife.
The Chipko movement of the 1970s also saved trees by hugging them.
Sacred groves across India are forests protected by villages.
We can help by planting trees, saving paper and caring for animals.

glossary.d: A community that follows Guru Jambheshwar's teachings of protecting nature
Food for farm animals like leaves and grass
A hardy desert tree with deep roots
Animals and plants living in the wild
A patch of forest protected by a community

rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch5-anita-and-the-hon.title: Anita and the Honeybees
rd-school-c4-evs-a.ch5-anita-and-the-hon.subtitle: A girl from Bihar who learnt to keep bees, and a scientist who spent his life watching birds

sections.md:
Have you ever seen a bee land on a flower, wiggle about, and fly away? Where is it going? What is it carrying? And how does a jar of golden **honey** end up in your kitchen?

In a village called **Bochaha** in Muzaffarpur district of **Bihar**, a girl named **Anita Kushwaha** became curious about the same questions. Her family was poor, and she had to work hard. But she loved learning. She went to school, kept studying, and one day she decided to learn **beekeeping** — the work of keeping honeybees in boxes and collecting their honey.

Anita watched the bees carefully. She learnt how they live, what they eat and how they make honey. Soon she was selling honey and earning money for her family and her studies. People in her village and even far away began to know her as the 'honey girl'.

> **Did you know?** Muzaffarpur is famous for **litchi**. Bees that visit litchi flowers make a special sweet-smelling litchi honey!

Anita's story is special for one more reason. In many villages, girls from poor families were (and sometimes still are) kept at home to look after younger children, graze goats or help in the fields. Anita too had to work as a child. But she kept going to school and later went on to college, studying while she earned.

She learnt beekeeping from people who already knew it, and from a training programme. She started with only a few boxes of bees. As she sold honey, she bought more boxes. Slowly her small work became a real business, and she also helped other girls and women in her area to begin keeping bees.

**What can we learn from her?**
- Learning does not stop at school — you can learn a skill by watching and asking.
- A small beginning, done patiently, can grow big.
- Earning your own money gives you confidence to make choices for your life.

> **Talk about it:** Do you know any child who works as well as studies? What kind of work do they do? Do you think every child should get a chance to study? Why?

check.q: How did Anita's honey business grow?
options: She got hundreds of boxes free on day one
She started small and bought more boxes from what she earned
She took honey from wild hives only
check.why: Anita began with a few boxes and used her earnings to slowly add more, growing her business step by step.

sections.h: Inside a beehive: a city of bees
sections.md:
A beehive is like a busy city. Thousands of bees live together, and each has a job. There are three kinds of bees:

| Bee | How many | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Queen bee** | only one in a hive | lays eggs — thousands of them! |
| **Worker bees** | thousands | collect nectar and pollen, make honey and wax, clean, guard, look after babies |
| **Drones** | a few hundred | male bees; they mate with the queen |

The worker bees are all females. They are the smallest but do almost all the work. The queen is the biggest bee in the hive.

The hive is made of **wax**, which the worker bees make from their own bodies. They shape it into little six-sided rooms called **cells**. Some cells store honey, some store pollen, and in some the queen lays eggs.

fig.alt: Hexagon honeycomb and a flying bee

check.q: Which bee lays eggs in the hive?
check.why: There is only one queen in a hive and her job is to lay eggs.

sections.md:
How do bees make honey? Follow a worker bee:

1. She flies to a flower and sucks up sweet juice called **nectar** with her long tongue.
2. She stores it in a special 'honey stomach' and also collects yellow **pollen** dust on her legs.
3. Back at the hive, she passes the nectar to other bees. They chew it and mix it with juices from their bodies.
4. They put it in wax cells and fan it with their wings to dry out the extra water.
5. The nectar slowly turns thick and sweet — **honey**! Then they seal the cell with wax.

While moving from flower to flower, bees carry pollen with them. This helps flowers make **fruits and seeds**. So bees do not just make honey — they help us get mangoes, apples, litchis and many vegetables.

**How do bees tell each other where flowers are?** They **dance**! A bee that finds lots of flowers comes back and does a special waggle dance. The way she moves tells the others which direction to go and how far.

check.q: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
check.why: Bees suck up sweet nectar from flowers and slowly turn it into honey in the hive.

sections.md:
Beekeepers like Anita keep bees in wooden boxes with frames inside. The bees build their comb on the frames. When the comb is full of honey, the beekeeper lifts the frame out, gently brushes off the bees, and spins out the honey. She also leaves enough honey for the bees.

Beekeepers wear a net over their face and gloves, and use a little smoke to calm the bees. Bees sting only when they feel their hive is in danger.

We get two useful things from bees:

- **Honey** — food, and used in many home remedies.
- **Wax** — used for candles, polish and creams.

Bees are in danger today because of too many pesticides (poison sprays) and fewer flowering plants. Without bees many crops would fail!
keyTerms: Nectar — sweet juice inside flowers
Pollen — yellow powder in flowers that helps make seeds
Beekeeping — keeping bees in boxes to get honey and wax
Hive — the home of bees

sections.md:
Bees are not the only animals that live in big families. Look around:

| Animal | How they live together |
|---|---|
| **Ants** | a colony with a queen and many workers; they march in a line, share food and build nests underground |
| **Elephants** | herds led by the oldest female; aunts and sisters help care for babies |
| **Monkeys** | troops that groom each other and warn about danger |
| **Birds** like parakeets, crows and sparrows | flocks that feed and roost together |

Living in a group helps animals find food, protect babies and stay safe from enemies. Some animals, like the tiger or the leopard, mostly live **alone**.

**Activity:** Put a small grain of sugar near an ant line. Watch from a distance. How long does it take for the first ant to find it? Do more ants come later? How do you think they 'told' each other?

> **Did you know?** Ants leave an invisible smell-trail on the ground so other ants can follow the path to food!

check.q: Who leads an elephant herd?
check.why: An elephant herd is led by the oldest and most experienced female, who remembers where food and water are.

sections.h: Salim Ali, the Birdman of India
sections.md:
Bees are not the only creatures that people love to watch. **Salim Ali** spent his whole life watching **birds**. As a boy, he once shot a sparrow with a toy gun and noticed it had an unusual yellow patch. He wanted to know what kind of bird it was — and that curiosity turned into a lifetime of study. Later he wrote the story of his life in a book called *The Fall of a Sparrow*.

He travelled across India, watching birds, writing down their colours, nests, calls, and food. He wrote famous books about Indian birds. He is called the **Birdman of India**. He helped protect places where birds live, like the **Bharatpur bird sanctuary** (Keoladeo National Park) in Rajasthan, where thousands of birds come every winter, some from very cold faraway lands like Siberia.

To watch birds like Salim Ali, you need: **patience**, a **notebook**, and if possible, **binoculars** — a tool that makes far things look near.

check.q: Who is called the Birdman of India?
check.why: Salim Ali spent his life studying Indian birds and helped protect bird sanctuaries.

sections.md:
You can watch nature just like Anita and Salim Ali. Try this:

- Sit quietly near a garden or tree for 15 minutes.
- Note down every bird, insect or animal you see.
- Draw one of them. What colour is it? What does it eat? Where does it go?

| What I saw | Colour | What it was doing |
|---|---|---|
| e.g. Mynah | brown, yellow beak | hopping on grass, eating insects |

Which birds come to your area only in winter? Ask your grandparents whether they saw more sparrows when they were young. Many people say house sparrows have become fewer in cities — you could keep a small water bowl and some grain to welcome them back.

check.q: Which tool helps us see faraway birds clearly?
check.why: Binoculars make distant objects look closer, so birdwatchers can see birds without disturbing them.

parts.md: The litchi trees were white with flowers. Anita stood still as a statue, watching a bee climb into a blossom. 'Where will you take that nectar?' she whispered. The bee buzzed off toward the wooden boxes the village uncle kept behind his field.

'Can I learn?' she asked him. The uncle smiled and handed her a net for her face. 'Move slowly. Bees like calm people.' For weeks, Anita came after school. She learnt to spot the big queen, the busy workers, the lazy-looking drones.

One day she lifted a frame heavy with golden comb. Her hands shook — but not a single bee stung her. That evening, she poured her very first jar of honey and held it up to the setting sun. It glowed like a little lamp. 'This,' she told her mother, 'will pay for my books.'

summary: Anita Kushwaha from Bochaha, Muzaffarpur (Bihar), learnt beekeeping and kept studying.
She started small and grew her honey business with what she earned.
Bees live together in a hive made of wax cells.
A hive has one queen (lays eggs), many worker bees and some drones.
Worker bees collect nectar and pollen, make honey and wax, and guard the hive.
Bees turn nectar into honey and dance to show where flowers are.
Bees carry pollen and help plants make fruits and seeds.
We get honey and wax from bees.
Ants, elephants, monkeys and many birds also live in groups.
Salim Ali, the Birdman of India, studied birds all his life.
Bharatpur (Keoladeo) is a famous bird sanctuary in Rajasthan.
Patience, a notebook and binoculars help in watching birds.

glossary.d: The only egg-laying bee in a hive
A male bee
A large group of animals like ants living together
A protected place where animals and birds live safely
An instrument to see faraway things clearly

How did Anita manage to study as well as earn?

How do bees make honey? Write the steps.
How do bees tell other bees where flowers are?
Name two things we get from bees.
Name three animals that live in groups and one that lives alone.
Who was Salim Ali? Why is he famous?
Name a bird sanctuary in Rajasthan.

rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch10-hu-tu-tu.title: Hu Tu Tu, Hu Tu Tu
rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch10-hu-tu-tu.subtitle: Kabaddi, a single breath, and why every girl and boy deserves a place on the field

sections.md:
Take a deep breath. Now walk across the room saying *'kabaddi-kabaddi-kabaddi'* without stopping for breath. How far did you get? That is the heart of one of India's oldest games — **kabaddi**, also called **hu-tu-tu** in some places, *chedugudu* in others.

In this chapter we watch girls play kabaddi in a village, meet a famous sportswoman, and ask some important questions:

- What are the rules of kabaddi?
- Why are rules needed in any game?
- Do girls get the same chance to play as boys?
- What makes someone a great player?

Kabaddi is played between **two teams**, usually **seven players** on each side on the court. A line divides the field into two halves.

1. One player, the **raider**, goes into the other team's half, saying 'kabaddi-kabaddi' continuously **in one breath**.
2. The raider tries to **touch** one or more players of the other team and get back to their own half.
3. Every player touched is **out**, and the raider's team gets points.
4. The other team tries to **catch** the raider and stop them from returning. If the raider is held or runs out of breath, the raider is out.
5. Out players can come back in when their team scores.

Kabaddi needs **strength, speed, quick thinking, team-work and good breath control**. No ball, no bat — just a flat ground and a line!

fig.caption: A raider (red) crosses the line, tags a defender and races back before losing breath.
fig.alt: Kabaddi court with a raider moving into the other half and back

check.q: What must a kabaddi raider do while raiding?
check.why: The raider must chant 'kabaddi' continuously in a single breath while trying to tag opponents.

sections.md:
Imagine a cricket match where one team says it gets 20 overs and the other only 10. Or a kabaddi raid where the raider can breathe as much as they like. It would not be fair or fun!

**Rules** make a game:

- **fair** — everyone gets the same chance,
- **safe** — no dangerous pushing or hitting,
- **clear** — everyone knows how to win.

Many games are played differently in different places — the rules of *gilli-danda*, *kho-kho*, *pitthu* (lagori) change from street to street. That's fine as long as everyone agrees before starting. In big tournaments there are fixed rules and a **referee** or **umpire** to make sure they are followed.

> **Activity:** Write the rules of a game you play with your friends. Do your friends agree with all of them?

check.q: Why do games need rules?
options: To make them fair, safe and clear
So only one team can win
check.why: Rules give everyone an equal chance, protect players, and make clear how to win.

sections.h: Team games and games you play alone
sections.md:
Let us sort the games we know. Some need a team, some can be played by just one or two people. Some are played inside the house, some need open ground.

| Game | Team or alone? | Indoor or outdoor? | Things needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kabaddi | team | outdoor | flat ground, a line |
| Kho-kho | team | outdoor | ground, two poles |
| Cricket | team | outdoor | bat, ball, stumps |
| Skipping | alone or group | outdoor | a rope |
| Chess | two players | indoor | board and pieces |
| Ludo / chaupar | 2–4 players | indoor | board, dice |
| Carrom | 2–4 players | indoor | board, striker, coins |

**Survey activity:** Ask ten children in your class which game they like most. Make a tally of girls and boys. Then ask: *Which games do girls in your area usually play? Which do boys play? Are there games only one group is allowed to play? Why?*

You may find that girls are often expected to play quiet games near home, while boys go to the open ground. Talk about whether this is fair. A game does not belong to girls or boys — it belongs to whoever wants to play it.

> **Think:** Which games do you play only at certain times — like kite-flying around Makar Sankranti, or marbles in the dry season?

check.q: Which of these is an indoor game for two players?
check.why: Chess is played by two people sitting at a board, usually indoors, while the others need an open ground and teams.

sections.md:
In the chapter, a group of girls play kabaddi in the village, but some people say, 'Girls should not play such rough games' or 'Girls should help at home instead.' Is that fair?

Playing is important for **every child**. Games make our bodies strong, help us make friends, teach us to win and lose gracefully, and make us happy. Girls and boys both have the **right to play**.

Today India has many famous sportswomen:

- **Karnam Malleswari** — weightlifter from Andhra Pradesh, the first Indian woman to win an **Olympic medal** (bronze, Sydney 2000).
- **Mary Kom** — boxing champion from Manipur.
- **P.V. Sindhu** — badminton, Olympic medals.
- **Mithali Raj** — cricket captain.

India's women's kabaddi team has also won medals at the Asian Games.

head: Player
Sport
From
fig.caption: Some Indian women who changed sport.

check.q: Karnam Malleswari became famous for —
check.why: Karnam Malleswari won a bronze medal in weightlifting at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, the first Olympic medal by an Indian woman.

sections.md:
Karnam Malleswari grew up in a small village near Srikakulam in Andhra Pradesh, one of several sisters. Her sisters went to a gym to learn weightlifting, and young Malleswari went along to watch. At first some people thought she looked too thin and weak for such a heavy sport. She did not argue — she simply began to practise.

Her mother encouraged all her daughters, even when neighbours said weightlifting was not a sport for girls. Malleswari trained with simple equipment, ate healthy food, and kept lifting a little more each month. She won national competitions, then world championships, and in the year 2000 at the Sydney Olympics she won a **bronze medal**. India celebrated: it was the first Olympic medal ever won by an Indian woman.

What do we learn from her?
- Do not let others decide what you can or cannot do.
- Family support makes a huge difference.
- Big results come from small daily efforts.

> **Talk about it:** Do you know a girl or a woman in your area who plays a sport? Interview her: how did she start, and who helped her?

check.q: What helped Malleswari most when people doubted her?
options: Her mother's support and her own daily practice
check.why: Her mother encouraged her and she trained steadily, proving the doubters wrong with her results.

sections.md:
Champions are not born — they are made by:

- **Practice** — again and again, even when it's boring.
- **Healthy food and sleep** — the body needs fuel and rest.
- **Support** — family, coaches and friends who believe in them.
- **Never giving up** — losing, learning, and trying again.

Sport also teaches **team spirit**. In kabaddi, one great raider is not enough; the defenders must hold hands and work as one chain.

> **Did you know?** Kabaddi is the state game of several Indian states, and there is now a professional kabaddi league watched by millions on TV.
keyTerms: Raider — the kabaddi player who goes into the other team's half
Referee/umpire — the person who makes sure rules are followed
Team spirit — working together for the team

sections.md:
India has a treasure of traditional games: **kho-kho**, **gilli-danda**, **pitthu/lagori**, **langdi**, **kancha** (marbles), **chaupar**, **pallanguzhi**. Many need no costly equipment — just a few stones, a stick, chalk or a ground.

Ask your grandparents which games they played. Write their names and rules. Teach one old game to your friends!

| Game | What you need | Players |
|---|---|---|
| Kho-kho | open ground | 2 teams |
| Pitthu | 7 flat stones, a ball | 2 teams |
| Gilli-danda | a small and a big stick | 2 or more |

check.q: Which game needs seven flat stones and a ball?
check.why: In pitthu (lagori), players knock down a pile of seven flat stones with a ball and then try to rebuild it.

parts.md: The harvest was in, and the threshing ground was flat and empty. 'Kabaddi!' shouted Bhagwati, and the girls came running. A few boys sat on the wall, laughing. 'Girls can't play kabaddi,' one said. Bhagwati only tightened her dupatta and drew the line in the dust with her toe.

She took a giant breath. 'Kabaddi-kabaddi-kabaddi…' She slipped past one girl, ducked another, and — tap! — touched Reena's shoulder. Three girls grabbed for her ankle. She twisted, stretched her arm across the line, still chanting. Point!

The boys on the wall had stopped laughing. 'Can we play too?' one asked quietly. Bhagwati grinned. 'Only if you follow the rules.' By sunset there were two mixed teams, dusty and shouting. And years later, when Bhagwati played for her state, she still remembered that first raid on the threshing ground.

summary: Kabaddi (hu-tu-tu) is an old Indian team game.
Each team usually has seven players on court.
The raider enters the other half chanting 'kabaddi' in one breath.
The raider tries to touch opponents and return; defenders try to catch the raider.
Kabaddi needs strength, speed, breath control and team-work.
Rules make games fair, safe and clear; local rules must be agreed first.
Games can be team or individual, indoor or outdoor.
Every child, girl or boy, has the right to play any game.
Karnam Malleswari was the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal (weightlifting bronze, 2000).
Her mother's support and her daily practice made her a champion.
Practice, good food, support and never giving up make champions.
India has many traditional games like kho-kho, pitthu and gilli-danda.

What are two qualities a good kabaddi player needs?
Why are rules important in a game?
Name two team games and two games for one or two players.
Who is Karnam Malleswari? What did she achieve?
Who supported Malleswari, and how?
Should girls and boys get equal chances to play? Give reasons.
Name three traditional Indian games and what you need to play them.
Write the rules of one game you play.
What did you learn from a game you lost?

rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch6-omanas-journey.title: Omana's Journey
rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch6-omanas-journey.subtitle: Pack your bag — a long train ride across India, through tunnels, rivers and many languages

sections.md:
*Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk… paaaaam!* The whistle blows, the platform starts to slide backwards, and you are off on a journey that will last more than a day and a night. That is exactly how **Omana** felt when her family boarded a long-distance train to go home to **Kerala** for the holidays.

Omana kept a **diary** of her journey. A travel diary is a lovely habit — you write down what you see, hear, smell and eat, and the time and place. Years later it brings the whole trip back.

In this read we will travel with Omana and learn:

- how to read a **train ticket**,
- how to plan and pack for a long journey,
- what life inside a train is like,
- how the land, trees and houses **change** as we cross India,
- why there are **tunnels and bridges**, and
- how languages change from place to place.

Before the journey, Omana's father showed her the ticket. A train ticket is full of information! Let us look at a pretend ticket:

| On the ticket | What it means |
|---|---|
| Train No. & name | which train to catch (e.g. 16xxx Express) |
| From / To | the starting station and the destination |
| Date & departure time | when the train leaves |
| Class | e.g. SL = Sleeper, 3A = AC 3-tier |
| Coach & Berth | e.g. S5, 33 Lower — your coach and your bed |
| Distance | how many kilometres you will travel |
| Fare | how much money the ticket cost, in ₹ |
| Name, age, sex | details of each passenger |

The distance can be more than 2,000 km on long journeys! Indian Railways is one of the largest railway networks in the world. Every day millions of people travel on it.

> **Activity:** If a ticket says the train leaves at 21:30 on Monday and arrives at 06:30 on Wednesday, how long is the journey? (Answer: 33 hours.)

check.q: On a ticket, what does 'S5, 33' most likely tell you?
options: Your coach number and berth number
check.why: S5 is the sleeper coach number and 33 is the berth (seat/bed) where you will sit and sleep.

sections.h: Planning and packing for a long journey
sections.md:
A journey of a day and a half needs planning. Omana's mother made a list a week before. Here is a list like hers:

- **Tickets** and an identity card for the grown-ups.
- **Food and water** — home-made puris, lemon rice, fruit, and filled water bottles.
- **A bedsheet and small pillow** (in sleeper class you carry your own).
- **A small bag** with toothbrush, soap, towel, comb and medicines.
- **Something to do** — a book, cards, a diary and pencil.
- **A chain and lock** for the big suitcase.
- Gifts for relatives — Omana carried sweets for her grandmother.

People also check the **railway timetable**. A timetable shows each station where the train stops, the arrival time, the departure time and the distance from the start.

| Station | Arrives | Departs | Km from start |
|---|---|---|---|
| Station A | — | 21:30 | 0 |
| Station B | 02:10 | 02:15 | 310 |
| Station C | 11:40 | 11:50 | 1,020 |
| Station D | 06:30 | — | 2,050 |

At Station B the train waits 5 minutes; at Station C it waits 10 minutes. From A to C the train covers 1,020 km.

> **Think:** What would you pack that Omana did not?

check.q: In the timetable, how long does the train stop at Station C?
check.why: It arrives at 11:40 and departs at 11:50, so it waits for 10 minutes.

sections.md:
Inside the train, Omana found a whole little world. There were **berths**: lower, middle, upper and side berths. At night, the middle berth folds down and everyone sleeps. In the day it folds up so people can sit.

At every big station, vendors called out: *Chai! Chai! Vada, samosa, idli!* Some foods were new to her. The family had also packed food from home — puris, lemon rice, bananas.

Omana made friends with a girl from another state. They could not speak the same language very well, but they played cards and laughed together.

Rules for a safe, happy train journey:

- Do not lean out of the door or windows.
- Keep your luggage chained or close to you.
- Do not throw rubbish out — use the dustbin.
- Do not pull the emergency chain unless there is a real emergency.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#e3f2fd'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='60' fill='#8d6e63'/><g stroke='#5d4037' stroke-width='4'><line x1='0' y1='210' x2='600' y2='210'/><line x1='0' y1='225' x2='600' y2='225'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-420 0;620 0' dur='9s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='0' y='120' width='110' height='75' rx='10' fill='#c62828'/><rect x='115' y='130' width='120' height='65' rx='6' fill='#1565c0'/><rect x='240' y='130' width='120' height='65' rx='6' fill='#1565c0'/><g fill='#fff59d'><rect x='125' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='150' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='175' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='200' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='250' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='275' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='300' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='325' y='140' width='18' height='16'/><rect x='10' y='130' width='30' height='20'/></g><g fill='#222'><circle cx='25' cy='198' r='9'/><circle cx='85' cy='198' r='9'/><circle cx='140' cy='198' r='9'/><circle cx='210' cy='198' r='9'/><circle cx='265' cy='198' r='9'/><circle cx='335' cy='198' r='9'/></g></g><g fill='#2e7d32'><circle cx='80' cy='70' r='22'/><circle cx='520' cy='80' r='26'/></g><text x='200' y='40' font-size='18' fill='#0d47a1'>Fields → rivers → hills → coconut trees</text></svg>
fig.caption: A long-distance train races across the country; the view outside changes as you go.
fig.alt: A red engine pulling blue coaches across the screen

sections.h: The land changes outside the window
sections.md:
Omana spent hours looking out of the window. She noticed that the land kept changing:

- Near the start, there were **flat fields** of wheat, cotton or groundnut, and houses with flat roofs.
- Then came **rivers** — the train rattled loudly over long **bridges**.
- Later, **hills and forests** appeared, and the train went into dark **tunnels**.
- Near Kerala, she saw **coconut trees**, **paddy fields**, backwaters, and houses with **sloping roofs** because it rains a lot there.

Why did the houses change? Because people build houses to suit the **weather** and the **materials** available nearby. In places with heavy rain, sloping roofs let water run off quickly.

The railway along the western coast between Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka is called the **Konkan Railway**. It goes through many tunnels cut through hills and over high bridges across rivers — a great engineering feat.

check.q: Why do many houses in Kerala have sloping roofs?
options: Because it rains a lot and water slides off
check.why: Kerala gets heavy rain, so sloping roofs let rainwater run off quickly instead of collecting on top.

sections.md:
Why do railways need tunnels and bridges? Trains cannot climb steep slopes or cross deep water. So engineers:

- build **bridges** across rivers and valleys,
- dig **tunnels** through hills and mountains.

Inside a tunnel, it suddenly becomes dark, the sound becomes louder, and your ears may feel funny. Children often shout 'Hoooo!' to hear the echo.

Building tunnels is very hard work. Workers use big machines and sometimes explosives to cut through rock, and make the walls strong so they do not fall.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#b3e5fc'/><path d='M0 200 Q150 30 300 200 Z' fill='#6d8b4a'/><path d='M100 200 a50 50 0 0 1 100 0 Z' fill='#222'/><rect x='300' y='220' width='300' height='60' fill='#4fc3f7'><animate attributeName='fill' values='#4fc3f7;#29b6f6;#4fc3f7' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='0' y='200' width='300' height='80' fill='#7b5e3b'/><g stroke='#555' stroke-width='6' fill='none'><path d='M300 200 L600 200'/><path d='M330 200 L330 260 M400 200 L400 260 M470 200 L470 260 M540 200 L540 260'/><path d='M330 200 Q365 240 400 200 Q435 240 470 200 Q505 240 540 200'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-60 0;640 0' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='0' y='175' width='60' height='24' rx='5' fill='#c62828'/></g><text x='90' y='240' font-size='16' fill='#fff'>Tunnel</text><text x='420' y='255' font-size='16' fill='#01579b'>Bridge</text></svg>
fig.caption: Tunnels let trains pass through hills; bridges let them cross rivers.
fig.alt: A train passing through a tunnel and over a bridge

check.q: Why are tunnels built for railways?
options: So trains can pass through hills instead of climbing steep slopes
check.why: Trains cannot climb steep hills, so tunnels let them go straight through.

sections.md:
At each station Omana saw the station's name board written in **three scripts** — often the language of that state, Hindi and English. As the train moved through Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala, she heard people speaking **Gujarati, Marathi, Konkani, Kannada and Malayalam**.

India has many languages, foods and ways of dressing. A long train journey is like a moving lesson in how big and varied our country is.

> **Activity:** Look at a map of India. Trace a railway route from your town to a place you want to visit. Which states will you pass through? Which languages are spoken there?
keyTerms: Berth — a bed on a train
Tunnel — a passage cut through a hill
Bridge — a structure across a river or valley
Konkan Railway — railway along India's western coast

check.q: Why are station names written in more than one script?
options: So that people who know different languages can read them
check.why: Travellers speak many languages, so names in the state's language, Hindi and English help everyone.

sections.md:
Trains are not the only way to travel a long distance. Each way has good and not-so-good points:

| Way to travel | Good points | Not-so-good points |
|---|---|---|
| Train | can sleep, walk about, cheaper for long trips | takes a long time |
| Bus | reaches small towns and hills | cramped on very long trips |
| Aeroplane | very fast | costly, cannot see the land up close |
| Ship/boat | crosses seas, e.g. to islands | slow, depends on weather |

To reach the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, people go by ship or aeroplane, because no train or bus can cross the sea.

> **Talk about it:** Have you ever made a long journey? How did you go? How long did it take? What did you see on the way?

> **Did you know?** Many Indian trains are named after rivers, places or famous people — try finding three such names on a railway chart!

check.q: Which is the best way to reach an island far out at sea?
check.why: Only ships and aeroplanes can cross the sea; trains and buses need land.

parts.md: *Day 1, 9:30 pm.* The train has started! I am on the upper berth. Appa says I must not climb down at night without waking him. The fan above me goes round and round. I can hear someone snoring already.

*Day 2, 7 am.* Woke up to chai calls. Outside: red soil and hills. We went through eleven tunnels — I counted! In one long tunnel everyone screamed and laughed. I made a friend named Pooja. She taught me a card game.

*Day 2, evening.* Coconut trees everywhere, and water shining between them. The station boards are in Malayalam now — I can read them! Ammamma will be waiting at the station with banana chips. Home soon!

summary: Omana travelled by a long-distance train to Kerala and kept a diary.
A train ticket shows train number, stations, date, time, class, coach, berth, distance and fare.
A timetable shows arrival and departure times and distance at each station.
Plan a long journey: tickets, food, water, bedding, a lock, medicines.
Long train journeys can take more than a day.
Trains have lower, middle, upper and side berths.
Follow safety rules: don't lean out, keep luggage safe, don't litter.
The landscape changes: fields, rivers, hills, forests, coconut trees.
Houses are built to suit local weather; rainy places have sloping roofs.
Bridges cross rivers; tunnels pass through hills; the Konkan Railway has many of both.
Station names are written in several scripts because India has many languages.
Buses, aeroplanes and ships are other ways to travel far.

glossary.d: A book where you write daily events
The place you are travelling to
Money paid for a ticket
Raised place at a station where you board a train
A chart of times when trains reach and leave stations

practice: Write five pieces of information found on a train ticket.
Make a packing list for a two-day train journey.
How did the land change during Omana's journey?
Why do houses in rainy areas have sloping roofs?
Why are tunnels and bridges built for railways?
Write three safety rules for train travel.
A train leaves at 08:00 on Tuesday and arrives at 14:00 on Wednesday. How long was the journey?
Name four languages Omana might hear on her way to Kerala.
Compare travelling by train and by aeroplane.
Write a short diary entry about a journey you made.

rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch7-from-the-window.title: From the Window
rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch7-from-the-window.subtitle: Look out of a moving train: rivers, tunnels, the sea and a world that keeps changing

sections.h: The best seat in the train
sections.md:
Everyone wants the **window seat**. Why? Because a window on a moving train is like a television that shows real life — and the show never repeats!

Omana's journey continues. Now the train is running along the **Konkan coast**, between the hills of the **Western Ghats** and the **Arabian Sea**. Omana presses her nose to the glass and her younger brother keeps asking, 'What's that? What's that?'

In this read you will learn to be a sharp **observer**: to notice, compare, ask questions and record what you see — just like a scientist.

sections.h: Things look different when you move
sections.md:
Have you noticed something strange from a moving train?

- Trees and poles **close to the track** seem to rush past very fast.
- Hills and trees **far away** seem to move slowly.
- The **moon** seems to follow you!

This happens because nearby things change their place in your view quickly, while far things change very little. You are moving, not the trees — but it *feels* as if they are moving backwards.

Also, when another train passes on the next track in the opposite direction, it seems to whiz by super fast. If it moves in the same direction at the same speed, it seems to stand still!
