fig.caption: From a moving train, nearby trees seem to rush past while faraway hills move slowly.
fig.alt: View through a train window with fast-moving trees and slow hills

check.q: From a moving train, which seems to move fastest?
check.why: Things close to you change position in your view quickly, so nearby trees seem to rush past.

sections.md:
On the Konkan route, the train crosses many rivers flowing down from the hills into the Arabian Sea. In **Goa**, Omana sees the wide **Mandovi** river with boats on it. The bridges are long, and the train makes a hollow *dhadak-dhadak* sound on them.

She sees:

- **fishing boats** and nets drying in the sun,
- **coconut** and **cashew** trees,
- small red-tiled houses,
- the blue line of the **sea** far away.

People here eat a lot of fish and rice, because the sea and rivers give fish and the heavy rain helps rice grow.

check.q: Which sea lies along the Konkan coast?
check.why: The Konkan coast is on India's west side, along the Arabian Sea.

sections.md:
The Konkan Railway is famous for its many **tunnels**. When the train enters one:

1. It suddenly turns **dark** and the lights inside the coach come on.
2. The noise becomes **loud** because sound bounces off the tunnel walls.
3. The air may feel **cooler**.
4. Then — a flash of light — and you are out again!

Omana and her brother made a game of counting the tunnels and timing how long each one lasted. Some lasted a few seconds; one lasted several minutes.

| Tunnel | Time inside | What we felt |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 seconds | dark, loud |
| 2 | 45 seconds | ears felt blocked |
| 3 | 3 minutes | cool, everyone shouted |

The longer the tunnel, the longer the time — but also, the slower the train, the longer it takes!

> **Imagine:** What if a tunnel were so long that the train stayed inside for a whole hour? How would you feel? What would you do?

check.q: Why does it become louder inside a tunnel?
options: Sound bounces off the tunnel walls
check.why: Tunnel walls reflect sound back towards the train, so it sounds louder inside.

sections.h: From morning to night at the window
sections.md:
A long journey lets you watch a whole day change outside.

- **Early morning:** mist over the fields, people going to the river or the well, farmers walking out with animals, smoke rising from village kitchens.
- **Noon:** bright sun, shadows are short, cattle rest in the shade, the coach gets warm and many people doze.
- **Evening:** the sky turns orange and pink, birds fly back in flocks to their trees, children play in open grounds, lamps and tube-lights come on in houses.
- **Night:** you can see little except lights — a lit-up station, a moving bus on a highway, a temple lamp on a hill. If the coach lights are on, you may even see your own face reflected in the glass!

As night falls, the window becomes a mirror because it is brighter inside the coach than outside.

**Activity:** On your next journey, write one line every hour about what you see. Compare the morning line with the night line.

check.q: Why can you see your own reflection in the train window at night?
options: It is brighter inside the coach than outside
check.why: When it is dark outside and lit inside, the glass reflects the bright inside back to you like a mirror.

sections.md:
From the window you can also see the people and machines that keep the railway running:

- **Signals** — red means stop, green means go, yellow means go slow and be careful.
- **Signal cabins** and **level crossings** where gates close for road traffic.
- **Gangmen** (track workers) who check and repair the tracks.
- **Station masters** who wave flags and give the line clear signal.

At level crossings, buses, cycles and cows wait patiently while the train goes by. Never cross a railway track when the gate is closed!

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='300' height='300' fill='#eceff1'/><rect x='140' y='160' width='20' height='130' fill='#455a64'/><rect x='105' y='20' width='90' height='150' rx='20' fill='#263238'/><circle cx='150' cy='55' r='20' fill='#e53935'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;1;0.2;0.2;0.2;0.2;1' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='150' cy='97' r='20' fill='#fdd835'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0.2;0.2;1;1;0.2;0.2;0.2' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='150' cy='139' r='20' fill='#43a047'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0.2;0.2;0.2;0.2;1;1;0.2' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><text x='205' y='60' font-size='14'>Stop</text><text x='205' y='102' font-size='14'>Caution</text><text x='205' y='144' font-size='14'>Go</text></svg>
fig.caption: Railway signal lights: red stop, yellow caution, green go.
fig.alt: A signal post blinking red, yellow and green in turn

sections.md:
Not every train carries people. Sometimes, on the next track, Omana sees a very long train with no windows at all — a **goods train**. Count its wagons: sometimes there are more than fifty!

Goods trains carry:

| Wagon type | What it carries |
|---|---|
| Covered wagons | grain, cement, fertiliser |
| Open wagons | coal, iron ore, stones |
| Tank wagons (round) | petrol, diesel, milk, water |
| Flat wagons | containers, trucks, cars |

The salt, sugar, coal and petrol in your town may well have travelled by goods train. In this way the railway joins farms, mines, factories and markets across the country.

> **Did you know?** Along the Konkan Railway, trucks loaded with goods were carried on flat wagons of trains so they did not have to drive over the steep ghat roads.

check.q: Which wagon would carry petrol or milk?
check.why: Liquids are carried in round closed tank wagons so they do not spill.

sections.md:
A good observer:

- **looks** carefully, not just quickly,
- **compares** (Is this hill taller than that one? Is this river wider?),
- **asks** questions (Why are these roofs red? Why is the soil red here?),
- **records** in words, drawings or tables.

Next time you are in a bus, car or train, make a 'window list': 5 trees, 5 animals, 5 kinds of vehicles, 5 kinds of work people are doing.

> **Did you know?** The soil along much of the Konkan coast is red because it has a lot of iron in it — like rust! Bricks and tiles made from it are red too.
keyTerms: Observer — someone who watches carefully
Signal — a light or sign telling a train to stop or go
Level crossing — where a road crosses a railway line
Goods train — a train that carries things, not passengers

check.q: What does a yellow railway signal mean?
check.why: Yellow warns the driver to slow down and be ready to stop at the next signal.

parts.md: 'Amma, the moon is following our train!' said Omana's little brother Appu. He moved to the other window. 'It's still there!' Omana laughed. 'It's very, very far away, Appu. That's why it seems to stay with us.'

'But the trees are running away,' Appu said, puzzled. Omana thought hard. 'The trees are close to us. We're zooming past them, so they look like they're running backwards. The moon is so far that our moving hardly matters.' Appu stared, then grinned. 'So the moon is lazy and the trees are fast!'

Just then — darkness! A tunnel. Appu shrieked with joy and the whole coach shouted 'Hooooo!' When they came out, the moon was right there again, round and patient. 'See?' said Appu. 'It waited for us.'

summary: A train window lets us observe the changing land and people.
Nearby objects seem to move fast; distant objects seem to move slowly.
The Konkan Railway runs between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.
Many rivers flow to the sea and are crossed by long bridges; in Goa the train crosses the Mandovi.
Inside tunnels it becomes dark, loud and cooler; longer tunnels take more time.
The view changes from morning mist to evening birds to night lights.
At night the window acts like a mirror.
Signals: red stop, yellow caution, green go.
Track workers, station masters and signal staff keep trains safe.
Goods trains carry coal, grain, petrol, milk and containers.
Good observers look, compare, ask and record.
practice: Why do nearby trees seem to run backwards from a moving train?
Name two things you might see from the train in Goa.
What happens when a train enters a tunnel?
How does the view from the window change from morning to night?
What do the red, yellow and green signals mean?
Why should we never cross the tracks when the level-crossing gate is closed?
Name three things carried by goods trains.
Why is the soil red in many parts of the Konkan?
Make a 'window list' of 5 things you saw on your last journey.
Draw what you would see from a train window near the sea.

rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch8-reaching-grandmot.title: Reaching Grandmother's House
rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch8-reaching-grandmot.subtitle: Bus, boat, bullock cart or bamboo bridge — the many ways people travel to the ones they love

sections.md:
Grandmother's house is a magical place — mango pickle, stories at night, a courtyard to run in. But first you have to **reach** it! Some children reach Nani's house in ten minutes by scooter. Others travel for two days by train, bus, boat and finally on foot across a swaying bridge.

In this chapter, children travel through hills, rivers and villages to reach their grandmothers. On the way we learn about:

- different **means of transport**,
- different kinds of **bridges**,
- how rivers and floods change the way people travel and build,
- why people in different places travel differently.

> **Think:** How do you reach your grandparents' home? List every vehicle you use, in order.

We can sort ways of travelling by where they move:

| On land | On water | In the air |
|---|---|---|
| walking, cycle, bullock cart, camel cart, tonga, auto-rickshaw, bus, car, train, jeep | raft, rowing boat, ferry, motorboat, ship | aeroplane, helicopter |

We can also sort them by what makes them move:

- **Animal power** — bullock cart, horse cart (tonga), camel cart.
- **Human power** — walking, cycle, cycle-rickshaw, rowing boat.
- **Fuel or electricity** — bus, car, train, motorboat, aeroplane.

In hilly areas, people use **jeeps** on winding roads, or walk on steep paths. In deserts, the **camel** is useful because it can walk on sand and go many days without water. In places with many rivers and lakes, like parts of **Assam**, **Kerala** and **West Bengal**, **boats** are a part of everyday life.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='150' fill='#bbdefb'/><rect y='150' width='600' height='70' fill='#a5d6a7'/><rect y='220' width='600' height='80' fill='#4fc3f7'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-100 0;650 0' dur='12s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 60 L70 55 L90 45 L95 60 L70 66 L0 66 Z' fill='#eceff1' stroke='#546e7a'/><path d='M30 60 L45 40 L55 60' fill='#90a4ae'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='-120 0;650 0' dur='9s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='0' y='160' width='100' height='40' rx='8' fill='#fbc02d'/><g fill='#e3f2fd'><rect x='10' y='166' width='16' height='14'/><rect x='32' y='166' width='16' height='14'/><rect x='54' y='166' width='16' height='14'/><rect x='76' y='166' width='16' height='14'/></g><circle cx='22' cy='202' r='8' fill='#222'/><circle cx='80' cy='202' r='8' fill='#222'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='650 0;-150 0' dur='16s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 250 Q60 275 120 250 Z' fill='#6d4c41'/><line x1='60' y1='250' x2='60' y2='215' stroke='#4e342e' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M60 218 L90 245 L60 245 Z' fill='#fff'/></g><g font-size='14' fill='#0d47a1'><text x='10' y='20'>Air</text><text x='10' y='145'>Land</text><text x='10' y='290'>Water</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Transport moves through the air, on land and on water.
fig.alt: An aeroplane, a bus and a boat moving in three bands

check.q: Which of these is moved by animal power?
check.why: A bullock cart is pulled by bullocks, so it uses animal power.

sections.md:
When there is a river or a deep valley on the way, people need a **bridge** — or a boat. Children in this chapter cross several kinds of bridges:

- **Cement / concrete bridges** — strong, wide, buses and trucks can cross.
- **Iron (steel) bridges** — often used for railways.
- **Bamboo bridges** — made by villagers in places like the North-East, tied with ropes; light and cheap, but they must be repaired often.
- **Rope bridges** — hang across valleys in hills; they swing as you walk!
- **Living root bridges** — in **Meghalaya**, people guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams for many years until they grow into a strong bridge.

Each bridge is made from materials found nearby and suits what needs to cross it — people only, or heavy vehicles.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#e8f5e9'/><path d='M0 120 L120 120 L160 300 L0 300 Z' fill='#6d8b4a'/><path d='M600 120 L480 120 L440 300 L600 300 Z' fill='#6d8b4a'/><rect x='160' y='260' width='280' height='40' fill='#4fc3f7'><animate attributeName='x' values='160;150;160' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><path d='M120 115 Q300 190 480 115' stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/><path d='M120 85 Q300 160 480 85' stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><g stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='2'><line x1='180' y1='108' x2='180' y2='136'/><line x1='240' y1='124' x2='240' y2='152'/><line x1='300' y1='130' x2='300' y2='158'/><line x1='360' y1='124' x2='360' y2='152'/><line x1='420' y1='108' x2='420' y2='136'/></g><g><animateMotion path='M120 105 Q300 180 480 105' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><circle cx='0' cy='-22' r='7' fill='#5d4037'/><rect x='-5' y='-15' width='10' height='16' fill='#e53935'/></g><text x='170' y='40' font-size='18' fill='#1b5e20'>A swaying rope bridge across a valley</text></svg>
fig.caption: A rope bridge hangs across a deep valley; a walker crosses carefully.
fig.alt: A person walking across a hanging rope bridge over a river

check.q: Where are living root bridges found?
check.why: In Meghalaya, people grow the roots of rubber fig trees across streams to form living bridges.

sections.h: Life by the river: boats and floods
sections.md:
In parts of Assam and Bihar, big rivers like the **Brahmaputra** and the **Kosi** flood almost every monsoon. Water spreads over fields and roads for weeks. For families here, the **boat** is as important as a bicycle is elsewhere.

- Children may go to school by boat, and some places even have **boat clinics** that carry doctors and medicines to island villages.
- Many houses are built on **stilts** (tall poles of bamboo or wood), so the floor stays above the flood water.
- People keep a small boat or a **banana-stem raft** ready, and store grain and fodder on a raised platform.
- After the flood, the river leaves behind fresh soil that is good for crops.

| In a flood area | Why |
|---|---|
| Houses on stilts | water passes below the floor |
| Boats kept ready | roads go under water |
| Raised storage | grain stays dry |

> **Talk about it:** What would be hard for you if your road were under water for a month? What would be fun?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#e1f5fe'/><g stroke='#6d4c41' stroke-width='6'><line x1='170' y1='150' x2='170' y2='270'/><line x1='250' y1='150' x2='250' y2='270'/><line x1='330' y1='150' x2='330' y2='270'/></g><rect x='150' y='110' width='200' height='45' fill='#d7a86e'/><path d='M135 115 L250 50 L365 115 Z' fill='#8d6e63'/><rect x='230' y='120' width='30' height='35' fill='#5d4037'/><rect y='190' width='600' height='90' fill='#4fc3f7' opacity='0.85'><animate attributeName='y' values='230;190;230' dur='8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='600 0;-120 0' dur='12s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 205 Q50 225 100 205 Z' fill='#5d4037'/><circle cx='50' cy='192' r='7' fill='#4e342e'/></g><text x='380' y='60' font-size='15' fill='#01579b'>House on stilts: water rises</text><text x='380' y='80' font-size='15' fill='#01579b'>but the floor stays dry</text></svg>
fig.caption: A house on stilts stays dry while flood water rises and falls; a boat carries people.
fig.alt: A house raised on poles above rising water with a boat passing

check.q: Why are some houses in flood areas built on stilts?
options: So flood water passes under the floor
check.why: Raising the house on poles keeps the floor above the level the flood water usually reaches.

sections.md:
Why do people choose one way of travel over another? It depends on:

- **Distance** — short distance: walk or cycle; long: train or bus.
- **Land** — hills, desert, rivers, snow.
- **Cost** — buses and trains cost less per person than taxis or planes.
- **Time** — aeroplanes are fastest.
- **Load** — carrying many goods? A truck, cart or boat.

**Try this sum:** A family of 4 can go by bus at ₹60 each, or hire a taxi for ₹400. The bus costs 4 × 60 = ₹240, so it is ₹160 cheaper — but the taxi may be faster and drop them at the door. Which would you choose for an old grandparent with heavy bags?

Old means of transport like bullock carts, tongas and country boats are slowly being replaced by motor vehicles in many places. These are faster but use **fuel** (petrol, diesel) that makes the air dirty. Walking, cycling and buses are kinder to the air.

> **Did you know?** In snowy Ladakh and Himachal, people once used yaks to carry loads across high passes.

check.q: Which travels the fastest over a very long distance?
check.why: Aeroplanes fly at very high speeds and do not have to go around hills or rivers.

sections.md:
Ask your grandparents how *they* travelled when they were your age. You may hear stories like these:

- They walked many kilometres to school or to the market.
- A wedding party travelled to the next village in a line of decorated bullock carts.
- A trip to the city happened only once or twice a year, by a steam train with a black-smoke engine.
- Letters, not phone calls, told relatives that someone was coming.

Today, many villages have roads, buses and mobile phones. Journeys are faster. But some things have not changed: the excitement of the journey, a packed tiffin, and a grandmother waiting at the door.

**Interview activity:** Ask an elder these questions and write the answers:
1. How did you go to your grandmother's house?
2. How long did it take?
3. What was the most exciting journey of your life?

check.q: Why did journeys take longer in your grandparents' childhood?
options: There were fewer roads and motor vehicles
check.why: With fewer roads, buses and cars, people often walked or used animal carts, which take much longer.

sections.h: Asking for directions and reading maps
sections.md:
On the way to grandmother's house, the children ask people for directions: *Which bus goes to the village? Which side of the river is the ferry ghat?*

You can help yourself by learning:

- **Landmarks** — a big temple, a school, a water tank, a bridge — help you remember the way.
- **Directions** — North, South, East, West. In the morning, the Sun rises in the **East**.
- **Maps** — show roads, rivers and places from above.

Always travel with an adult, keep your family's phone number written down, and ask a police officer, bus conductor or shopkeeper if you are lost.
keyTerms: Transport — ways of carrying people and goods from place to place
Ferry — a boat that carries people (and sometimes vehicles) across water
Landmark — an easy-to-spot place that helps you find your way
Stilts — tall poles that lift a house above the ground

check.q: In the morning, the Sun rises in the —
check.why: The Sun always rises in the East, which helps us find other directions.

parts.md: Bina and her father caught the early bus from town. It bumped along the road, past paddy fields shining with water. 'Two more stops,' said the conductor, clicking his ticket punch. At the river ghat, the bus stopped. The road ended — the water began.

A big flat ferry was waiting. Cycles, goats, sacks of rice and people all squeezed on. The boatman pushed off with a long pole. Bina watched a kingfisher dive. On the far bank, a bamboo bridge crossed a little stream. It creaked. 'Step where I step,' said Father.

Across the bridge, a narrow path led through banana trees — and there was Nani, waving from her doorway with a plate of pithas. 'How did you come?' she asked. Bina counted on her fingers: 'Bus, ferry, bamboo bridge and my own two feet!' Nani laughed. 'The best vehicle of all.'

summary: People travel in many ways: on land, on water and in the air.
Transport can use human power, animal power or fuel/electricity.
Hilly areas use jeeps and footpaths; deserts use camels; river areas use boats.
Bridges may be made of cement, iron, bamboo, rope or even living roots.
Living root bridges are found in Meghalaya.
In flood areas people keep boats ready and build houses on stilts.
People choose transport by distance, land, cost, time and load.
Motor vehicles are fast but pollute; walking and cycling don't.
Our grandparents often walked or used bullock carts and steam trains.
Landmarks, directions and maps help us find our way; the Sun rises in the East.
practice: Name three means of transport each on land, water and air.
Which transport uses animal power? Give two examples.
Name four kinds of bridges and the material each is made of.
Why is the camel useful in the desert?
How do people in flood areas protect their homes and grain?
What things do we think of when choosing how to travel?
A bus ticket costs ₹45. How much will 3 people pay?
Ask an elder how they travelled as a child and write three points.
What should you do if you get lost on a journey?
Draw the route from your home to your grandparents' home and mark landmarks.

rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch9-changing-families.title: Changing Families
rd-school-c4-evs-b.ch9-changing-families.subtitle: New babies, weddings, moving cities — how families grow, shrink and change

sections.md:
Look at an old family photo. Who is in it? Who is missing? Who was not even born then? Families are like trees — they grow new branches, some leaves fall, and the tree keeps changing with the seasons.

In this chapter, we meet children whose families changed:

- a little sister or brother was **born**,
- an aunt got **married** and went to live in another house — or a new aunt came to live with them,
- a father or mother **moved** to another city for a job,
- a grandparent **passed away**, or came to live with them.

These changes can make us happy, sad, excited, or a little bit confused — all at once. That is completely normal.

sections.h: A new baby in the house
sections.md:
When a new baby arrives, everything changes! The house is full of visitors and sweets. The baby cries at night, needs feeding every few hours and cannot do anything by itself.

An older brother or sister may feel:

- **happy** — 'I have someone to play with!'
- **jealous** — 'Everyone only looks at the baby now.'
- **proud** — 'I am the big sister now.'

All these feelings are fine. You can help by talking to your parents about how you feel and by helping a little: fetching a nappy, singing to the baby, keeping the house quiet when the baby sleeps.

> **Did you know?** A newborn baby sleeps 14–17 hours a day, in short bits — that's why parents look sleepy!

check.q: If you feel a little jealous of a new baby, the best thing to do is —
options: Talk to your parents about how you feel
check.why: Talking about feelings helps parents understand and reassure you, and the feeling usually passes.

sections.md:
It is not only the family that changes — **you** change every year. Find a photo of yourself as a baby and compare it with today:

| As a baby | Now |
|---|---|
| could not walk or talk | runs, talks, reads and writes |
| no teeth | milk teeth falling, new teeth coming |
| fed by others | eats by yourself |
| tiny clothes and shoes | clothes and shoes several sizes bigger |

**Activity — measure your growth:** Stand against a wall and ask someone to mark your height with a pencil and the date. Do it again after six months. How many centimetres did you grow? Ask your parents what your height and weight were when you were born.

Old clothes that no longer fit can be passed on to a younger cousin or given to someone who needs them. In many families, a dress or sweater travels from the eldest child to the youngest!

> **Think:** What can you do now that you could not do two years ago? What would you like to learn next year?

check.q: What is a good thing to do with clothes you have outgrown?
options: Pass them to a younger child or someone in need
check.why: Clothes that are still good can be reused by a smaller child, so nothing is wasted.

sections.md:
Families come in many sizes and shapes:

| Kind of family | Who lives together |
|---|---|
| Small (nuclear) family | parents and their children |
| Big (joint) family | grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, cousins |
| Single-parent family | one parent and children |
| Other families | children with grandparents, or other relatives |

No kind is better than another. What matters is love and care.

A family can change from one kind to another. When an uncle gets married and moves out, a joint family may become smaller. When grandparents come to live with you, your family becomes bigger.

fig.caption: A family tree keeps growing — watch a new baby join it.
fig.alt: Family tree with grandparents, parents, children and a new baby appearing

check.q: A family with grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins living together is called —
check.why: In a joint family many generations and relatives live together under one roof.

sections.md:
When someone in the family gets married, it is a big celebration with music, food and relatives from far away. After the wedding, the couple may live with one of their families or set up a new home. So one family may 'lose' a member and another may 'gain' one — both families grow bigger in love.

Sometimes a parent has to **move to another city** for work, or gets a **transfer** in a government or company job. Many people from villages and small towns go to big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru or even other countries to earn money. The family then keeps in touch by **phone calls, video calls and letters**, and meets during festivals and holidays.

Sometimes the whole family moves. Then children have to make new friends, join a new school, and maybe learn a new language. It can be hard at first, but it is also an adventure.

check.q: Why do some parents move to another city?
options: For work, to earn money for the family
check.why: Many people move to cities where they can find jobs and send money home to support their family.

sections.h: Sharing the work when things change
sections.md:
When a family changes, the work at home changes too. Think about these situations:

- **A new baby comes:** the mother needs rest. Father, grandparents and older children take over cooking, washing and shopping.
- **Father moves to the city:** mother may now handle the bank, the fields or the shop as well as the house; children help with small jobs.
- **A grandparent falls ill:** someone must give medicines on time and take them to the doctor.

Good families **share work** — it should not all fall on one person, and jobs are not 'only for women' or 'only for men'. Boys can cook and sweep; girls can fix a cycle or go to the market.

**Activity — the home helper chart:**

| Job | Who does it now? | Can I help? |
|---|---|---|
| Filling water bottles | | |
| Folding clothes | | |
| Watering plants | | |
| Laying the table | | |

Fill in your chart and choose one new job to do every day this week.

check.q: When the mother comes home with a new baby, what is the fairest thing to do?
options: Everyone shares the housework so she can rest
Only the girls in the house help
check.why: Sharing the work among all family members lets the mother rest and look after the baby.

sections.h: When someone grows old or passes away
sections.md:
Grandparents get older and may need more help — with walking, remembering medicines, or reading small print. Children can help by reading the newspaper aloud, fetching water, or simply sitting and listening to their stories.

Sometimes a dear family member **passes away**. The family feels very sad and misses them. People remember them by sharing stories, looking at photos, and following the good things they taught. It is okay to cry, and okay to ask questions. Slowly, the sadness becomes softer, and the happy memories stay.

> **Think:** What is one thing you learnt from an elder in your family?

A **family tree** is a drawing that shows how members of a family are related. Grandparents are at the top, their children (your parents, uncles, aunts) below them, and their children (you, your siblings, cousins) below that.

**Activity:**

1. Ask your elders the names of your grandparents and their children.
2. Draw it like a tree with branches.
3. Add a star next to people who were born after you, and a flower for people who joined by marriage.

You will see how your family has changed over the years. You might even find a great-grandparent whose name you never knew!
keyTerms: Nuclear family — parents and their children
Joint family — many relatives living together
Transfer — being sent by an employer to work in another place
Family tree — a chart showing how family members are related

check.q: In a family tree, who is usually shown at the top?
check.why: Family trees start with the oldest generation at the top and branch down to younger generations.

parts.md: At the start of summer, Sonu's Bua got married. The courtyard was full of lights, dholaks and laddoos. Sonu danced till his legs hurt. But on the last day Bua left with her new family, and the house suddenly felt too quiet.

A week later, Papa got a job in Pune. 'I will call every night,' he promised, hugging Sonu at the bus stand. Every night at nine, the phone rang, and Sonu told Papa everything — the mango that fell on Dadi's head, the cricket score, the new puppy next door.

Then, at the end of summer, Mummy came home from hospital with a tiny baby wrapped in a yellow cloth. 'Your little sister,' she said. Sonu learnt to make tea for Mummy and fold the baby's clothes. The baby grabbed Sonu's finger and wouldn't let go. That night, on the video call, Papa cried happy tears. 'Our family keeps changing,' said Dadi, 'but the love only grows.'

summary: Families change over time.
Changes include births, marriages, moving for work, and death of elders.
A new baby needs a lot of care; older children may feel many mixed feelings.
We ourselves grow and change every year — height, teeth, skills.
Families can be nuclear, joint, single-parent or other kinds.
No kind of family is better than another — love and care matter most.
Marriage can make one family smaller and another bigger.
People often move to cities for work and keep in touch by phone and visits.
When families change, everyone should share the housework fairly.
Elders need care and respect; their stories teach us a lot.
A family tree shows how members are related.
practice: Write two changes that can happen in a family.
How might a child feel when a new baby is born? How can they help?
Write three ways in which you have changed since you were a baby.
What is the difference between a nuclear family and a joint family?
Why do some family members move to other cities?
How do families stay in touch when someone lives far away?
How should housework be shared when a family changes?
How can you help elderly people in your family?
Draw your family tree up to your grandparents.
Ask an elder how your family has changed in the last 20 years and write about it.

rd-school-c4-evs-c.ch11-the-valley-of-fl.title: The Valley of Flowers
rd-school-c4-evs-c.ch11-the-valley-of-fl.subtitle: A Himalayan valley that bursts into colour — and the flowers we eat, wear and celebrate with

sections.md:
In 1931, a group of British mountaineers led by **Frank Smythe** were climbing in the Himalayas. Tired and lost, they walked over a ridge — and stopped in amazement. In front of them lay a valley carpeted with **thousands of flowers** of every colour: blue, yellow, pink, purple, white. Smythe later wrote a book that made it famous as the **Valley of Flowers**.

Of course, the local shepherds and villagers already knew about the valley; they had grazed animals there for generations and called it *Bhyundar valley*. Today it is a **National Park** in **Uttarakhand** and a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

In this read we explore the valley, look closely at flowers, and discover how flowers are part of our food, festivals and daily life.

sections.h: A valley that blooms for a few months
sections.md:
The Valley of Flowers lies high up in the mountains — about **3,500 metres** above sea level. For most of the year it is covered in **snow**. When the snow melts and the **monsoon** rains come (roughly July to September), the valley wakes up and bursts into bloom.

You can find hundreds of kinds of flowers there, including the beautiful **Himalayan blue poppy**, wild roses, marigolds, primulas and orchids. Butterflies, bees and birds visit them. Animals like the musk deer and the Himalayan black bear live nearby.

The valley is protected: visitors may walk on the paths, but **must not pluck flowers**, camp in the valley, or leave plastic. If everyone picked just one flower, there would soon be none left!

fig.alt: Mountain valley changing from snow-covered to full of coloured flowers

check.q: In which state is the Valley of Flowers?
check.why: The Valley of Flowers National Park is high in the Himalayas of Uttarakhand.

sections.h: The botanist who stayed in the valley
sections.md:
After Smythe's book, many people wanted to see the valley. In 1939 a British woman named **Joan Margaret Legge** came there. She was a **botanist** — a scientist who studies plants. She walked across the slopes collecting and studying flowers.

One day, while collecting flowers on a steep, slippery rock, she slipped and fell, and lost her life. Her sister later came to the valley and built a small stone **memorial** for her. Even today, trekkers stop at this quiet grave among the flowers and remember a person who loved plants so much.

What do scientists like her do?
- **Observe** plants carefully and note where they grow.
- **Collect and press** samples to study later.
- **Name and record** new kinds of plants so others can learn about them.

But today, in a National Park, even scientists collect only with permission, so that the valley stays safe.

> **Think:** Would you like to be a botanist? Which plant would you study first?

check.q: What is a botanist?
check.why: Botanists are scientists who observe, collect, name and study plants.

sections.md:
Pick up a fallen flower (don't pluck a fresh one!) and look carefully:

- **Petals** — the colourful parts. Count them! A mustard flower has 4, a hibiscus (gudhal) 5, a lily 6.
- **Sepals** — small green leaf-like parts under the petals that protected the bud.
- **Centre parts** — thin threads with yellow powder (**pollen**) and a sticky tip in the middle.
- **Smell** — some are sweet (jasmine, rose), some have none.

Flowers are not just pretty. They are how many plants make **fruits and seeds**. Bees and butterflies visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen from one flower to another. Then the flower can turn into a fruit with seeds inside.

| Flower | Colour | No. of petals | Smell? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hibiscus | red | 5 | no |
| Mustard | yellow | 4 | slight |
| Rose | pink/red | many | yes |

fig.alt: Five-petalled red flower opening and closing

check.q: How do bees help flowers?
options: They carry pollen from flower to flower so fruits and seeds can form
check.why: While collecting nectar, bees carry pollen between flowers, which helps the flower make fruit and seeds.

sections.h: From bud to bloom, morning to night
sections.md:
Flowers do not stay the same. Watch one plant for a week:

1. A tight green **bud** appears, wrapped in sepals.
2. The bud swells and shows a hint of colour.
3. It **opens** into a full flower.
4. After some days the petals **wilt** and fall.
5. The part left behind may grow into a **fruit** with seeds.

Flowers also open at different **times of day**:
- **Lotus** and **sunflower** open with the morning sun.
- **Parijat** (night jasmine) and **raat ki rani** open and smell sweetest at night; parijat flowers fall to the ground by morning.
- The **four o'clock flower** is named for opening in the late afternoon!

**Activity — press a flower:** Place a fallen flower between two sheets of newspaper inside a heavy book. After a week it will be flat and dry. Stick it on a card to make a bookmark, and write its name, colour and the date you found it.

check.q: Which flower opens and smells sweetest at night?
check.why: Raat ki rani, whose name means 'queen of the night', opens and spreads its smell after dark.

sections.md:
Did you know you eat flowers? Some foods are actually flowers or flower buds:

- **Cauliflower** and **broccoli** — tight bunches of flower buds.
- **Banana flower** (kele ka phool) — cooked as a vegetable in Kerala, Bengal and the North-East.
- **Pumpkin flowers** — fried as fritters (pakoras).
- **Cloves** (laung) — dried flower buds used as a spice.
- **Saffron** (kesar) — threads from the crocus flower; grown in **Kashmir**; very costly because each flower gives only three tiny threads.
- **Gulkand** — a sweet jam made from rose petals.
- **Mahua** flowers — eaten and used by many tribal communities in central India.

check.q: Which of these is a dried flower bud used as a spice?
check.why: Cloves are the dried flower buds of the clove tree.

sections.md:
Flowers are everywhere in Indian life:

- **Garlands** of marigold and jasmine at weddings, temples and to welcome guests.
- **Rangoli** and **pookalam** — beautiful floor designs made with petals, especially during **Onam** in Kerala.
- **Gajra** — jasmine strings worn in the hair.
- **Perfumes** and **attar** — Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh is famous for perfume made from flowers.
- **Medicines** — some flowers, like hibiscus, are used in home remedies and hair oils.
- **Colours** — the flame-of-the-forest (palash/tesu) flower was traditionally used to make Holi colours.

Many people earn a living from flowers: farmers who grow them, sellers in **phool mandis**, garland-makers, perfume-makers.
keyTerms: Petal — the coloured part of a flower
Pollen — fine yellow powder in a flower
Bud — a flower before it opens
National Park — protected area for plants and animals
Pookalam — flower carpet made during Onam

sections.md:
Wild flowers are disappearing in many places because:

- people **pluck** them or dig them out,
- too many animals **graze**,
- forests and meadows are cleared for buildings and roads,
- **plastic and garbage** are thrown on mountains.

What can you do?

1. Enjoy flowers with your eyes and camera, not your hands.
2. Grow flowering plants at home or school.
3. Use flowers from plants grown for selling, not wild ones.
4. Carry your rubbish back when you visit a hill or park.

> **Did you know?** The **Neelakurinji** flower in Kerala's hills blooms only **once in 12 years**, turning whole hills blue!

check.q: Neelakurinji, which turns hills blue in Kerala, blooms once in —
check.why: Neelakurinji blooms together only once every twelve years, painting the hills of Munnar blue.

parts.md: Ritu's chacha was a forest guide near the Valley of Flowers. One August morning he took her up the path, past waterfalls and wet stones. Mist rolled over the slopes. 'Look,' he whispered, pointing.

Among the rocks stood a flower so blue it looked painted by the sky itself — a Himalayan blue poppy. Ritu reached out, then stopped. 'Can I take it home for Ma?' Chacha shook his head gently. 'If it stays, it makes seeds. Next year there will be five.'

So Ritu drew it in her notebook instead, colouring each petal carefully. Back home, Ma pinned the drawing on the kitchen wall. 'This one,' Ma said, 'will never wilt.' And on the mountain, the poppy kept nodding in the wind, scattering tiny seeds.

summary: The Valley of Flowers is in Uttarakhand, high in the Himalayas.
Frank Smythe made it famous in 1931; local people already knew it.
It is a National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It is snow-covered most of the year and blooms in the monsoon.
Botanist Joan Margaret Legge studied flowers there; a memorial to her stands in the valley.
Visitors must not pluck flowers or litter.
Flowers have petals, sepals and a centre with pollen.
A flower grows from a bud, blooms, wilts and may form a fruit.
Some flowers open in the morning, some at night.
We eat flowers: cauliflower, banana flower, clove, saffron, gulkand.
Flowers are used in garlands, rangoli, pookalam, perfumes and colours.
Neelakurinji blooms once in 12 years in Kerala; we must protect wild flowers.
practice: Where is the Valley of Flowers? When does it bloom?
Why are visitors not allowed to pluck flowers there?
Who was Margaret Legge and why is she remembered?
Name the parts of a flower you can see.
Write the stages from bud to fruit.
Name one flower that opens in the morning and one that opens at night.
Name four flowers or flower parts that we eat.
How are flowers used during festivals? Give two examples.
Why is saffron so costly?
Collect three fallen flowers and make a table of their colour, petals and smell.

rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch24-home-and-abroad.title: Home and Abroad
rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch24-home-and-abroad.subtitle: When your cousin lives across the sea, what changes — and what stays the same?

sections.md:
Imagine the postman, or a phone ping, bringing a message from your cousin who lives in another country. She writes: *"It is snowing here! I wore two sweaters and a cap to school. What are you wearing in Chennai?"* You look out of the window — it is hot and sticky, and you are in a cotton shirt.

This chapter is about exactly that feeling. Many Indian families have someone living **abroad** — in another country. When they visit, or when we visit them, we notice that many things are different: the **money**, the **language**, the **weather**, the **food**, even the **time on the clock**. And yet many things are the same: families love each other, children go to school, people celebrate festivals.

**Home** means the place where we live and feel we belong. **Abroad** means outside our own country. To go abroad, you usually need a **passport** (a small booklet from your government saying who you are and which country you belong to) and often a **visa** (permission from the other country to enter).

In this read we will travel in our minds, compare, and learn to respect differences.
keyTerms: Abroad — in a country other than your own
Passport — official booklet that shows your identity and nationality
Visa — permission to enter another country

check.q: Which document shows your identity and nationality when you travel to another country?
check.why: A passport is issued by your own country's government and proves who you are and which country you belong to.

sections.h: Money is different in every country
sections.md:
In India we pay with **rupees** (₹) and paise. If your uncle lives in the USA he pays with **dollars** ($). In England people use the **pound** (£), in Japan the **yen** (¥), in many European countries the **euro** (€), and in Bangladesh the **taka**.

The coins and notes look different too. Indian notes carry a picture of Mahatma Gandhi and have the value written in many Indian languages. Other countries print their own leaders, buildings, animals or birds.

One dollar is **not** equal to one rupee. The value changes from day to day. Suppose on some day 1 dollar = ₹83. Then a chocolate costing 2 dollars would cost about 2 × 83 = ₹166 in our money. That is why travellers **exchange** money at a bank or money-changer before they go abroad.

| Country | Money |
|---|---|
| India | Rupee (₹) |
| USA | Dollar ($) |
| UK | Pound (£) |
| Japan | Yen (¥) |
| France, Germany | Euro (€) |
| Nepal | Nepalese rupee |

*Did you know?* Nepal and Sri Lanka also call their money "rupee", but their rupees are not the same as ours.

check.q: If 1 dollar = ₹80 on a day, how many rupees is 3 dollars?
check.why: 3 × 80 = 240, so 3 dollars is worth ₹240 on that day.

sections.md:
When your cousin's classmates speak, you may hear **English, Arabic, French, Japanese** or many other languages. Even inside India we have over twenty officially listed languages! Learning a few words — *hello*, *thank you*, *please* — in another language is a lovely way to make friends.

**Food** also changes. A family in India may eat rice, dal, roti and sabzi. In Japan people often eat rice with fish and use chopsticks. In Italy, pasta and bread are common. In the Gulf countries, dates and flatbreads. Indians abroad often cook their home food too — so you will find idli, poha and parathas in kitchens across the world.

**Clothes** depend on weather and custom. Where winters are snowy, people wear thick coats, gloves, boots and woollen caps. Where it is hot, they choose light, loose cotton.

Notice: different does **not** mean better or worse. Every way of living suits its own place and people.
keyTerms: Custom — a usual way of doing things in a place
Culture — the language, food, clothes, festivals and beliefs of a group of people

check.q: Why do people in very cold countries wear thick coats and boots?
options: To keep warm in the cold weather
Because cotton is not sold there
check.why: Clothing mostly depends on climate, and thick woollen clothes trap warmth in cold places.

sections.md:
Your cousin in the USA calls at 8 o'clock in the morning — but for her it is still the evening before! How?

The Earth is round and keeps **spinning**. Only half of it faces the Sun at a time. When India faces the Sun, it is day here, while the other side of the Earth is in darkness and has night. So clocks in different countries show different times.

For example, when it is 12 noon in Delhi, it is around 6:30 in the morning in London, and around 1:30 at night in New York (the exact difference changes a little in different seasons). That is why families abroad plan their phone and video calls carefully!

Seasons can be opposite too. When India has summer in May, Australia, which is in the southern half of the Earth, has cool weather.

check.q: Why is it night in the USA when it is day in India?
options: The Earth is spinning and the USA is on the side away from the Sun
Clocks in the USA are broken
check.why: Only half of the spinning Earth faces the Sun at a time, so places on the other side have night.

sections.h: Missing home and making a new home
sections.md:
People go abroad for many reasons: to **study**, to **work**, to join family, or sometimes because they had to leave a difficult situation. Many Indians work in Gulf countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, and send money home to their families in Kerala, Punjab, Bihar and other states.

Living far away can feel lonely at first. People miss their grandparents, festival sweets, the smell of rain, their own language. So they form groups, celebrate Diwali, Eid, Onam, Christmas and Gurpurab together, and teach their children Indian songs and stories.

At the same time, they learn new things from the new place and make friends from many countries. Your cousin may come home with stories of a library on wheels, or a friend from Ghana!

**Think:** Has anyone from your family or neighbourhood gone to another state or country? What did they miss most? What new things did they learn?

check.q: Which of these is a common reason for people to go abroad?
check.why: Studying and working are among the most common reasons people move to other countries.

sections.md:
Let's make a comparison chart. It helps us see that every place has its own good things.

The big idea of the chapter is **respect**. When we meet people from other places — whether another country or another state of India — we should be curious, ask politely, and never make fun of their food, clothes or way of speaking.

*Did you know?* India's own people living abroad are often called the **Indian diaspora**, and they number in crores, living in almost every country in the world.

left.title: At home (India)
points: Languages: Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and many more

right.title: Abroad (example: Canada)
points: Festivals: Christmas, Thanksgiving — and Diwali by Indian families

parts.md: Meera in Patna woke up early because Bua was calling from Toronto. "Good morning, Meera!" said Bua — but behind her the window was dark. "Why is it dark there?" Meera asked. Bua laughed. "It's nine at night here. Your morning is my night!" Her little son Aarav waved, wearing a thick sweater. "It's minus ten degrees outside," he said proudly. Meera, fanning herself in the September heat, couldn't believe it.

Aarav held up a coin with a bird on it. "This is a loonie — one Canadian dollar!" Meera ran to fetch a ten-rupee coin. They compared — different size, different picture, different writing. "Can I buy samosas with a loonie in Patna?" Aarav asked. "Not unless you change it at a bank," said Papa from behind Meera. They promised to swap coins when Bua visited for Chhath. As the call ended, Aarav said one Hindi word he had learnt: "Dhanyavaad!" Meera smiled — so far away, and still family.

summary: Home is where we live and belong; abroad means another country.
Travelling abroad usually needs a passport and often a visa.
Each country has its own money: rupee, dollar, pound, yen, euro and more.
One dollar is not equal to one rupee; money is exchanged at banks.
Languages, food and clothes differ from place to place.
Clothes suit the climate — woollens for cold, cotton for heat.
The Earth spins, so when it is day in India it is night on the other side.
Seasons can be opposite in the northern and southern halves of the Earth.
People go abroad to study, work or join family.
Indians abroad keep their festivals and food alive and also learn new ways.
Different does not mean better or worse — respect all ways of living.

glossary.d: The money used in a country
Changing one country's money into another's
People who live away from their home country

practice: What is the difference between a passport and a visa?
Name the money used in India, the USA, the UK and Japan.
Why can't you use rupees directly to buy things in England?
Explain why your cousin in America may be sleeping when you are at school.
Make a chart comparing food and clothes in your home town with any one other country.
Write three questions you would ask a child who lives abroad.
Why should we never make fun of someone's food or language?
If 1 euro = ₹90, what is the cost of a 4-euro book in rupees?

rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch25-spicy-riddles.title: Spicy Riddles
rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch25-spicy-riddles.subtitle: Close your eyes, sniff the masala box — can you guess what's inside?

sections.h: The mystery of the masala dabba
sections.md:
In many Indian kitchens there is a round steel box with small bowls inside — the **masala dabba**. Open it and a cloud of smells rises: warm, sharp, sweet, smoky. Each bowl holds a **spice**.

This chapter plays a game of **riddles**. Someone describes a spice — its colour, shape, smell, taste — and you guess its name. Try this one:

> *I am small and black and round, I make you sneeze, I'm in rasam and in pepper-chicken.* Who am I?

Yes — **black pepper**! Now try:

> *I am yellow powder, I colour your dal and I'm put on cuts by grandmothers.* — **Turmeric (haldi)**.

We use our **senses** to recognise spices: **eyes** (colour, shape), **nose** (smell), **tongue** (taste) and even **fingers** (rough, smooth, powdery). Spices are **parts of plants** — seeds, bark, buds, roots, fruits or flowers — which are dried and used in small amounts to add flavour.
keyTerms: Spice — a dried plant part used in small amounts for flavour, smell or colour
Masala dabba — a box holding everyday spices

check.q: Which sense do we NOT usually use to identify a spice?
check.why: Spices do not make sounds, so we recognise them by how they look, smell, feel and taste.

sections.md:
Every spice comes from a plant, but from different parts:

| Spice | Plant part |
|---|---|
| Cumin (jeera), mustard (rai), coriander (dhaniya), fenugreek (methi) | Seeds |
| Cinnamon (dalchini) | Bark of a tree |
| Clove (laung) | Dried flower bud |
| Turmeric (haldi), ginger (adrak) | Underground stem (rhizome), often called root |
| Black pepper (kali mirch) | Dried fruit/berry of a climbing vine |
| Red chilli | Fruit, dried |
| Saffron (kesar) | Thin threads from a flower |
| Cardamom (elaichi) | Seed pods |

Isn't it amazing? Plants give us bark, buds, roots and seeds as spices. Saffron is the costliest spice of all — it takes many thousands of crocus flowers to make a small amount, and in India it grows mainly in Kashmir.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>text{font-family:sans-serif;font-size:15px;fill:#3a2a12}.l{stroke-dasharray:300;stroke-dashoffset:300;animation:d 3s ease forwards infinite}@keyframes d{to{stroke-dashoffset:0}}</style><rect width='600' height='330' fill='#fff8ec'/><rect y='250' width='600' height='80' fill='#a4744a'/><rect x='285' y='90' width='26' height='170' fill='#7b4a24'/><circle cx='298' cy='80' r='75' fill='#5aa646'/><circle cx='250' cy='60' r='9' fill='#e64a7a'><animate attributeName='r' values='7;11;7' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='340' cy='70' r='6' fill='#c43'/><circle cx='330' cy='100' r='6' fill='#c43'/><path d='M298 260 q-30 30 -70 40 M298 260 q20 35 60 45' stroke='#6b3c1c' stroke-width='6' fill='none'/><ellipse cx='228' cy='300' rx='18' ry='10' fill='#e8a317'/><g stroke='#333' stroke-width='2' fill='none'><path class='l' d='M250 60 L120 40'/><path class='l' d='M335 85 L480 50'/><path class='l' d='M290 180 L130 170'/><path class='l' d='M228 300 L110 290'/></g><text x='20' y='40'>Bud → clove</text><text x='470' y='45'>Fruit → pepper</text><text x='20' y='170'>Bark → cinnamon</text><text x='10' y='285'>Root → turmeric</text><text x='300' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='19'>Spices come from different plant parts</text></svg>
fig.caption: Bud, fruit, bark and root — spices come from many parts of plants (shown together on one imaginary plant).
fig.alt: A cartoon plant with labels pointing to bud, fruit, bark and root, each naming a spice.

check.q: Cinnamon (dalchini) comes from which part of a plant?
check.why: Cinnamon is the dried, rolled inner bark of a tree, which is why it looks like little scrolls of wood.

sections.h: Vegetable riddles: which part do we eat?
sections.md:
The chapter's riddles are not only about spices — vegetables can be riddles too! Try these:

> *I grow under the ground, I have eyes but cannot see.* — **Potato**

> *Peel me and you will cry, layer after layer.* — **Onion**

> *Green outside, red when ripe, I bite your tongue.* — **Chilli**

Like spices, every vegetable is a part of a plant:

| Part we eat | Examples |
|---|---|
| Root | carrot, radish (mooli), beetroot, sweet potato |
| Underground stem | potato, ginger, turmeric |
| Bulb (fleshy leaves) | onion, garlic |
| Stem | sugarcane, lotus stem (kamal kakdi) |
| Leaves | spinach (palak), methi, cabbage, coriander leaves |
| Flowers | cauliflower, broccoli, banana flower |
| Fruits | tomato, brinjal, ladyfinger (bhindi), cucumber, pumpkin |
| Seeds | peas, beans, corn, all the dals |

Some plants give us more than one thing: the coriander plant gives fresh **leaves** (hara dhaniya) and dried **seeds** (sabut dhaniya). Methi gives leaves to cook and seeds as a spice. Mustard gives leaves (*sarson ka saag*), seeds, and oil from the seeds!

> **Activity:** Look at today's lunch. Write each vegetable and spice, and the plant part it came from.

check.q: Which part of the plant is the potato?
check.why: A potato is a swollen underground stem; its 'eyes' are buds that can sprout into new plants.

sections.md:
India has many languages, so one spice may have many names. Here is how a few spices are called in some languages:

| English | Hindi | Tamil | Bengali | Marathi |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Turmeric | Haldi | Manjal | Holud | Halad |
| Cumin | Jeera | Seeragam | Jeere | Jire |
| Mustard | Rai / Sarson | Kadugu | Sorshe | Mohari |

Ask your grandparents or neighbours what they call the spices in their language and make your own chart. You will discover the same smell connects homes from Kashmir to Kanyakumari.

check.q: 'Manjal' in Tamil and 'Holud' in Bengali are names for which spice?
check.why: Both words mean turmeric, showing that one spice has different names in different Indian languages.

sections.h: Spices did more than flavour food
sections.md:
Spices are not only for taste. People use them in many ways:

- **Home remedies:** ginger-tulsi tea for a cold, ajwain for a stomach ache, turmeric milk at night. (A doctor should always be consulted when someone is really ill.)
- **Keeping food longer:** salt, chilli, turmeric and mustard oil help pickles (achaar) last for months.
- **Colour:** haldi turns food yellow; saffron gives a golden colour to kheer and biryani.
- **Festivals and rituals:** turmeric is used in weddings and pujas in many communities.

*Did you know?* Long ago, traders from faraway lands sailed to India for spices, especially black pepper from the Malabar coast of Kerala. Pepper was so valuable it was called **"black gold"**. In 1498 the Portuguese sailor **Vasco da Gama** reached Calicut (Kozhikode) by sea, partly in search of spices.

check.q: Why was black pepper once called 'black gold'?
options: It was very valuable in trade
check.why: Traders paid high prices for Indian pepper, so it was as precious as gold to them.

sections.md:
How does cumin reach your dal? A farmer grows the plant, waits for it to ripen, cuts and **dries** it in the sun, beats out the seeds, cleans them and sells them. Traders pack them; shops sell them; and at home they are **roasted** or **ground** in a mixer or on a stone grinder (sil-batta).

Some spices are used **whole** (cloves in pulao, jeera tadka), and some are **ground** into powder (garam masala, red chilli powder). Many families still make masala at home by roasting and grinding — the whole house smells wonderful!

India grows and uses more spices than almost any other country. Kerala is famous for pepper and cardamom, Rajasthan and Gujarat for cumin, Andhra Pradesh for chillies, and Kashmir for saffron.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>text{font-family:sans-serif;font-size:14px}.dot{animation:m 5s linear infinite}@keyframes m{from{transform:translateX(0)}to{transform:translateX(480px)}}</style><rect width='600' height='200' fill='#f4fff0'/><line x1='60' y1='100' x2='540' y2='100' stroke='#8c6' stroke-width='6'/><g font-size='30'><text x='40' y='90'>🌱</text><text x='155' y='90'>☀️</text><text x='275' y='90'>🚚</text><text x='395' y='90'>🏪</text><text x='510' y='90'>🍲</text></g><g text-anchor='middle'><text x='60' y='135'>Grow</text><text x='175' y='135'>Dry</text><text x='295' y='135'>Transport</text><text x='415' y='135'>Shop</text><text x='530' y='135'>Kitchen</text></g><circle class='dot' cx='60' cy='100' r='9' fill='#c0392b'/></svg>
fig.caption: A spice's journey: grown, dried, transported, sold, cooked.
fig.alt: A line of five icons from plant to cooking pot with a red dot travelling along it.

sections.h: Grow your own: seeds from the kitchen
sections.md:
Many spices are seeds — and seeds can grow! Try this simple experiment with an adult's help:

1. Take a small pot or a cut plastic bottle with a hole at the bottom. Fill it with soil.
2. Sow a few **methi** seeds in one pot, a few whole **dhaniya** seeds (gently crushed into two halves) in another, and **mustard** seeds in a third.
3. Water them lightly every day and keep them where they get some sunlight.
4. Note the day each one sprouts.

| Seed | Day sown | Day it sprouted | Height after 10 days |
|---|---|---|---|
| Methi | | | |
| Dhaniya | | | |
| Mustard | | | |

Methi usually sprouts in just a few days. In two to three weeks you may be able to pick fresh leaves for a paratha!

Why don't the seeds sprout inside the masala dabba? Because seeds need **water, air and the right warmth** to grow. Dry seeds kept in a closed box stay asleep.

check.q: Why don't seeds sprout inside the masala dabba?
check.why: Seeds need water (along with air and warmth) to sprout, and the spices in the dabba are kept dry.

sections.md:
Now it is your turn. A good riddle gives **three clues**: one about looks, one about smell or taste, one about use.

- *I'm green, I come in a pod, I make chai smell royal.* (cardamom)
- *I look like a tiny nail, I'm dark brown, I help a toothache.* (clove)
- *I'm tiny and black, I pop and crackle in hot oil in South Indian tadka.* (mustard seeds)

**Activity:** With an adult's permission, put 5 spices in small bowls. Blindfold a friend and let them identify by smell only. Do NOT let anyone smell chilli powder closely — it stings the nose and eyes!

check.q: 'I'm tiny and black, I pop in hot oil for South Indian tadka.' Who am I?
check.why: Black mustard seeds crackle when they hit hot oil and are used in tadka across South India.

parts.md: It was raining, and the cousins were bored. Dadi brought out her masala dabba and a dupatta. 'Whoever guesses the most spices with eyes closed gets the first hot pakora,' she announced. Little Kabir went first, sniffing hard. 'Jeera!' Correct. 'Elaichi!' Correct again.

Then Meera got a bowl of black pepper and sniffed too close. 'Aaachoo!' Everyone laughed. 'Pepper,' she said, wiping her nose. 'It told me its own name!' Dadi kept the chilli powder far away. 'Some riddles,' she said, 'you solve with your eyes, not your nose.'

At the end, Dadi asked one last riddle: 'I grow under the ground, I'm yellow inside, and I'm in every curry in this house.' 'Haldi!' they shouted together. The pakoras came out golden — and everyone got the first one at the same time.

summary: Spices are dried plant parts used in small amounts for flavour, smell and colour.
We identify spices using sight, smell, taste and touch.
Seeds: cumin, mustard, coriander, fenugreek.
Bark: cinnamon. Bud: clove. Root/rhizome: turmeric, ginger.
Fruits: black pepper, chilli. Flower threads: saffron.
Vegetables too are plant parts: roots, stems, bulbs, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds.
Some plants give several things — coriander gives leaves and seeds; mustard gives leaves, seeds and oil.
One spice has many names in Indian languages.
Spices are used in home remedies, pickles, colouring and rituals.
Kerala's pepper was once called 'black gold'; Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.
Spices travel from farm to kitchen: grow, dry, transport, sell, cook.
Spice seeds like methi can sprout when given water, air and warmth.
practice: Name two spices that are seeds and one that is bark.
Write a three-clue riddle for turmeric.
Name one vegetable each that is a root, a leaf, a fruit and a seed.
Which plant gives us both leaves and seeds that we eat?
Why do pickles not spoil quickly?
Find the name of cumin in two languages of your choice.
Which spice is the costliest and where in India does it grow?
Why did foreign traders come to Kerala long ago?
What do seeds need to sprout?

rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch26-defence-officer-.title: Defence Officer: Wahida
rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch26-defence-officer-.subtitle: A girl who dreamed big grew up to serve the nation in uniform

sections.h: A dream that started in school
sections.md:
Picture a young girl watching aeroplanes roar across the sky and thinking, *"One day, I want to do something like that."* In this chapter we meet **Wahida**, a woman who grew up to become an officer in the **Indian Navy** — working as a doctor and proudly leading her fellow officers in a parade.

When she was in school, many people believed defence jobs were "only for men". Wahida did not let that stop her. She studied hard, joined the **NCC** (National Cadet Corps) in school and college, learnt discipline and teamwork, and later studied medicine. She then joined the Navy as a doctor.

Her story teaches us that **girls and boys can both dream of any career** — doctor, pilot, sailor, engineer, soldier — if they prepare well and keep trying.
keyTerms: Defence — protecting a country
Officer — a person with a rank who leads others in the forces
NCC — National Cadet Corps, a youth organisation in schools and colleges that trains cadets in discipline and service

check.q: Which organisation in school and college helped Wahida learn discipline and teamwork?
check.why: The National Cadet Corps trains students in drill, discipline and service, a common first step towards the forces.

sections.md:
The chapter tells Wahida's story partly through what she shares in an interview. Here is her path, retold simply:

1. **School days:** She was a curious student who liked science and enjoyed sports. Her family encouraged her studies.
2. **NCC cadet:** In NCC she learnt drill, camping, map-reading and how to work in a team. She went to camps and saw how officers lead.
3. **Medical college:** She studied for many years to become a doctor — hard work, long hours, many exams.
4. **Joining the Navy:** She was selected as a doctor in the Navy and trained to live and work like a naval officer — swimming, drill, life on ships.
5. **Leading the parade:** She was given the honour of leading a marching contingent in a big parade — a moment of great pride for her and her family.

Notice how each step built on the one before. None of it happened in one day.

> **Talk about it:** What would you like to be when you grow up? Write the steps you think you will need to get there, like Wahida's ladder.

items.what: Studies science, plays sports
Learns drill, discipline and teamwork
Becomes a doctor
Joins as a doctor-officer and trains for life at sea
Leads a contingent with pride

fig.caption: Wahida's ladder to her dream.

check.q: What did Wahida study to become a doctor in the Navy?
check.why: Navy doctors first study medicine at a medical college before joining the forces.

sections.md:
India's armed forces have three main parts:

| Force | Works on | Uniform colour (usual) | Examples of work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Army** | Land | Olive green | Guards borders, mountains and deserts |
| **Navy** | Sea | White (and navy blue) | Ships and submarines guard our coasts and seas |
| **Air Force** | Sky | Blue-grey | Fighter jets, transport planes, helicopters |

India has a long coastline of about 7,500 km, so the Navy has an important job. Its ships carry sailors, doctors, engineers, cooks and pilots — a little floating town!

All three forces also help during **disasters**: floods, earthquakes, cyclones and landslides. They rescue people by boat and helicopter, set up medical camps and deliver food. Doctors like Wahida treat the injured.

check.q: Which force guards India's seas and coasts?
check.why: The Navy uses ships and submarines to protect India's long coastline and the seas around it.

sections.md:
An officer's day begins early — often before sunrise — with **exercise** and **drill** (marching in step). Then there is work: for a doctor, checking patients; for an engineer, repairing machines; for a pilot, flying practice.

Officers must be:
- **Physically fit** — they run, swim and train regularly.
- **Disciplined** — on time, neat, following rules.
- **Brave and calm** — able to think in danger.
- **Team players** — nobody works alone on a ship or in a camp.

They may be posted far from home: snowy mountains, deserts, islands or ships at sea for weeks. Their families often move from city to city. On special days such as **Republic Day (26 January)** and **Navy Day (4 December)**, officers march in parades, and it is a great honour to lead one.

*Did you know?* Women today serve in all three forces — as pilots flying fighter jets, as doctors, engineers, and officers on warships.

check.q: On which day does India celebrate Republic Day with a grand parade?
check.why: India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated each year as Republic Day with a parade in New Delhi.

sections.md:
Have you noticed the stripes, stars and badges on uniforms? They show a person's **rank** — how senior they are. Ranks help everyone know who leads a team.

A few examples:
- **Army:** Lieutenant, Captain, Major, Colonel, General
- **Navy:** Sub-Lieutenant, Lieutenant, Commander, Captain, Admiral
- **Air Force:** Flying Officer, Flight Lieutenant, Squadron Leader, Wing Commander, Air Marshal

A uniform makes people look **equal** and part of one team, no matter which state, religion or language they come from. It also has practical uses: Army camouflage helps soldiers hide in forests; the Navy's white keeps sailors cooler in the sun at sea.

Medals are given for bravery and service. The highest wartime bravery award in India is the **Param Vir Chakra**.

check.q: What do the stripes and stars on a uniform mainly show?
check.why: Badges and stripes show rank, so everyone knows who leads and who follows orders.

sections.h: Other people in uniform who keep us safe
sections.md:
The armed forces are not the only people in uniform. Many others protect and help us every day:

| Who | What they do | How to reach them |
|---|---|---|
| **Police** | keep law and order, help lost children, control traffic | 112 (emergency) |
| **Fire brigade** | put out fires, rescue people trapped in buildings | 101 / 112 |
| **Ambulance staff** | carry sick and injured people to hospital | 108 in many states / 112 |
| **Coast Guard** | guard the sea near the coast, rescue fishermen | through the coastal authorities |
| **Disaster response teams** | rescue people in floods and earthquakes | called in by the government |

Each uniform is different so that people can recognise them quickly in a crowd or an emergency. Nurses, postal workers, bus conductors and school guards also wear uniforms.

**Activity:** Draw three uniforms you have seen near your home. Write who wears it and what work they do. Learn the emergency number **112** by heart, and tell a grown-up if you ever need help.

check.q: Which single number can you call for emergency help in India?
check.why: 112 is India's single emergency helpline that connects you to police, fire and ambulance services.

sections.h: Girls can, boys can — everyone can
sections.md:
Wahida's story is also about **breaking stereotypes**. A stereotype is a fixed idea like "girls can't be soldiers" or "boys can't cook". Such ideas are unfair and untrue.

Think of jobs around you: nurses, drivers, pilots, chefs, teachers, police officers. Each can be done by anyone who learns the skills. In defence, women once could join only a few branches; today their roles keep growing.

**Talk about it:** Who in your family or neighbourhood does a job people don't expect? How did they get there? What might stop a child from following a dream — and how can families and schools help?

To prepare for a defence career, students can join **NCC**, play sports, study well (especially science and maths for many roles), and later clear entrance exams like those for the National Defence Academy.

left.title: Stereotype says…
points: Only men can join the forces

right.title: Truth is…
points: Women serve in Army, Navy and Air Force
Women fly fighter jets for India

check.q: Which statement is a stereotype?
check.why: Saying girls can't be pilots is an unfair fixed idea; many Indian women fly aircraft today.

parts.md: Rain had fallen for three days. In a small village near the river, water climbed the steps of Zoya's house. Her grandfather had a fever and could not walk far. Then, through the rain, came the thud-thud of a helicopter and the hum of a rubber boat. Sailors in orange life jackets helped everyone in. A woman officer with a red-cross bag knelt by Grandpa, checked his pulse and gave him medicine.

At the relief camp, Zoya asked, "Are you a nurse?" The officer smiled. "I'm a Navy doctor. Surgeon Lieutenant, to be exact." "Girls can be in the Navy?" Zoya whispered. "Girls can be anything they prepare for," the doctor said, handing her a biscuit packet. That night, warm and dry, Zoya drew a ship in her notebook — with herself on the deck, in white uniform.

summary: Wahida became a doctor and officer in the Indian Navy and led a parade.
She prepared step by step: school, NCC, medical college, Navy training.
India's armed forces: Army (land), Navy (sea), Air Force (sky).
Forces protect borders and also rescue people in floods, earthquakes and cyclones.
Officers need fitness, discipline, courage and teamwork.
Badges and stripes show rank; uniforms make everyone equal and serve practical purposes.
Republic Day is 26 January; Navy Day is 4 December.
Police, fire brigade, ambulance staff and the Coast Guard also serve in uniform.
112 is India's single emergency number.
Women today serve in all three forces, including as fighter pilots.
Stereotypes about jobs for girls or boys are unfair and untrue.
practice: Name the three armed forces and where each works.
Write the steps Wahida took to become a Navy doctor.
Write two ways the forces help during disasters.
What qualities does a defence officer need?
Name three other people who wear uniforms and say what they do.
What number would you call in an emergency?
What is a stereotype? Give one example and explain why it is wrong.
Why do soldiers in forests wear camouflage uniforms?
Interview an adult about their job and write five lines about it.
Would you like to join the forces? Give reasons.

rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch27-chuskit-goes-to-.title: Chuskit Goes to School
rd-school-c4-evs-e.ch27-chuskit-goes-to-.subtitle: A wheelchair, a mountain village, and friends who built a way

sections.h: A girl who watched from the window
sections.md:
High in the mountains of **Ladakh**, where the sky is deep blue and winters are freezing, lives a girl named **Chuskit**. She is bright and curious and loves to learn — but for a long time she could only **watch** other children walk to school. Chuskit's legs did not work like theirs; she could not walk.

One day her father brought home a **wheelchair**. Now Chuskit could move around the house and courtyard. But the road to school had a big problem: a small **stream** with stones to hop across, and a rough path. A wheelchair could not cross it.

This chapter is about how a whole community — a friend, a teacher, children and villagers — found a way. It teaches us about **inclusion**: making sure that *everyone* can take part in school and life.
keyTerms: Wheelchair — a chair with wheels for people who cannot walk easily
Inclusion — making sure everyone is included and nobody is left out
Ladakh — a high, cold mountain region in the far north of India

check.q: What was the main thing stopping Chuskit's wheelchair from reaching school?
options: A stream and rough path on the way
check.why: The stream had only stepping stones, which a wheelchair cannot cross.

sections.md:
Let us walk through Chuskit's story slowly, in our own words.

**Scene 1 — The dream.** Chuskit is ten. Every morning she hears children laughing on their way to school. She has learnt some letters at home and she imagines sitting in a classroom, reading, drawing, playing at break time.

**Scene 2 — The wheelchair.** Her father brings home a wheelchair. Chuskit practises rolling across the courtyard, turning the wheels with her hands until her arms grow strong. Her family feels hopeful: maybe now she can go to school.

**Scene 3 — The problem.** Her family worries about the path. It is bumpy and steep in places, and the stream can only be crossed by jumping from stone to stone. Nobody can carry a wheelchair across that every day.

**Scene 4 — A friend notices.** Abdul, a boy from the neighbourhood, keeps thinking about Chuskit sitting at home. He decides that this is not just *her* problem.

**Scene 5 — The school acts.** The headmaster listens, and the whole school gets to work (see the next section).

**Scene 6 — The first day.** Chuskit rolls into her classroom. Her classmates cheer. She is no longer watching school from outside — she is part of it.

> **Think:** How do you think Chuskit felt on each of these days? Write one feeling word for each scene.

check.q: Why did Chuskit practise turning the wheels in the courtyard?
options: To make her arms strong enough to move the wheelchair herself
Because she was bored of school
check.why: Moving a wheelchair needs strong arms, so practising helped her move about on her own.

sections.md:
Chuskit's neighbour **Abdul**, a boy from the same school, wanted to help. He talked to the headmaster and his classmates. The headmaster called a meeting. The children and teachers decided: *we will build a small bridge and level the path!*

Everyone joined in. Children carried stones, teachers and parents helped dig and arrange them, and soon there was a **flat path** and a sturdy little **bridge** across the stream. On the first morning, Abdul pushed Chuskit's wheelchair along the new path — and she rolled right into her classroom, smiling.

What do we learn?
- One person's problem can become **everyone's project**.
- Children can **speak up** and make change happen.
- Small changes — a ramp, a bridge, a wider door — can open a whole world for someone.
