check.q: Who first decided to help Chuskit reach school?
check.why: Abdul, her schoolmate and neighbour, took the idea to the headmaster and classmates.

sections.md:
Chuskit's story happens in a special place. **Ladakh** is a cold desert high in the Himalayas, much of it more than 3,000 metres above sea level.

- **Winters** are extremely cold, often far below 0 °C. Rivers and streams can freeze.
- Very **little rain** falls; water comes mostly from melting snow and glaciers.
- Houses are made of **stone and mud bricks** with flat roofs, thick walls and small windows to keep warmth inside.
- People keep **yaks, goats and sheep**; the soft wool of the Changthangi goat gives **pashmina**.
- Children wear thick woollen clothes and caps. A common greeting is **"Julley!"**

Travelling in the mountains is hard for anyone, which makes Chuskit's journey even more special.

check.q: Why do houses in Ladakh have thick walls and small windows?
options: To keep the warmth inside in the cold
To keep out sunlight in summer only
check.why: Thick walls and small windows reduce heat loss, keeping homes warmer in Ladakh's freezing winters.

sections.h: Why a ramp works: a little science
sections.md:
Have you ever tried to push a loaded trolley or a cycle up a step? It gets stuck. But push it up a **gentle slope** and it rolls. Why?

- A wheel can roll smoothly over a surface that rises **little by little**.
- A step is a sudden jump up; the wheel hits its edge and stops.
- A ramp spreads the same height over a **longer distance**, so each push needs less effort.

**Try this:** Make a ramp from a book and a ruler. Roll a toy car or a round pencil up it. Now make the ramp steeper by adding more books. Which is easier to push the car up — the gentle ramp or the steep one?

This is why ramps for wheelchairs are long and gentle, not short and steep. Good ramps also have **handrails** and a rough surface so wheels do not slip.

> **Did you know?** The same idea is used on mountain roads in Ladakh: instead of climbing straight up, roads zig-zag in long bends so vehicles can climb slowly.

check.q: Which ramp is easiest to push a wheelchair up?
check.why: A long gentle slope spreads the climb over a bigger distance, so each push needs less force.

sections.md:
Some people cannot walk, some cannot see, some cannot hear, and some find reading or moving harder. These are called **disabilities** — but often the real problem is a place built without thinking of them. A staircase is a barrier for a wheelchair; a **ramp** is not.

Things that make a school **accessible**:
- **Ramps** next to steps, with handrails
- **Wide doors** and toilets a wheelchair can enter
- **Braille** books and talking computers for children who cannot see
- **Sign language** for children who cannot hear
- Desks at the right height, and friends who help without taking over

**Look around your school.** Can a classmate in a wheelchair reach the library, the toilet, the playground? Make a list and share it with your teacher.

*Did you know?* Louis Braille, who invented the dot alphabet used by blind people around the world, was himself blind and created it as a teenager.
keyTerms: Accessible — easy for everyone, including people with disabilities, to reach and use
Ramp — a gentle slope instead of steps
Braille — raised-dot writing read by touch

check.q: Which change would most help a wheelchair user enter a building with steps?
check.why: A gentle ramp lets wheels roll up where steps would block them.

sections.h: Every child has the right to learn
sections.md:
In India, every child between **6 and 14 years** has the right to free schooling under a law called the **Right to Education Act**. This includes children with disabilities. Schools are expected to welcome them and make the changes they need.

But a law alone is not enough. Chuskit reached school because **people cared**: a friend who noticed, a headmaster who listened, classmates who carried stones.

Around you there may be children who do not go to school — because they must work, because their family moves often, or because the school is hard to reach. What could your class do? You could:
- tell your teacher about a child who wants to study,
- share old books and stationery,
- help a new classmate feel welcome.

> **Talk about it:** If you could change one thing in your school to make it better for everyone, what would it be?

check.q: Under the Right to Education Act, which children have the right to free schooling?
check.why: The law gives every child from 6 to 14 years, including children with disabilities, the right to free schooling.

sections.md:
Being a good friend to someone with a disability is simple:

1. **Treat them as a friend first** — talk to them directly, not to the person with them.
2. **Ask before helping** — "Shall I push?" Don't just grab the wheelchair.
3. **Include them in games** — change the game a little if needed so everyone can play.
4. **Never tease or stare.**
5. **Speak up** if a place is not accessible.

Chuskit did not want pity — she wanted to learn, play and laugh like everyone else. With friends like Abdul and a school that cared, she could.

check.q: What is the polite thing to do before pushing someone's wheelchair?
check.why: Asking first respects the person's choice; they know best what help they need.

parts.md: On Saturday morning the whole school came to the stream with baskets. The little ones carried pebbles, the big ones rolled heavy flat stones, and Abdul's uncle brought planks of poplar wood. 'Julley!' everyone called to Chuskit, who watched from her wheelchair on the bank.

They made a chain — hand to hand to hand — passing stones down to the water. By lunch the path was smooth. By evening the planks lay across the stream, tied and wedged firm. Abdul jumped on it twice. 'It doesn't wobble!'

On Monday, Chuskit wore her new cap and a bag her mother had stitched. Abdul pushed, then let go. 'You do the bridge yourself,' he said. She rolled across, slowly, the water singing below. At the school gate, thirty children were waiting — clapping.

summary: Chuskit, a girl in Ladakh, could not walk and longed to go to school.
She got a wheelchair, but a stream and rough path blocked the way.
Her friend Abdul and the school community built a path and bridge.
Children can speak up and lead change.
Ladakh is a high, cold desert; houses have thick walls and small windows.
People in Ladakh keep yaks, goats and sheep; 'Julley' is a greeting.
A long gentle ramp is easier for wheels than a step or a steep slope.
Accessible places have ramps, wide doors, Braille and sign language.
Often the barrier is the building, not the person.
The Right to Education Act gives every child aged 6–14 the right to free schooling.
Ask before helping; include everyone in games; never tease.
Inclusion means nobody is left out.
practice: Why could Chuskit not go to school at first?
How did Abdul and the others solve the problem?
Retell Chuskit's story in six short sentences.
Write three features of houses in Ladakh and why they are built that way.
Why is a ramp easier than steps for a wheelchair?
Name four things that make a school accessible.
Survey your school: list two places a wheelchair user could not reach.
What is Braille? Who invented it?
How would you change a game of kho-kho so a friend in a wheelchair can play?
Write a short letter to your headmaster asking for a ramp.

rd-school-c4-evs-e.revision.title: Class 4 EVS — The Whole Book in One Read
rd-school-c4-evs-e.revision.subtitle: Revise all 27 chapters of Looking Around, chapter by chapter

sections.h: How to use this revision read
sections.md:
Your Class 4 EVS book, *Looking Around*, has **27 chapters**. It does not split into 'science' and 'social studies' — it looks at the world **around** you through big themes: **family and friends** (people, animals, plants), **food**, **water**, **shelter**, **travel**, and **things we make and do**.

This read goes through every chapter **in book order**, giving the key ideas you must remember. After each group there is a quick check. At the end you will find a summary and practice questions that mix all chapters.

| Chapters | What they are mostly about |
|---|---|
| 1–5 | school journeys, animals, trees, bees |
| 6–10 | travel, families, games |
| 11–16 | flowers, homes, rivers, farming, markets, animal homes |
| 17–21 | city life, water, plants, food |
| 22–27 | community, crafts, other countries, spices, careers, inclusion |

> **Tip:** Read one group a day, then try to explain it aloud to someone at home — that is the best way to remember.

**1. Going to School** — Children across India reach school in amazing ways: a **bamboo bridge** over a stream in Assam, a **trolley** pulled along ropes across a river, a **vallam** (small wooden boat) in Kerala, **camel carts** and **bullock carts** in deserts, cycles along village roads, and walking over snow in the hills. Children cross rivers, jungles and deserts because they want to learn.

**2. Ear to Ear** — Animals have very different ears: elephants have huge ones, while birds, snakes and lizards have only ear holes. Animals whose ears we can see usually have **hair or fur** on their skin and **give birth** to young ones. Animals without visible ears (like birds) usually **lay eggs**. Skin can be spotted, striped or patterned.

**3. A Day with Nandu** — Elephants live in **herds** of mostly females and young ones, led by the **oldest female**. Male elephants leave the herd at about 14–15 years. An elephant eats for many hours a day, needs a lot of water, loves mud baths that keep its skin cool and free of insects.

**4. The Story of Amrita** — In Khejadli near Jodhpur, the **Bishnoi** people protected khejri trees. When the king's men came to cut them, **Amrita Devi** and many villagers hugged the trees and gave their lives. The king then stopped tree-cutting in Bishnoi villages. The **Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award** honours nature protectors; the later **Chipko** movement also saved trees.

**5. Anita and the Honeybees** — Anita Kushwaha of Bochaha, Muzaffarpur (Bihar) learnt **beekeeping** and kept studying. A hive has one **queen** (lays eggs), many **workers** (collect nectar, make honey and wax) and some **drones**. Bees help flowers make fruits. **Salim Ali**, the *Birdman of India*, studied birds all his life.

check.q: Animals whose ears we can see usually —
options: give birth to young ones and have hair
check.why: In the chapter Ear to Ear, animals with visible ears usually have hair on their bodies and give birth to babies.

sections.md:
**6. Omana's Journey** — Omana travels by a long-distance train to Kerala and keeps a **diary**. A **ticket** shows train number, stations, date, time, class, coach, berth and fare. The view changes from fields to rivers to hills and coconut trees; houses change with the **climate**. **Tunnels** go through hills, **bridges** cross rivers.

**7. From the Window** — Along the **Konkan** coast the train crosses rivers like the **Mandovi** in Goa and passes many tunnels. Nearby trees seem to rush past while far hills move slowly. **Signals**: red stop, yellow caution, green go.

**8. Reaching Grandmother's House** — Transport on **land, water and air**, powered by people, animals or fuel. Bridges made of cement, iron, bamboo, rope, and Meghalaya's **living root bridges**. In flood areas, houses on stilts and boats are part of daily life.

**9. Changing Families** — Families change: a baby is born, someone marries, a parent moves for work, an elder passes away. Families may be **nuclear** or **joint**; all need love and shared work. A **family tree** shows how members are related.

**10. Hu Tu Tu, Hu Tu Tu** — **Kabaddi** is played by two teams; a **raider** chants in one breath, touches opponents and returns. **Rules** keep games fair and safe. Girls and boys both have the right to play. **Karnam Malleswari** became the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal (weightlifting, Sydney 2000).

fig.alt: A train moving towards a tunnel in a hill

check.q: In kabaddi, what must the raider do?
options: Chant in one breath while trying to touch opponents
check.why: The raider keeps chanting 'kabaddi' in a single breath while tagging opponents and returning home.

sections.h: Chapters 11–16: Flowers, homes, rivers, farms and markets
sections.md:
**11. The Valley of Flowers** — In **Uttarakhand**, a high valley blooms in the monsoon; Frank Smythe made it famous in 1931. Flowers have petals, sepals and pollen; bees carry pollen so fruits form. We eat flowers (cauliflower, banana flower, clove, saffron) and use them in garlands, rangoli and perfume. Neelakurinji blooms once in 12 years.

**12. Changing Times** — Houses have changed: once made of **mud, wood, stone and thatch**, now often of **bricks, cement, iron and glass**. People shift homes; houses in different places suit the local weather and materials. Building a house needs many workers — masons, carpenters, labourers.

**13. A River's Tale** — A river begins clean in the mountains, flows past villages and cities, and slowly becomes **dirty** from waste, sewage and factory waste. Dirty water harms fish, plants and people. We must not throw garbage in rivers.

**14. Basva's Farm** — Farmers **plough, sow, water, weed, spray and harvest**. Farm tools and machines (plough, sickle, tractor) help. Crops depend on rain and irrigation; natural manure keeps soil healthy.

**15. From Market to Home** — Vegetables and fruits travel from **farm → mandi → vendor → home**. Prices change with season; leafy vegetables spoil quickly. Hawkers, carts and big markets each play a part.

**16. A Busy Month** — Animals have busy routines: a **crow** builds a nest, an **ant** colony stores food, a **cat** cares for kittens, a **honeybee** collects nectar. Each animal works for food and shelter.

check.q: What makes a river dirty as it flows past cities?
check.why: In A River's Tale, waste and sewage from towns and factories pollute the river as it flows downstream.

sections.h: Chapters 17–21: City life, water, plants and food
sections.md:
**17. Nandita in Mumbai** — Nandita's family lives in a crowded part of a big city with little space and shared water. People move to cities for work. We should understand others' lives with respect, never look down on anyone.

**18. Too Much Water, Too Little Water** — Some places get **floods**, others suffer **drought** and must fetch water from far away. **Rainwater harvesting**, old tanks and **stepwells**, and saving every drop help.

**19. Abdul in the Garden** — **Roots** hold plants in the soil, take in water and may store food. Some roots are eaten (carrot, radish, beetroot, turnip). Roots can be thick tap roots or thin bunches of fibrous roots.

**20. Eating Together** — Eating together shows care and builds friendship. The government **mid-day meal** gives children a cooked meal in school. Everyone needs enough healthy food; we should not waste it.

**21. Food and Fun** — Children in a school or hostel share food, games and chores. Different regions have different foods, and festivals bring special dishes. Learning to share food and work is part of growing up.

head: Chapter
One-line memory hook
rows: Big city, small rooms, shared taps
Floods here, drought there — save rain
fig.caption: Quick hooks for chapters 17–21.

check.q: Which of these is a root that we eat?
check.why: Carrot is a swollen tap root that stores food; potato is a stem, onion a bulb and cauliflower a flower.

sections.md:
**22. The World in My Home** — Talks about fairness at home and in society: are boys and girls treated equally? Do all family members share work and respect? Everyone deserves equal care and respect.

**23. Pochampalli** — In **Pochampalli** (Telangana), weaver families make **ikat** sarees. Threads are **tied and dyed** in patterns *before* weaving, so the design appears as the cloth is woven on the **loom**. Cotton and silk threads are used.

**24. Home and Abroad** — Other countries have different **money** (dollar, pound, yen), **languages**, **clothes**, food and **time** of day. When it is morning in India, it may be night in the USA.

**25. Spicy Riddles** — Spices are plant parts: seeds (jeera, rai), bark (cinnamon), buds (clove), roots/rhizomes (haldi, ginger), fruits (pepper, chilli), flower threads (saffron). Vegetables too are roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. Pepper was once called 'black gold'.

**26. Defence Officer: Wahida** — Wahida, a Navy doctor, led a parade. The **Army** (land), **Navy** (sea) and **Air Force** (sky) protect India and help in disasters. Girls and boys can choose any career.

**27. Chuskit Goes to School** — In Ladakh, Chuskit, who used a wheelchair, could not cross a stream to school. Her friend **Abdul** and the school built a path and bridge. **Inclusion** and **accessible** places (ramps, wide doors, Braille) let everyone learn.

check.q: In ikat weaving, when are threads dyed?
options: Before weaving, by tying and dyeing
check.why: Ikat threads are tied and dyed in patterns before weaving, so the design appears as the cloth is woven.

sections.h: Big ideas that join the whole book
sections.md:
Look back and you will notice ideas that keep returning:

1. **Everything is connected.** Trees give shelter to birds, bees make fruits possible, rivers feed farms, farms feed markets, markets feed homes.
2. **People live differently because places are different.** Houses on stilts, sloping roofs, thick walls; boats, camels and jeeps — each suits its land and weather.
3. **Respect for everyone.** Girls and boys can play kabaddi and join the Navy; children with disabilities have a right to school; every job and every family deserves dignity.
4. **Care for nature.** Amrita Devi's trees, the Valley of Flowers, a clean river, saved water — protecting nature protects us.
5. **Observe and ask.** From Omana's window to Salim Ali's birds, the book wants you to look carefully, ask *why*, and record what you find.

> **Final challenge:** Pick any three chapters and draw one picture that connects them — for example, a river (ch. 13) watering Basva's farm (ch. 14) whose vegetables go to market (ch. 15).

check.q: Which chapter pair best shows that 'everything is connected'?
options: Basva's Farm and From Market to Home
Hu Tu Tu and Home and Abroad
Ear to Ear and Defence Officer
check.why: Crops grown on Basva's farm travel to the market and then to our homes, linking farming to the food we eat.

summary: Class 4 EVS has 27 chapters grouped around family and friends, food, water, shelter, travel and things we make and do.
Children reach school by bamboo bridges, boats, trolleys, carts and on foot (ch. 1).
Animals with visible ears usually have hair and give birth; birds have ear holes and lay eggs (ch. 2).
Elephant herds are led by the oldest female (ch. 3).
The Bishnois and Amrita Devi protected khejri trees (ch. 4).
Bees live in colonies of queen, workers and drones (ch. 5).
Train journeys, tunnels, bridges and signals (ch. 6–8).
Families change; kabaddi teaches rules and teamwork (ch. 9–10).
Flowers, changing houses, a polluted river, farming and markets (ch. 11–15).
Animals are busy finding food and shelter (ch. 16).
City life, floods and droughts, roots, and sharing food (ch. 17–21).
Ikat weaving at Pochampalli; different money and time abroad (ch. 23–24).
Spices are plant parts; Wahida served in the Navy; Chuskit's bridge shows inclusion (ch. 25–27).

rd-school-c4-english-b.revision.title: Class 4 English · Revision & Practice
rd-school-c4-english-b.revision.subtitle: All ten units of the book in one friendly journey

sections.md:
You have read ten units this year — poems that sing and stories that surprise. This read walks through every unit quickly so you can remember the **characters, events, lessons and words**. Use it before your exam, and keep your textbook open beside you.

Each unit pairs **one poem** with **one story**:

| Unit | Poem | Story |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Wake Up! | Neha's Alarm Clock |
| 2 | Noses | The Little Fir Tree |
| 3 | Run! | Nasruddin's Aim |
| 4 | Why? | Alice in Wonderland |
| 5 | Don't be Afraid of the Dark | Helen Keller |
| 6 | The Donkey / I Had a Little Pony | The Milkman's Cow |
| 7 | Hiawatha | The Scholar's Mother Tongue |
| 8 | A Watering Rhyme | The Giving Tree |
| 9 | Books | Going to Buy a Book |
| 10 | The Naughty Boy | Pinocchio |

sections.md:
**Unit 1 · Wake Up!** A cheerful poem calling a sleepy child to get up because the morning is full of life — birds singing, the sun shining, flowers opening.
**Neha's Alarm Clock**: Neha dislikes her loud alarm clock. One day it stops working, but she still wakes on time — because nature (a bird, the light, sounds of the morning) is the best alarm clock!

**Unit 2 · Noses** A funny poem about the poet looking at his own nose in the mirror and wondering about its shape and holes.
**The Little Fir Tree**: a small fir tree is unhappy with its needles and wishes for leaves of gold, then glass, then soft green leaves — each wish goes wrong (stolen, broken, eaten). At last it happily wants its own needles back. *Lesson: be happy as you are.*

**Unit 3 · Run!** A poem full of action words about running and racing.
**Nasruddin's Aim**: the clever Mulla Nasruddin shoots arrows and misses each time, but has a witty excuse for every miss — and when he finally hits, he claims that one as his own shot!

check.q: In The Little Fir Tree, what did the tree want at the end?
check.why: After every new kind of leaf caused trouble, the fir tree realised its own needles suited it best.

sections.md:
**Unit 4 · Why?** A poem about a curious child who keeps asking *why* — the best way to learn.
**Alice in Wonderland** (by Lewis Carroll): Alice falls down a rabbit-hole, very slowly, past cupboards and shelves, wondering if she will come out on the other side of the Earth. She lands in a hall full of locked doors.

**Unit 5 · Don't be Afraid of the Dark** A gentle poem that comforts a child: the dark is just the night resting, and stars and Moon keep watch.
**Helen Keller**: Helen (1880–1968) could not see or hear from the age of about two. Her teacher **Anne Sullivan** spelled words into her hand. At a water pump, Helen understood that the letters w-a-t-e-r meant the cool thing flowing over her hand. She went on to study, write books and help many people. *Lesson: courage and a patient teacher can open the world.*

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#eef7ff'/><rect x='120' y='60' width='30' height='120' fill='#555'/><path d='M150 80 L200 80 L200 95' stroke='#555' stroke-width='12' fill='none'/><g fill='#3a8ee6'><rect x='194' y='100' width='12' height='10'><animate attributeName='y' values='100;200' dur='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='194' y='140' width='12' height='10'><animate attributeName='y' values='140;220' dur='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><ellipse cx='200' cy='225' rx='40' ry='10' fill='#9fd0ff'/><g font-family='monospace' font-size='34' fill='#c0392b'><text x='300' y='140'>W<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='340' y='140'>A<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;1;1' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='380' y='140'>T<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;0;1;1' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='420' y='140'>E<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;0;0;1;1' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='460' y='140'>R<animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;0;0;0;0;1' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text></g></svg>

fig.alt: Water flowing from a pump while the letters W A T E R appear one by one.

check.q: Who taught Helen Keller by spelling words into her hand?
check.why: Anne Sullivan was Helen's patient teacher who spelled words into her hand.

sections.md:
**Unit 6 · The Donkey** and **I Had a Little Pony** — two short animal poems. One is a kind poem to a donkey; in the other, a child lends a pony to a lady who rides it too hard, so the child will never lend it again. *Lesson: be kind to animals.*
**The Milkman's Cow**: a cow wanders off and sits in a street, refusing to move. People try pushing and pulling with no luck — until someone simply holds out some hay, and the cow follows. *Lesson: kindness and good sense beat force.*

**Unit 7 · Hiawatha** (from Longfellow's long poem): young Hiawatha, a Native American boy, learns the language of birds and animals, the names of stars and the secrets of the forest from his grandmother.
**The Scholar's Mother Tongue**: a scholar who speaks many languages challenges the court of Raja Krishnadeva Raya to guess his mother tongue. Clever **Tenali Raman** steps on his foot by surprise — and the scholar cries out in his real mother tongue! *Lesson: in sudden moments we speak the language closest to our heart.*

check.q: How did Tenali Raman discover the scholar's mother tongue?
options: He surprised him so he cried out
check.why: When surprised or hurt, people shout in their mother tongue, so Tenali Raman's trick revealed it.

sections.md:
**Unit 8 · A Watering Rhyme** — water big plants well and tiny seedlings gently.
**The Giving Tree** (Shel Silverstein) — a tree gives a boy apples, branches and trunk through his life; at the end, the old man rests on her stump and she is happy.

**Unit 9 · Books** — books are like ships and magic carpets for the mind.
**Going to Buy a Book** — children save pocket money and find that choosing one book from a shop full of them is the most exciting part.

**Unit 10 · The Naughty Boy** (John Keats) — the boy runs to Scotland and finds everything the same as at home.
**Pinocchio** (Carlo Collodi) — Mastro Cherry's talking log becomes Geppetto's puppet, whose nose grows; he runs off as soon as he has feet.

check.q: Which unit has a story by Shel Silverstein?
check.why: The Giving Tree, by Shel Silverstein, is the story in Unit 8.

sections.md:
| Skill | Example |
|---|---|
| Nouns (naming words) | tree, Neha, Kolkata, book |
| Verbs (action words) | run, give, ask, read |
| Adjectives (describing) | tall, sleepy, colourful |
| Past tense | give → gave, take → took, run → ran |
| Opposites | big–small, early–late, dark–light |
| Rhyming words | tree–free, flower–shower |
| 'as … as' comparisons | as brave as a lion |
| Question words | who, what, why, where, when, how |
| Punctuation | . ? ! , and capital letters |

**Quick tips for exam answers:**
- Read the question twice. Underline the question word.
- Answer in a full sentence that uses words from the question.
- Check capital letters and full stops.

check.q: Which of these is an adjective?
check.why: 'Sleepy' describes a person or animal, so it is an adjective (a describing word).

sections.md:
Exams in Class 4 often ask you to **write** a short paragraph or a note. Use this plan:

1. **Beginning** — one sentence that says what you are writing about.
2. **Middle** — three or four sentences with details: who, what, where, when, why.
3. **End** — one sentence with your feeling or a lesson.

**Example — 'My Morning'**: *I wake up at six when the sparrows start chirping outside my window. I brush my teeth, drink a glass of milk and pack my school bag. My grandmother waters the tulsi plant while I tie my shoes. The school bus honks at seven. I love mornings because the world feels fresh and new.*

**Speaking practice:** Recite your favourite poem from the book with expression. Retell one story in your own words to your family in two minutes. Act out the Tenali Raman or Pinocchio scene with a friend.

**Dictionary skill:** words are arranged in **alphabetical order**. Put these in order: *tree, alarm, nose, book, pony* → alarm, book, nose, pony, tree.

check.q: Which word comes first in a dictionary?
check.why: 'Alarm' begins with 'a', the first letter of the alphabet, so it comes first.

sections.md:
- **Nature is a friend**: it wakes Neha, gives us trees and water.
- **Be yourself**: the Little Fir Tree.
- **Keep asking why**: curiosity, like Alice.
- **Courage**: Helen Keller and the child not afraid of the dark.
- **Kindness to animals**: the pony, the donkey, the milkman's cow.
- **Cleverness**: Nasruddin and Tenali Raman.
- **Give back**: The Giving Tree.
- **Love reading**: Books.
- **Honesty**: Pinocchio.

> Did you know? The Class 4 textbook is named *Marigold* — the bright genda phool that we see in garlands at Diwali and weddings across India.

summary: Unit 1: Wake Up! and Neha's Alarm Clock — nature is the best alarm.
Unit 2: Noses and The Little Fir Tree — be happy as you are.
Unit 3: Run! and Nasruddin's Aim — a witty excuse for every miss.
Unit 4: Why? and Alice in Wonderland — curiosity and a long fall down a rabbit-hole.
Unit 5: Don't be Afraid of the Dark and Helen Keller — courage and a patient teacher.
Unit 6: animal poems and The Milkman's Cow — kindness beats force.
Unit 7: Hiawatha and The Scholar's Mother Tongue — Tenali Raman's clever trick.
Unit 8: A Watering Rhyme and The Giving Tree — give back to nature.
Unit 9: Books and Going to Buy a Book — the joy of reading and choosing.
Unit 10: The Naughty Boy and Pinocchio — mischief and honesty.

rd-school-c4-english-b.unit10.title: Unit 10 · The Naughty Boy / Pinocchio
rd-school-c4-english-b.unit10.subtitle: A boy who ran away to find something new, and a piece of wood that wouldn't keep quiet

sections.md:
Have you ever wished you could just run off to a faraway land, where everything would be amazing and different? And have you ever heard a cupboard creak at night and wondered, *was that a voice?*

This last unit of the book gives us two famous mischief-makers:

- **The Naughty Boy** — a poem by the great English poet **John Keats** (1795–1821). A restless boy runs away to Scotland hoping everything will be different.
- **Pinocchio** — from the Italian story by **Carlo Collodi**, first published in the 1880s. A log of wood that talks becomes the most mischievous puppet in the world.

Both pieces are funny. Both also quietly teach us something.

check.q: Who wrote the poem The Naughty Boy?
check.why: The Naughty Boy is a playful poem by the English poet John Keats.

sections.md:
In 1818 the young Keats went on a long **walking tour** of Scotland with a friend. From there he wrote cheerful letters home to his little sister **Fanny**. In one letter he scribbled a long, playful song about a naughty boy — and the boy was really Keats himself, laughing at his own restless feet!

Your textbook gives part of that song. Because it began as a joke in a letter to a child, it is simple, bouncy and full of fun. Keats wanted to make his sister smile and to tell her: *I came all this way, and guess what — Scotland is not so different after all!*

> Did you know? Keats walked hundreds of kilometres on that tour, climbing hills and crossing to Ireland and back.

check.q: To whom did Keats send the poem in a letter?
check.why: Keats wrote the playful song in a letter to his young sister Fanny during his walking tour of Scotland.

sections.md:
In our own words:

There was a naughty boy who could not stay quietly at home. He packed a few things and ran away to **Scotland**, the country to the north of England, sure that he would find wonderful new things there.

And what did he find? He found that:

- the **ground** was just as hard,
- a **yard** was just as long,
- a **song** sounded just the same,
- a **cherry** was just as red,
- a **pound of lead** was just as heavy,

as they were back home in England. So he **stood there wondering** — he had travelled so far, and everything was the same!

**The joke:** you can run far away, but the basic facts of the world come with you. A metre is a metre in Delhi or in Chennai.

**The deeper idea:** travel is wonderful, but happiness and newness do not come only from going far. Sometimes the boy himself needed to change, not his place.

fig.caption: The boy runs to Scotland and finds cherries just as red and a yard just as long.
fig.alt: A boy walks from England to Scotland; the same cherry and same yard appear on both sides.

check.q: What surprised the naughty boy in Scotland?
options: Things were the same as in England
check.why: He expected wonders, but found the ground, a yard, a song and a cherry were all just the same as at home.

sections.h: Rhythm and repetition in the poem
sections.md:
Keats uses **repetition**: the same pattern comes again and again — *the ground was as hard… a yard was as long… a cherry was as red*. Repetition makes the poem bouncy and funny, like a chant.

He also uses **comparisons with 'as … as'**:

- as hard as at home
- as red as at home

You can make your own:

- as cold as ice
- as busy as a bee
- as brave as a lion
- as light as a feather

The lines are very **short**, so the poem feels quick, like the boy's running feet. Read it aloud and tap the beat on your desk.

**Did you know?** Keats is one of the most famous poets in English. He lived only 25 years, yet his poems are still read all over the world.
keyTerms: repetition — saying the same words or pattern again
yard — an old unit of length, a little less than one metre
wonder — to feel surprised and think deeply

check.q: Complete the comparison: as light as a ____
check.why: A feather weighs almost nothing, so 'as light as a feather' is the usual comparison.

sections.md:
Now to Italy, and the story of **Pinocchio**. Here is the part in your book, retold in our own words:

An old carpenter called **Mastro Cherry** — nicknamed so because his nose was red and shiny like a ripe cherry — found an ordinary-looking log. He decided to make a table leg out of it. But as soon as he struck it with his axe, a tiny voice cried out, begging him not to hit so hard! Cherry looked everywhere. No one was there. Shaking with fright, he tried again with a plane, and the voice giggled that it tickled!

Just then his friend **Geppetto** arrived. Geppetto wanted to make a wonderful **wooden puppet** that could dance and do tricks, so he could travel and earn his bread. Cherry happily gave him the strange log.

The log was mischievous even then: it bumped Geppetto's shins, and the two old friends ended up quarrelling, each thinking the other had done it! Finally they made peace, and Geppetto carried the log home.

At home Geppetto carved a puppet and named him **Pinocchio**. As soon as the eyes were made, they stared; when the nose was made, it began to **grow longer and longer**; the mouth laughed and stuck out its tongue; the hands snatched Geppetto's wig! The moment the feet were ready, Pinocchio ran out of the door and down the street.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#fff3e0'/><rect x='250' y='150' width='60' height='110' rx='10' fill='#d8a46a'/><circle cx='280' cy='110' r='40' fill='#e8bf8a'/><circle cx='268' cy='100' r='5' fill='#222'/><circle cx='292' cy='100' r='5' fill='#222'/><path d='M265 130 Q280 140 295 130' stroke='#a0522d' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><rect x='318' y='108' width='20' height='8' rx='4' fill='#d8a46a'><animate attributeName='width' values='20;180;20' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><path d='M250 60 L310 60 L300 40 L260 40Z' fill='#c0392b'/><rect x='255' y='260' width='15' height='40' fill='#d8a46a'/><rect x='290' y='260' width='15' height='40' fill='#d8a46a'/><text x='60' y='300' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#5a3a1a'>The nose keeps growing!</text></svg>
fig.caption: In the story, Pinocchio's wooden nose grows as Geppetto carves it.
fig.alt: A wooden puppet whose nose grows longer and shorter.

check.q: What did Mastro Cherry first plan to make from the log?
check.why: Cherry wanted a table leg, but the log talked, so he gave it to Geppetto, who made a puppet.

sections.md:
| Character | What he is like |
|---|---|
| Mastro Cherry | an old carpenter; easily frightened; kind enough to give the log away |
| Geppetto | a poor, gentle old man; dreams of a dancing puppet; loses his temper but forgives quickly |
| Pinocchio | naughty, cheeky and curious; does not obey; runs away at once |

In the full book, Pinocchio gets into many troubles because he lies, skips school and listens to bad advice. When he tells a lie, his nose grows! A wise Talking Cricket and a kind Fairy try to guide him. In the end he learns to be honest, kind and hardworking, looks after Geppetto, and becomes a real boy.

**Funny moments to notice:** the voice from the log, the two old men fighting, the puppet snatching Geppetto's wig, and the long nose.

check.q: In the full Pinocchio story, what happens when he tells a lie?
check.why: Pinocchio's nose grows each time he lies, which is why the story is famous for teaching honesty.

sections.md:
| | The Naughty Boy | Pinocchio |
|---|---|---|
| Type | poem | story |
| Writer | John Keats (England) | Carlo Collodi (Italy) |
| Mischief | runs away from home | talks, kicks, snatches, runs away |
| Lesson | the world is the same everywhere; change starts inside you | naughtiness brings trouble; honesty and obedience matter |

Both characters **run away**, and both are a bit foolish — but they make us laugh, and they make us think.

**Grammar corner — exclamations:** sentences that show strong feeling end with **!** e.g. *What a strange log!* *Oh no, my wig!* Find three exclamations in your textbook story.

**Grammar corner — naming words for workers:** a *carpenter* works with wood, a *tailor* with cloth, a *potter* with clay, a *cobbler* with shoes, a *blacksmith* with iron.

check.q: Which sign ends an exclamation?
check.why: An exclamation shows strong feeling like surprise or anger, so it ends with an exclamation mark (!).

sections.md:
**Make a puppet:** draw a face on an old sock or a paper bag, add button eyes and wool hair, and put on a puppet show of the talking-log scene. India has a rich puppet tradition too — like *kathputli* string puppets of Rajasthan.

**Role-play:** two friends act as Cherry and Geppetto quarrelling, then making up. Use voices to show fear, anger and laughter.

**Model answers**

*Q: Why did the naughty boy run away?*
A: He was restless and could not stay quietly at home, so he ran to Scotland hoping to find new and wonderful things.

*Q: Why was Mastro Cherry frightened?*
A: When he struck the log, he heard a small voice even though no one else was in the room, so he was scared and amazed.

*Q: How do we know Pinocchio was naughty from the start?*
A: As soon as he was carved he laughed at Geppetto, stuck out his tongue, snatched his wig and ran away the moment he had feet.

summary: The Naughty Boy is a funny poem by John Keats.
Keats wrote it in a letter to his sister during a walking tour of Scotland in 1818.
The boy runs away to Scotland expecting new wonders.
He finds the ground, a yard, a song and a cherry just the same as in England.
Repetition, short lines and 'as … as' comparisons give the poem its bounce.
Pinocchio is by the Italian writer Carlo Collodi.
Mastro Cherry found a log that talked and gave it to Geppetto.
Geppetto carved a puppet and named him Pinocchio.
Pinocchio's nose grew, he snatched the wig and ran off as soon as he had feet.
In the full story his nose grows when he lies; he learns honesty and becomes a real boy.
Exclamations end with ! and show strong feelings.

glossary.d: a person who makes things from wood
a doll moved by strings or by hand
false hair worn on the head
naughty in a playful way
a carpenter's tool for smoothing wood

practice: Where did the naughty boy run to?
Name four things that were the same in Scotland.
What lesson does the poem The Naughty Boy teach?
Why was Mastro Cherry called by that name?
What frightened Mastro Cherry about the log?
Why did Geppetto want a puppet?
Describe two naughty things Pinocchio did after he was carved.
Make four 'as … as' comparisons of your own.
Write three exclamations a person might say on seeing a talking log.
If you had a puppet that came alive, what would you teach it first?

rd-school-c4-english-b.unit8.title: Unit 8 · A Watering Rhyme / The Giving Tree
rd-school-c4-english-b.unit8.subtitle: How do plants drink? And what does a tree give a boy who keeps asking?

sections.md:
Imagine a hot May afternoon in Jaipur. The sun is a big orange ball. The tulsi pot on the balcony looks tired, its leaves drooping like sleepy eyelids. Your grandmother fills a small steel lota and pours the water slowly at the roots. By evening the leaves stand up again!

This unit is all about **giving**. In the poem *A Watering Rhyme*, we learn how to give water to plants in the right way. In the story *The Giving Tree*, we meet a tree that gives and gives to a boy all through his life.

As you read, keep asking yourself two questions:

- **Who gives?**
- **Who receives, and do they say thank you?**

> Did you know? A big tree can pull up hundreds of litres of water from the soil on a hot day, and most of it goes out into the air through tiny holes in its leaves.

check.q: What is the common idea that joins the poem and the story in this unit?
check.why: Both pieces are about giving: we give water to plants, and the tree gives everything it has to the boy.

sections.h: About the poem: A Watering Rhyme
sections.md:
*A Watering Rhyme* is a short, musical poem with a rhyming, bouncy beat. It speaks to a young gardener and gives a simple rule: **plants are not all the same, so they should not all be watered the same way.**

Here is what the poem tells us, in our own words:

- **Big, grown plants and trees** have deep, strong roots. They can take a good, heavy shower of water.
- **Tiny new plants and seedlings** are delicate. Their roots are thin like threads. A heavy splash can wash away the soil or knock them over. So they need only a gentle sprinkle, a little at a time.
- The poem also hints at *when* we water — not in a rush, but with care, like looking after a baby.

The poem uses **opposites** to make its point: big and small, much and little, strong and weak. It is almost like a recipe for a happy garden.

**Why it rhymes:** rhyming words at the ends of lines make a poem easy to remember. Gardeners long ago may have sung such rhymes while working.

fig.caption: Big plants can take lots of water; tiny seedlings need a few gentle drops.
fig.alt: A tree getting many falling drops and a small seedling getting one slow drop.

check.q: According to the poem, how should we water a tiny seedling?
options: With a big bucket all at once
Gently, a little at a time
check.why: Seedlings have thin, weak roots, so a gentle, small amount of water keeps them safe and healthy.

sections.h: Words and sounds in the poem
sections.md:
Poems are like songs. Read the poem aloud from your textbook and clap on the beat. You will feel a steady rhythm.

**Rhyming pairs** — words that end with the same sound. Can you make more pairs?

| Word | Rhymes with |
|---|---|
| flower | shower, tower |
| tree | free, bee |
| rain | grain, chain |
| small | tall, ball |

**Opposites** you can practise:

- big — small
- heavy — light
- much — little
- old — young
- strong — weak

**A gardening word bank:** seed, seedling, sapling, root, stem, leaf, bud, soil, watering can, hose, sprinkle, pour.
keyTerms: seedling — a very young plant just come out of a seed
sprinkle — to drop small drops of water lightly
rhyme — words that end with the same sound

check.q: Which word rhymes with 'shower'?
check.why: 'Flower' and 'shower' both end with the same '-ower' sound, so they rhyme.

sections.h: The Giving Tree: the story in our words
sections.md:
*The Giving Tree* was written by the American author **Shel Silverstein**. It is a gentle story with a big heart. Here is the story retold briefly in our own words.

**When the boy is small**, he comes to an apple tree every day. He gathers her leaves and makes crowns, climbs her trunk, swings from her branches, eats her apples and naps in her shade. They play hide-and-seek. The boy loves the tree, and **the tree is happy.**

**When the boy grows older**, he visits less. One day he says he wants money to buy things. The tree has no money, but she offers her apples so he can sell them. He takes them all. The tree is happy.

**When he is a grown man**, he wants a house for a family. The tree offers her branches to build one. He cuts them and carries them away. The tree is happy.

**When he is older still**, he is sad and wants a boat to sail far away. The tree offers her trunk. He cuts it down, makes a boat and leaves. The tree is happy — but only a little.

**At the end**, the boy comes back as a very old man. The tree has nothing left but an old stump. He says he needs nothing much now, only a quiet place to sit and rest. The tree straightens herself as much as she can and invites him to sit. He sits. And **the tree is happy.**

items.what: Plays with leaves, climbs, eats apples, sleeps in the shade
Wants money — takes the apples to sell
Wants a house — takes the branches
Wants a boat — takes the trunk
Wants rest — sits on the stump

fig.caption: The boy's life, and what he took from the tree at each stage.

check.q: What did the boy take from the tree to build a house?
check.why: When the boy wanted a house, the tree gave him her branches to build it.

sections.md:
**The tree** is loving, patient and generous. She gives without asking for anything back. Her only wish is to see the boy happy and to have him near.

**The boy** begins as a joyful child who truly loves the tree. As he grows, he becomes busy with wants — money, a house, a boat. He keeps taking. He rarely says thank you, and he does not give anything back.

Notice how the tree's happiness changes:

- When the boy plays with her — she is fully happy.
- When he takes her trunk — she is happy, "but not really".
- At the end, when he simply sits with her — she is happy again.

This tells us something deep: **what made the tree happiest was not giving things, but being together.**

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><style>.l{animation:g 6s ease-in-out infinite;transform-origin:150px 150px}@keyframes g{0%,20%{opacity:1}50%,100%{opacity:0}}</style><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff8e8'/><rect y='250' width='600' height='50' fill='#9cc56b'/><rect x='135' y='150' width='30' height='100' fill='#7a4a1e'/><g class='l'><circle cx='150' cy='120' r='70' fill='#3c9a3c'/><circle cx='120' cy='110' r='7' fill='#d62b2b'/><circle cx='175' cy='135' r='7' fill='#d62b2b'/></g><rect x='420' y='225' width='50' height='25' fill='#7a4a1e'/><ellipse cx='445' cy='225' rx='25' ry='6' fill='#c9915a'/><text x='70' y='40' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#5a3a1a'>A full tree...</text><text x='380' y='200' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#5a3a1a'>...becomes a stump</text><path d='M260 180 L370 220' stroke='#5a3a1a' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#a)'/><defs><marker id='a' markerWidth='10' markerHeight='10' refX='5' refY='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10z' fill='#5a3a1a'/></marker></defs></svg>
fig.caption: Bit by bit, the tree gave away leaves, apples, branches and trunk.
fig.alt: A leafy apple tree fading away, with an arrow to a tree stump.

check.q: When was the tree happiest?
options: When the boy took her trunk
When the boy simply spent time with her
check.why: The story shows the tree was truly happy when the boy played or sat with her, because she loved his company.

sections.h: What does the story teach us?
sections.md:
Different readers find different lessons. That is the beauty of this story. Here are some:

1. **Love means giving.** Parents, grandparents and teachers often give to us like the tree — time, care, food, money.
2. **Remember to give back.** The boy only took. We can say thank you, help at home, and spend time with those who love us.
3. **Respect nature.** Trees give us fruit, wood, shade, oxygen and homes for birds. If we only cut and never plant, one day only stumps will be left.

**Link to the poem:** the poem shows us how to give *to* plants; the story shows how much plants give *to us*. Watering a sapling is one small way to thank a tree.

> Activity idea: plant a seed in a paper cup. Water it the poem's way — gently — and keep a diary of how it grows for two weeks.

check.q: Which is a good way to 'give back' to trees?
check.why: Planting and caring for saplings returns some of what trees give us and keeps nature healthy.

sections.md:
The story is told in the **past tense** because it already happened. Look at these pairs:

| Now (present) | Then (past) |
|---|---|
| give | gave |
| take | took |
| come | came |
| climb | climbed |
| play | played |
| sit | sat |

Some past forms just add **-ed** (play → played). Others change completely (give → gave). We have to learn those by heart.

**Parts of a tree** are naming words (nouns): root, trunk, branch, twig, leaf, bark, fruit, flower, seed.

**Write it:** make three sentences about what you got from a tree, e.g. *I ate a mango from our tree.* *I sat in the shade of the neem.*
keyTerms: past tense — a verb form for something that already happened
noun — a naming word
generous — happy to give

check.q: What is the past tense of 'take'?
check.why: 'Take' is an irregular verb, so its past form is 'took', not 'taked'.

summary: The unit's theme is giving and caring.
A Watering Rhyme teaches that big plants can take more water and tiny seedlings need a gentle sprinkle.
The poem uses rhyme, rhythm and opposites like big–small.
The Giving Tree is by Shel Silverstein.
The tree gives the boy shade, play, apples, branches and finally her trunk.
The boy takes at every stage of life and rarely gives back.
At the end the old man rests on the stump, and the tree is happy again.
The tree was happiest with the boy's company, not with giving things.
Lessons: give back, say thank you, respect and plant trees.
Grammar: past tense forms like give–gave, take–took, sit–sat.

glossary.d: a young plant
the bottom part of a tree left after it is cut
a cool place out of the sun
happy to give and share

practice: Why should a seedling be watered gently?
Write two pairs of opposites used to talk about plants.
List everything the tree gave the boy, in order.
Why did the boy want money, a house and a boat?
How did the tree feel after giving away her trunk?
What did the old man want at the end of the story?
Do you think the boy was fair to the tree? Give reasons.
Write five things a tree gives us.
Write the past tense of: give, take, come, sit, play.
Write a short thank-you letter from you to a tree near your home.

rd-school-c4-english-b.unit9.title: Unit 9 · Books / Going to Buy a Book
rd-school-c4-english-b.unit9.subtitle: A book is a door. Where will yours open?

sections.md:
Close your eyes. You are sitting on a mat under a fan in Kolkata. It is raining outside. You open a book — and suddenly you are on a camel in the Thar desert, or deep under the sea with a whale, or flying past the Moon in a rocket.

Nobody moved. Only the pages turned.

That is the magic this unit celebrates. The poem **Books** praises what books can do for us. The story **Going to Buy a Book** shows the excitement of choosing a book of your very own from a bookshop.

While you read, think: *What is the best book you have ever read? Why did you love it?*

check.q: What is the main topic of this unit?
check.why: Both the poem and the story are about books: what they give us and how we choose them.

sections.md:
The poem *Books* is a joyful poem about the wonders hidden between two covers. In our own words, the poet says:

- Books are like **ships and magic carpets** — they carry us to far lands without a ticket.
- Books hold **stories of kings, animals, heroes and ordinary children** from every corner of the world.
- Books are **friends** that never get tired of us. We can open them any time, again and again.
- Books help us **learn** — about stars, plants, history and people.

The poem uses **comparisons**. When we say "a book is a magic carpet", we do not mean it really flies. We mean it takes our *mind* on a journey. This kind of comparison makes writing colourful.

**Read aloud tip:** read the poem slowly with feeling. Pause at commas. Let your voice rise with excitement at the wonders. Read the full poem in your Marigold textbook (free on the NCERT website).

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='n' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#1b2a5a'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#4a5fa8'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='320' fill='url(#n)'/><path d='M200 260 Q300 230 300 260 Q300 230 400 260 L400 290 Q300 265 300 290 Q300 265 200 290Z' fill='#fff8e0' stroke='#c9a24a' stroke-width='3'/><g font-size='34'><text x='280' y='240'>🚀<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-150 -170;0 0' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='290' y='240'>🐋<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;150 -120;0 0' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text><text x='300' y='240'>🏰<animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;20 -200;0 0' dur='8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></text></g><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='25' fill='#fff4b0'/><text x='160' y='40' fill='#fff' font-size='20' font-family='sans-serif'>Open a book... worlds fly out!</text></svg>
fig.caption: A book can take your imagination anywhere — to space, the sea or a castle.
fig.alt: An open book with a rocket, whale and castle floating up out of it.

check.q: When the poet compares a book to a magic carpet, what does it mean?
options: Books take our imagination to far places
check.why: It is a comparison: a book carries our mind to new places, just as a magic carpet would carry our body.

sections.md:
Here is how to understand any poem like *Books*, part by part:

1. **The opening** names the subject and shows the poet's excitement. Ask: *what feeling do the first lines give you?* (Joy, wonder.)
2. **The middle** lists the many things found inside books — places, people, creatures, adventures. Lists like this make the poem feel full and rich, like a treasure box being emptied.
3. **The ending** returns to the reader: books are always waiting for *you*. Ask: *what does the poet want us to do?* (Pick up a book and read!)

**Rhyme and rhythm:** say the poem aloud and clap the beats. Find pairs of rhyming words at the ends of lines and write them down. Rhyme makes a poem musical and easy to remember.

**Imagery:** poets help us *see* pictures. Draw one picture that comes to your mind when you read the poem.

check.q: Why do poets often use lists of wonderful things?
options: To make it feel full and rich, like a treasure box
check.why: A list of exciting things shows how much a book contains and builds the reader's wonder.

sections.h: Going to Buy a Book: the story
sections.md:
This story is about the thrill of buying a book with your own money. Here is the gist in our own words (read the textbook for the exact names and details):

- The children in the story have **saved up their pocket money** for a long time — coins kept carefully in a box.
- At last they set off for the **bookshop** in the market. They are so excited that the walk feels long.
- Inside the shop, they see **rows and rows of books** — fat ones and thin ones, picture books, adventure stories, books about animals and books of jokes.
- Choosing becomes the hardest part! One book has bright pictures. Another has an exciting cover. Another is too costly. They turn pages, read a few lines, put books back and pick them up again.
- The shopkeeper is patient and helps them.
- Finally they choose **one special book**, pay for it and carry it home proudly, eager to start reading.

The story is not about a big adventure. Its adventure is the **joy of choosing** — and the feeling of owning a book that is truly yours.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fdf1dc'/><rect x='40' y='40' width='520' height='200' fill='#8b5a2b'/><g><rect x='55' y='60' width='490' height='8' fill='#5c3a17'/><rect x='55' y='140' width='490' height='8' fill='#5c3a17'/><rect x='55' y='220' width='490' height='8' fill='#5c3a17'/></g><g><rect x='70' y='80' width='20' height='60' fill='#d64545'/><rect x='92' y='85' width='18' height='55' fill='#3b82c4'/><rect x='112' y='78' width='24' height='62' fill='#e0b030'/><rect x='138' y='88' width='16' height='52' fill='#4aa35a'/><rect x='300' y='160' width='22' height='60' fill='#9b59b6'/><rect x='324' y='165' width='18' height='55' fill='#e67e22'/><rect x='344' y='158' width='24' height='62' fill='#16a085'><animate attributeName='y' values='158;120;158' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><text x='170' y='280' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' fill='#5a3a1a'>Which one shall we choose?</text></svg>
fig.caption: So many books, so little pocket money! Choosing is the exciting part.
fig.alt: A bookshelf full of colourful books with one book lifting out.

check.q: What was the hardest part for the children at the bookshop?
check.why: There were so many good books that deciding on only one was the hardest and most exciting part.

sections.md:
- **Saving pays off.** Small coins saved over weeks became enough for something precious.
- **Choose wisely.** The children looked at the pictures, read a few lines and checked the price before deciding. That is smart shopping.
- **Books are treasures.** They did not buy sweets that finish in a minute; they bought something that lasts for years.
- **Respect books.** Keep them clean, don't fold the corners, use a bookmark, and share with friends.

> Did you know? Many Indian cities hold big book fairs. The Kolkata Book Fair and the New Delhi World Book Fair draw huge crowds every year.

check.q: Why is buying a book a good use of saved money?
options: It lasts long and teaches us
check.why: A book can be read many times and shared, so it gives joy and learning for a long time.

sections.h: How to choose a good book
sections.md:
Next time you visit a library or shop, try this checklist:

1. **Look at the cover and title.** Does it make you curious?
2. **Read the back cover.** It tells you what the book is about.
3. **Read the first page.** Do you want to know what happens next?
4. **Check the level.** Too many hard words? Maybe keep it for later.
5. **Check the price** (if buying) — or the due date (if borrowing).

**Parts of a book**

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Cover | the outside front of the book |
| Title | the name of the book |
| Author | the person who wrote it |
| Illustrator | the person who drew the pictures |
| Contents | a list of chapters with page numbers |
| Spine | the narrow back edge you see on a shelf |
| Publisher | the company that printed the book |
keyTerms: author — the writer of a book
illustrator — the artist who draws pictures for a book
library — a place where you can borrow books

check.q: Which part of a book lists the chapters and their page numbers?
check.why: The contents page lists all the chapters and tells you the page where each begins.

sections.md:
Not everyone can buy many books — but a **library** lets everyone read for free or for a tiny fee. Your school library, a public library in your town, or a mobile library van all lend books.

**How a library works:**

1. You become a member and get a **library card**.
2. You choose a book and the librarian notes it.
3. You get a **due date** to return it, usually one or two weeks.
4. You return it on time, clean and undamaged, so the next reader can enjoy it.

Books in a library are arranged by **subject** and by **author's name** so they are easy to find.

**Activity:** Start a class library. Each child brings one book they have finished. Make a register with the book's name, the borrower and the date.

check.q: Why must library books be returned by the due date?
options: So others can read them too
So they can be thrown away
check.why: A library shares books among many people, so each one must come back on time for the next reader.

sections.md:
**Words with 'book'** (compound words — two words joined): bookshop, bookshelf, bookmark, bookworm, notebook, storybook, bookcase.

A *bookworm* is someone who loves to read a lot — not a real worm!

**Describing words (adjectives)** for books: thick, thin, colourful, funny, scary, exciting, old, new.

- *I bought a* **colourful** *book of jokes.*
- *Grandpa has a* **thick, old** *book of stories.*

**Punctuation tip:** book titles begin with capital letters, e.g. *The Jungle Book*, *Panchatantra Tales*.

**Speaking:** In pairs, act out a scene at a bookshop — one is the shopkeeper, one is the buyer. Use polite words: *May I see…? How much is this? Thank you.*

**Write it:** Describe your favourite book in five sentences. Say its name, who wrote it, what happens, your favourite part, and why you would tell a friend to read it.

check.q: What does 'bookworm' mean?
check.why: 'Bookworm' is a fun word for a person who reads a lot and loves books.

sections.md:
**Q: Why are books called our friends?**
A: Books are called our friends because they are always with us, they never get tired of us, they teach us new things and they cheer us up with stories whenever we open them.

**Q: How did the children manage to buy a book?**
A: They saved their pocket money little by little for a long time until they had enough to buy a book of their own.

**Q: What did the children do before choosing their book?**
A: They looked at many books, saw the pictures and covers, read a few lines inside and checked the price before choosing the one they liked best.

**Make your own book:** fold four sheets of paper in half, staple the fold, and write and draw a short story. Add a cover, a title, your name as author and illustrator, and a contents page!

rd-school-c4-hindi.padhna-likhna.title: पढ़ना-समझना और लिखना (कक्षा 4)
rd-school-c4-hindi.padhna-likhna.subtitle: अपठित गद्यांश, कविता-समझ, चित्र-वर्णन, अनुच्छेद, पत्र, कहानी और संवाद — सब आसान तरीके से

sections.md:
सोचो, तुम एक जासूस हो। तुम्हारे सामने एक कहानी है और कुछ सवाल हैं। उत्तर कहीं छिपे हैं — बस उन्हें ढूँढना है! **अपठित गद्यांश** (बिना पहले पढ़ा हुआ अनुच्छेद) ऐसा ही खेल है।

इस पाठ में तुम सीखोगे:

1. ध्यान से पढ़ना और समझना
2. प्रश्नों के सही उत्तर ढूँढना
3. अपठित कविता (पद्यांश) समझना
4. चित्र देखकर लिखना
5. अनुच्छेद लिखना
6. पत्र लिखना
7. कहानी पूरी करना और संवाद लिखना
8. सूचना, विज्ञापन और सुंदर लिखावट

**रिमझिम** की कहानियाँ और कविताएँ — जैसे मन के भोले-भाले बादल, जैसा सवाल वैसा जवाब, किरमिच की गेंद, पापा जब बच्चे थे, दोस्त की पोशाक, नाव बनाओ नाव बनाओ, दान का हिसाब, कौन?, स्वतंत्रता की ओर, थप्प रोटी थप्प दाल, पढ़क्कू की सूझ, सुनीता की पहिया कुर्सी, हुदहुद, मुफ़्त ही मुफ़्त — इसी अभ्यास के लिए बहुत अच्छी हैं। इनके प्रश्न भी यही कौशल माँगते हैं: ढूँढो, सोचो, अपने शब्दों में लिखो।

check.q: 'अपठित गद्यांश' का अर्थ क्या है?
check.why: 'अपठित' यानी जो पहले न पढ़ा हो — परीक्षा में नया अनुच्छेद देकर समझ परखी जाती है।

sections.h: अपठित गद्यांश हल करने के पाँच कदम
sections.md:
1. **पहले पूरा अनुच्छेद एक बार आराम से पढ़ो।** मोटा-मोटा समझो कि बात किसके बारे में है।
2. **अब प्रश्न पढ़ो।** प्रश्नवाचक शब्द पर ध्यान दो — *कौन, क्या, कहाँ, कब, क्यों, कैसे, कितने*।
3. **अनुच्छेद दोबारा पढ़ो** और उत्तर वाली पंक्ति के नीचे पेंसिल से हल्की रेखा खींचो।
4. **पूरे वाक्य में उत्तर लिखो**, प्रश्न के शब्दों का प्रयोग करके।
5. **जाँच करो** — मात्राएँ, पूर्ण विराम (।) और साफ़ लिखावट।

**उदाहरण अनुच्छेद:**
*रानी हर सुबह अपनी दादी के साथ छत पर जाती है। वहाँ वे गमलों में पानी डालती हैं। तुलसी, गुलाब और गेंदे के पौधे खिल उठते हैं। एक दिन रानी ने देखा कि गुलाब के पौधे पर एक नन्ही चिड़िया ने घोंसला बनाया है। उस दिन से वह पौधे को और ध्यान से सींचने लगी।*

- प्रश्न: रानी किसके साथ छत पर जाती है? → **रानी अपनी दादी के साथ छत पर जाती है।**
- प्रश्न: चिड़िया ने घोंसला कहाँ बनाया? → **चिड़िया ने गुलाब के पौधे पर घोंसला बनाया।**
- प्रश्न: छत पर कितने तरह के पौधे थे? → **छत पर तीन तरह के पौधे थे — तुलसी, गुलाब और गेंदा।**

**प्रश्नों के प्रकार पहचानो:**
- *सीधे प्रश्न* — उत्तर अनुच्छेद में लिखा है।
- *सोच वाले प्रश्न* — जैसे 'रानी पौधे को ध्यान से क्यों सींचने लगी?' उत्तर तुम्हें सोचकर लिखना है: *क्योंकि वह नहीं चाहती थी कि चिड़िया का घोंसला टूटे।*
- *शब्द-प्रश्न* — विलोम (सुबह–शाम), पर्यायवाची (पानी–जल), शीर्षक।
- *शीर्षक* — छोटा और मुख्य बात बताने वाला, जैसे 'रानी और नन्ही चिड़िया'।

check.q: उत्तर लिखते समय सबसे अच्छा तरीका क्या है?
options: पूरे वाक्य में, प्रश्न के शब्दों के साथ
check.why: पूरे वाक्य में उत्तर लिखने से बात साफ़ और सही रहती है और पूरे अंक मिलते हैं।

sections.md:
कविता गद्य से अलग होती है — उसमें **लय**, **तुक** और **भाव** होते हैं। कविता समझने के लिए:

1. कविता को **दो बार ज़ोर से** पढ़ो, ताल के साथ।
2. पूछो: *कविता किसके बारे में है?* (बादल, चिड़िया, माँ, नदी…)
3. पूछो: *कवि क्या महसूस कर रहा है?* — ख़ुशी, उदासी, अचरज, प्यार।
4. **तुकांत शब्द** खोजो — जिनका अंत मिलता हो: *गाना–खाना, पानी–रानी, बादल–पागल*।
5. कठिन शब्द का अर्थ आस-पास की पंक्तियों से अनुमान लगाओ।

**उदाहरण (हमारी अपनी छोटी कविता):**
> *काले-काले बादल आए, संग में ठंडी हवा भी लाए।*
> *मोर नाचे, कोयल गाए, बच्चे काग़ज़ की नाव बहाए।*

- कविता किस ऋतु की है? → **यह कविता वर्षा ऋतु की है।**
- तुकांत शब्द → *आए–लाए, गाए–बहाए।*
- बच्चे क्या कर रहे हैं? → **बच्चे काग़ज़ की नाव बहा रहे हैं।**

रिमझिम की कविताओं में भी यही करो: 'मन के भोले-भाले बादल' में बादलों को शरारती बच्चों जैसा बताया गया है; 'नाव बनाओ नाव बनाओ' में बच्चा बड़ों से काग़ज़ की नाव बनाने की ज़िद करता है; 'कौन?' कविता पहेली की तरह एक चूहे की शरारतों के बारे में पूछती है। हर कविता की मूल बात अपने शब्दों में एक-दो वाक्य में लिखने का अभ्यास करो।

check.q: 'पानी' का तुकांत शब्द कौन-सा है?
check.why: 'पानी' और 'रानी' दोनों का अंत 'आनी' से होता है, इसलिए ये तुकांत हैं।

sections.md:
परीक्षा में अक्सर एक चित्र देकर कहा जाता है — *इसे देखकर पाँच वाक्य लिखो।* इसके लिए **'क्या, कौन, कहाँ, क्या कर रहे हैं, कैसा लग रहा है'** सोचो।

**मान लो चित्र है — मेले का दृश्य:**

1. यह एक गाँव के मेले का चित्र है।
2. मेले में बड़ा-सा झूला घूम रहा है।
3. बच्चे गुब्बारे और खिलौने खरीद रहे हैं।
4. एक दुकान पर गरम-गरम जलेबियाँ बन रही हैं।
5. सब लोग बहुत ख़ुश दिखाई दे रहे हैं।

**सुझाव:** हर वाक्य में कुछ नया बताओ। रंग, आवाज़ और ख़ुशबू वाले शब्द जोड़ो — *रंग-बिरंगे गुब्बारे, ढोल की आवाज़, जलेबी की ख़ुशबू।* शुरू में बताओ चित्र किसका है, अंत में बताओ लोग कैसा महसूस कर रहे हैं।

check.q: चित्र-वर्णन को सुंदर बनाने के लिए क्या जोड़ना चाहिए?
options: रंग, आवाज़ और ख़ुशबू वाले शब्द
check.why: रंग, आवाज़ और ख़ुशबू वाले शब्द पढ़ने वाले के मन में चित्र जीवित कर देते हैं।

sections.md:
**अनुच्छेद** किसी एक विषय पर लिखे गए जुड़े हुए वाक्यों का छोटा समूह है।

**ढाँचा:**
- **शुरुआत** — विषय का परिचय (1–2 वाक्य)
- **बीच** — मुख्य बातें (3–5 वाक्य)
- **अंत** — अपनी भावना या सीख (1 वाक्य)

**उदाहरण — 'मेरा प्रिय त्योहार: दीवाली'**

मेरा प्रिय त्योहार दीवाली है। यह कार्तिक महीने की अमावस्या को मनाया जाता है। इस दिन हम घर की सफ़ाई करते हैं और रंगोली बनाते हैं। शाम को दीये जलाकर पूरे घर को रोशन करते हैं। हम लक्ष्मी जी की पूजा करते हैं और मिठाइयाँ बाँटते हैं। मुझे दीवाली इसलिए अच्छी लगती है क्योंकि इस दिन सब मिल-जुलकर ख़ुशियाँ मनाते हैं।

**दूसरा उदाहरण — 'वर्षा ऋतु'**

गर्मी के बाद वर्षा ऋतु आती है। आसमान में काले बादल छा जाते हैं और रिमझिम बारिश होती है। खेतों में हरियाली आ जाती है और किसान ख़ुश हो जाते हैं। बच्चे पानी में काग़ज़ की नाव चलाते हैं। कभी-कभी ज़्यादा बारिश से सड़कों पर पानी भर जाता है। फिर भी मुझे बारिश की सोंधी ख़ुशबू बहुत प्यारी लगती है।

**अन्य विषय:** मेरा विद्यालय, मेरी माँ, मेरा प्रिय खेल, पेड़ हमारे मित्र, मेरा प्रिय जानवर, रेल यात्रा।

check.q: अनुच्छेद के अंत में क्या लिखना अच्छा रहता है?
check.why: अंत में अपनी भावना या सीख लिखने से अनुच्छेद पूरा और प्रभावशाली लगता है।

sections.md:
कक्षा 4 में हम दो तरह के पत्र सीखते हैं: **अनौपचारिक** (परिवार, दोस्तों को) और **औपचारिक** (प्रधानाचार्य आदि को)।

**प्रार्थना-पत्र (छुट्टी के लिए) का ढाँचा:**

> सेवा में,
> प्रधानाचार्य जी,
> सरस्वती विद्यालय, लखनऊ
>
> विषय: दो दिन के अवकाश हेतु प्रार्थना-पत्र
>
> महोदय/महोदया,
> सविनय निवेदन है कि मुझे कल रात से तेज़ बुख़ार है। डॉक्टर ने आराम करने को कहा है। अतः मुझे 12 और 13 तारीख का अवकाश देने की कृपा करें।
>
> धन्यवाद।
> आपका आज्ञाकारी शिष्य,
> अमन, कक्षा 4-ब
> दिनांक: 11 जुलाई

**अनौपचारिक पत्र का उदाहरण (दादाजी को):**

> 15, गांधी नगर, भोपाल
> दिनांक: 5 मई
>
> पूज्य दादाजी,
> सादर प्रणाम।
> मैं यहाँ ठीक हूँ और आशा करती हूँ कि आप और दादीजी भी स्वस्थ होंगे। मेरी गर्मी की छुट्टियाँ शुरू हो गई हैं। इस बार मैं आपके पास गाँव आना चाहती हूँ। मुझे आपके साथ आम के बग़ीचे में घूमना और कहानियाँ सुनना बहुत अच्छा लगता है। दादीजी को मेरा प्रणाम कहिएगा।
>
> आपकी प्यारी पोती,
> मीना

**याद रखो:** पता और दिनांक ऊपर, संबोधन (पूज्य/प्रिय), अभिवादन (प्रणाम/नमस्ते/ढेर सारा प्यार), मुख्य बात, अंत में नाम।

check.q: प्रधानाचार्य को पत्र किससे शुरू होता है?
check.why: औपचारिक प्रार्थना-पत्र 'सेवा में' से शुरू होता है, जो आदर दिखाता है।

sections.h: कहानी पूरी करो और संवाद लिखो
sections.md:
**कहानी पूरी करना:** परीक्षा में आरंभ दिया जाता है, जैसे — *एक प्यासा कौआ पानी ढूँढ रहा था…* तुम्हें बीच और अंत लिखना है।

- पात्र कौन हैं? समस्या क्या है?
- पात्र क्या उपाय करता है?
- अंत में क्या होता है और **सीख** क्या है?
- अंत में एक शीर्षक भी दो।

**उदाहरण:** कौए को एक घड़ा मिला, पर पानी बहुत नीचे था। उसने पास पड़े कंकड़ एक-एक करके घड़े में डाले। पानी ऊपर आ गया और कौए ने प्यास बुझाई। **सीख:** सूझ-बूझ से हर समस्या हल हो सकती है। **शीर्षक:** चतुर कौआ।

**संवाद लेखन:** दो लोगों की बातचीत। हर बोलने वाले का नाम लिखकर कोलन (:) लगाओ।

> **माँ:** बेटा, स्कूल से आकर हाथ धोए?
> **राजू:** अभी धोता हूँ, माँ।
> **माँ:** शाबाश! फिर खाना खा लो।
> **राजू:** आज क्या बना है?
> **माँ:** तुम्हारी पसंद की दाल और रोटी।

संवाद छोटे, स्वाभाविक और विषय से जुड़े हों — जैसे रिमझिम के पाठ 'जैसा सवाल वैसा जवाब' में बीरबल के मज़ेदार उत्तर।

check.q: कहानी पूरी करने के बाद अंत में क्या देना अच्छा है?
check.why: शीर्षक और सीख कहानी को पूरा और अर्थपूर्ण बनाते हैं।

sections.h: सूचना, विज्ञापन, सुंदर लेख और पढ़ने की आदत
sections.md:
**सूचना लिखना:** विद्यालय के सूचना-पट के लिए छोटी बात — *क्या, कब, कहाँ, किसके लिए*।

> **सूचना** — 20 अगस्त को सुबह 9 बजे विद्यालय के मैदान में चित्रकला प्रतियोगिता होगी। कक्षा 3 से 5 के इच्छुक विद्यार्थी अपना नाम कक्षा-अध्यापक को दें। — प्रधानाचार्य

**विज्ञापन/पोस्टर:** बड़े अक्षर, छोटा नारा, चित्र — *'पानी बचाओ, जीवन बचाओ!'*

**सुंदर लेख:** शिरोरेखा सीधी, मात्राएँ साफ़, शब्दों के बीच बराबर दूरी, हर वाक्य के अंत में पूर्ण विराम (।)। प्रश्न के अंत में प्रश्नवाचक चिह्न (?) और अचरज में विस्मयादिबोधक चिह्न (!) लगाओ।

**अच्छा पढ़ने की आदत:**
- रोज़ 15 मिनट कोई कहानी, अख़बार का बच्चों वाला पन्ना या पत्रिका पढ़ो।
- नए शब्द एक कॉपी में लिखो और उनका वाक्य बनाओ।
- जो पढ़ा, उसे घर पर किसी को सुनाओ।
- पुस्तकालय से हर सप्ताह एक किताब लो।

> क्या तुम जानते हो? ज़ोर से पढ़ने से उच्चारण भी सुधरता है और याद भी जल्दी होता है।

check.q: सूचना में कौन-सी बातें ज़रूर होनी चाहिए?
check.why: सूचना का काम सही बात सही लोगों तक पहुँचाना है, इसलिए क्या-कब-कहाँ-किसके लिए ज़रूरी है।

summary: अपठित गद्यांश पहले पूरा पढ़ो, फिर प्रश्न पढ़ो।
प्रश्नवाचक शब्द — कौन, क्या, कहाँ, कब, क्यों, कैसे — पर ध्यान दो।
उत्तर पूरे वाक्य में और प्रश्न के शब्दों के साथ लिखो।
शीर्षक छोटा और मुख्य बात बताने वाला हो।
कविता में लय, तुक और भाव खोजो।
चित्र-वर्णन में क्या, कौन, कहाँ, क्या हो रहा है — सोचो।
रंग, आवाज़, ख़ुशबू वाले शब्द लेखन को जीवित बनाते हैं।
अनुच्छेद — शुरुआत, बीच, अंत।
औपचारिक पत्र 'सेवा में' से शुरू होता है और उसमें विषय होता है।
अनौपचारिक पत्र प्यार भरी भाषा में परिवार या मित्र को लिखा जाता है।
कहानी पूरी करते समय समस्या, उपाय, अंत, सीख और शीर्षक दो।
संवाद में बोलने वाले का नाम और कोलन लगाओ।
सूचना में क्या, कब, कहाँ, किसके लिए लिखो।
रोज़ पढ़ने और नए शब्द लिखने की आदत डालो।
practice: ऊपर दिए रानी वाले अनुच्छेद पर दो और प्रश्न बनाकर उनके उत्तर लिखो।
'बरसात का दिन' चित्र की कल्पना करके पाँच वाक्य लिखो।
'मेरा विद्यालय' पर अनुच्छेद लिखो।
'पेड़ हमारे मित्र' पर छह वाक्य लिखो।
प्रधानाचार्य को बहन की शादी के लिए तीन दिन की छुट्टी का प्रार्थना-पत्र लिखो।
अपने दादाजी को गर्मी की छुट्टियों के बारे में पत्र लिखो।
कहानी पूरी करो: 'एक दिन जंगल में शेर जाल में फँस गया…'
दुकानदार और ग्राहक के बीच छह पंक्तियों का संवाद लिखो।
विद्यालय में वृक्षारोपण दिवस की सूचना लिखो।
अपनी पसंद की एक कविता के तुकांत शब्द लिखो।

rd-school-c4-hindi.vyakaran.title: हिंदी व्याकरण (कक्षा 4)
rd-school-c4-hindi.vyakaran.subtitle: वर्ण से वाक्य तक — संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, लिंग, वचन, विशेषण, क्रिया, काल, शब्द-भंडार और विराम चिह्न

sections.h: भाषा का घर: वर्ण, शब्द, वाक्य
sections.md:
सोचो, एक घर ईंटों से बनता है। भाषा का घर भी ऐसे ही बनता है — **वर्ण** ईंटें हैं, **शब्द** दीवारें हैं और **वाक्य** पूरा कमरा!

- **वर्ण** — भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि, जिसके टुकड़े नहीं हो सकते: अ, क, म।
- **वर्णमाला** — वर्णों का क्रम से समूह।
- **स्वर** — जो अपने-आप बोले जाते हैं: अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ए ऐ ओ औ (11)।
- **व्यंजन** — जो स्वर की मदद से बोले जाते हैं: क ख ग घ ङ … ह।
- **शब्द** — वर्णों का सार्थक मेल: क + म + ल = कमल।
- **वाक्य** — शब्दों का सार्थक मेल जो पूरी बात कहे: *कमल तालाब में खिलता है।*

**मात्राएँ:** स्वर जब व्यंजन से मिलता है तो उसका चिह्न लगता है — का, कि, की, कु, कू, के, कै, को, कौ, कं। **अ** की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती।

**संयुक्त व्यंजन:** क्ष (क्+ष), त्र (त्+र), ज्ञ (ज्+ञ), श्र (श्+र)।

check.q: किस स्वर की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती?
check.why: 'अ' हर व्यंजन में पहले से मिला रहता है, इसलिए इसकी अलग मात्रा नहीं होती।

sections.md:
किसी **व्यक्ति, वस्तु, स्थान, प्राणी या भाव** के नाम को **संज्ञा** कहते हैं।

| प्रकार | अर्थ | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| व्यक्तिवाचक | किसी ख़ास एक का नाम | गंगा, दिल्ली, सचिन, ताजमहल |
| जातिवाचक | पूरी जाति/समूह का नाम | नदी, शहर, लड़का, पेड़ |
| भाववाचक | भाव या गुण का नाम (छू नहीं सकते) | प्यार, ख़ुशी, मिठास, बचपन |

**पहचान का खेल:** *सीमा ने बाज़ार से मीठे आम ख़रीदे।* — सीमा (व्यक्तिवाचक), बाज़ार, आम (जातिवाचक)।

**भाववाचक बनाना:** मीठा → मिठास, बच्चा → बचपन, अच्छा → अच्छाई, हँसना → हँसी।

check.q: 'ख़ुशी' कौन-सी संज्ञा है?
check.why: ख़ुशी एक भाव है जिसे महसूस किया जाता है, छुआ नहीं जा सकता — इसलिए भाववाचक संज्ञा।

sections.md:
बार-बार नाम दोहराने से वाक्य भारी लगता है: *राम स्कूल गया। राम ने राम की किताब खोली।* इसकी जगह: *राम स्कूल गया। उसने अपनी किताब खोली।*

संज्ञा के स्थान पर आने वाले शब्द **सर्वनाम** हैं: मैं, हम, तुम, आप, वह, वे, यह, ये, कोई, कुछ, कौन, क्या, अपना।

- बोलने वाला अपने लिए — **मैं, हम**
- सुनने वाले के लिए — **तुम, आप**
- किसी और के लिए — **वह, वे, यह, ये**

'आप' आदर के लिए बोला जाता है — बड़ों से *आप* कहो।

check.q: 'सीता ने खाना खाया। ___ बहुत भूखी थी।' खाली जगह में क्या आएगा?
check.why: सीता किसी और व्यक्ति के बारे में बात है, इसलिए 'वह' सर्वनाम सही है।

sections.md:
**लिंग** — शब्द से पता चलता है कि वह पुरुष जाति का है या स्त्री जाति का।

| पुल्लिंग | स्त्रीलिंग |
|---|---|
| लड़का | लड़की |
| घोड़ा | घोड़ी |
| शेर | शेरनी |
| राजा | रानी |
| मोर | मोरनी |
| धोबी | धोबिन |
| बैल | गाय |

**वचन** — शब्द से पता चलता है कि वह एक है या अनेक।

| एकवचन | बहुवचन |
|---|---|
| कपड़ा | कपड़े |
| किताब | किताबें |
| नदी | नदियाँ |
| चिड़िया | चिड़ियाँ |
| लड़का | लड़के |
| बात | बातें |

**ध्यान दो:** लिंग और वचन बदलने पर क्रिया भी बदलती है — *लड़का खेलता है, लड़की खेलती है, लड़के खेलते हैं।*

check.q: 'नदी' का बहुवचन क्या है?
check.why: ई से अंत होने वाले स्त्रीलिंग शब्दों में 'ई' को 'इ' करके 'याँ' जोड़ते हैं — नदियाँ।

sections.md:
जो शब्द संज्ञा या सर्वनाम की **विशेषता** (गुण, रंग, आकार, संख्या, मात्रा) बताएँ, वे **विशेषण** हैं। जिसकी विशेषता बताई जाए, उसे **विशेष्य** कहते हैं।

- गुण: *ईमानदार* लड़का, *मीठा* आम
- रंग: *लाल* गुलाब, *हरा* तोता
- आकार: *बड़ा* हाथी, *छोटी* चींटी
- संख्या: *पाँच* केले, *कुछ* बच्चे
- मात्रा: *दो लीटर* दूध, *थोड़ा* पानी

**उदाहरण:** *मेरी दादी के पास एक सफ़ेद, बूढ़ी, प्यारी बिल्ली है।* — सफ़ेद, बूढ़ी, प्यारी विशेषण; बिल्ली विशेष्य।

check.q: 'ऊँचा पहाड़' में विशेषण कौन-सा है?
check.why: 'ऊँचा' पहाड़ का गुण बता रहा है, इसलिए वह विशेषण है और पहाड़ विशेष्य।

sections.md:
**क्रिया** — जिन शब्दों से किसी काम का करना या होना पता चले: खाना, पढ़ना, दौड़ना, सोना, हँसना, बरसना।

*चिड़िया आसमान में **उड़ती** है।* *बच्चे मैदान में **खेल रहे हैं**।*

**काल** — क्रिया के होने का समय:

| काल | पहचान | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| भूतकाल (बीता समय) | था, थी, थे, या, ई | मैंने कल फ़िल्म देखी। |
| वर्तमान काल (अभी) | है, हैं, रहा है | मैं पढ़ रहा हूँ। |
| भविष्यत् काल (आने वाला) | गा, गी, गे | हम कल मेला जाएँगे। |
