check.q: 'हम कल दिल्ली जाएँगे' — कौन-सा काल है?
check.why: 'जाएँगे' में 'गे' आने वाले समय का काम बताता है, इसलिए भविष्यत् काल।

sections.h: शब्द-भंडार: विलोम, पर्यायवाची, अनेक शब्दों के लिए एक शब्द, मुहावरे
sections.md:
**विलोम (उलटे अर्थ):** दिन–रात, सुख–दुख, आगे–पीछे, अमीर–ग़रीब, सच–झूठ, ठंडा–गरम, जीत–हार।

**पर्यायवाची (समान अर्थ):** पानी — जल, नीर; सूरज — सूर्य, दिनकर; फूल — पुष्प, सुमन; घर — गृह, भवन; माँ — माता, जननी।

**अनेक शब्दों के लिए एक शब्द:**
- जो दूसरों की मदद करे — परोपकारी
- जो सच बोले — सच्चा/सत्यवादी
- जहाँ पुस्तकें रखी हों — पुस्तकालय
- जो खेती करे — किसान

**मुहावरे (विशेष अर्थ वाले वाक्यांश):**
- *आँखों का तारा* — बहुत प्यारा: बेटी माँ की आँखों का तारा है।
- *नौ दो ग्यारह होना* — भाग जाना: पुलिस को देख चोर नौ दो ग्यारह हो गया।
- *फूला न समाना* — बहुत ख़ुश होना: पहला इनाम पाकर रिया फूली न समाई।

**तुकांत/समान ध्वनि वाले शब्द** (रिमझिम के अभ्यासों में आते हैं): ओला–बोला, झोला–डोला।

check.q: 'सुख' का विलोम क्या है?
check.why: सुख का उलटा अर्थ देने वाला शब्द दुख है।

sections.md:
बोलते समय हम रुकते हैं; लिखते समय यह रुकना **विराम चिह्न** बताते हैं।

| चिह्न | नाम | कब |
|---|---|---|
| । | पूर्ण विराम | वाक्य पूरा होने पर |
| , | अल्प विराम | थोड़ा रुकने पर, गिनती में |
| ? | प्रश्नवाचक | प्रश्न पूछने पर |
| ! | विस्मयादिबोधक | ख़ुशी, दुख, अचरज में |
| " " | उद्धरण | किसी की कही बात |

*अरे! तुम कब आए? मैं, माँ और पापा बाज़ार गए थे। माँ ने कहा, "जल्दी लौटना।"*

**शुद्ध लेखन की बातें:** चंद्रबिंदु (ँ) और अनुस्वार (ं) सही लगाओ — *माँ, हँसना / गंगा, संत*। नुक्ता और छोटी-बड़ी मात्रा पर ध्यान दो — *दिन (छोटी इ), दीया (बड़ी ई)*।

check.q: 'तुम्हारा नाम क्या है' के अंत में कौन-सा चिह्न लगेगा?
check.why: यह प्रश्न है, इसलिए अंत में प्रश्नवाचक चिह्न (?) लगेगा।

summary: वर्ण भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि है; वर्णों से शब्द और शब्दों से वाक्य बनते हैं।
स्वर अपने-आप बोले जाते हैं; व्यंजन स्वर की मदद से।
'अ' की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती।
संज्ञा के तीन प्रकार — व्यक्तिवाचक, जातिवाचक, भाववाचक।
सर्वनाम संज्ञा के बदले आता है — मैं, तुम, वह, आप।
लिंग — पुल्लिंग/स्त्रीलिंग; वचन — एकवचन/बहुवचन।
लिंग-वचन बदलने पर क्रिया भी बदलती है।
विशेषण गुण, रंग, आकार, संख्या, मात्रा बताता है; विशेष्य वह जिसकी विशेषता बताई जाए।
क्रिया काम बताती है; काल उसका समय — भूत, वर्तमान, भविष्यत्।
विलोम उलटे अर्थ, पर्यायवाची समान अर्थ वाले शब्द हैं।
मुहावरे का अर्थ शब्दों से अलग, विशेष होता है।
विराम चिह्न — । , ? ! " " — सही जगह लगाओ।
practice: पाँच व्यक्तिवाचक और पाँच जातिवाचक संज्ञाएँ लिखो।
इनसे भाववाचक संज्ञा बनाओ: मीठा, बच्चा, अच्छा, बूढ़ा।
लिंग बदलो: राजा, शेर, मोर, धोबी, घोड़ा।
वचन बदलो: किताब, नदी, कपड़ा, चिड़िया, बात।
इस वाक्य में विशेषण और विशेष्य छाँटो: 'हरी घास पर पाँच सफ़ेद ख़रगोश बैठे हैं।'
'खेलना' क्रिया से तीनों कालों के वाक्य बनाओ।
विलोम लिखो: आगे, सच, अमीर, जीत, ठंडा।
'आँखों का तारा' और 'फूला न समाना' मुहावरों से वाक्य बनाओ।
विराम चिह्न लगाओ: अरे तुम कहाँ थे मैंने कहा जल्दी आओ

rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch1-building-with-b.title: Building with Bricks
rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch1-building-with-b.subtitle: Faces, patterns, jaalis, kilns and counting bricks in a stack — maths hiding in every wall

sections.h: A walk past a building site
sections.md:
On the way to school, Meena passes a house being built in her lane in Jaipur. A truck tips out a mountain of red bricks. Workers pass them hand to hand — *tak, tak, tak* — and a wall grows taller every hour. Meena wonders: **why are bricks shaped like this? Why are walls built in that zig-zag way? And how many bricks are in that pile?**

This chapter answers all three. You will learn:

1. The faces of a brick and the shapes they make
2. How bricks are arranged in walls and why
3. Patterns on floors, paths and *jaalis*
4. How bricks are made in a kiln
5. How to count bricks in a stack without counting each one

Bricks have been used in India for over 4,000 years — the Harappan cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Lothal were built with baked bricks of carefully equal shape.

check.q: Which ancient Indian civilisation used baked bricks for its cities?
check.why: Harappan towns like Mohenjo-daro and Lothal were built of baked bricks more than 4,000 years ago.

sections.h: The six faces of a brick
sections.md:
A brick is a **cuboid**: it has **6 faces**, **12 edges** and **8 corners**. Every face is a **rectangle**, and opposite faces are the same.

A common brick measures about **22 cm long, 11 cm wide, 7 cm high**. So it has three different pairs of faces:

| Face pair | Size | Called |
|---|---|---|
| Top & bottom | 22 cm × 11 cm (biggest) | bed face |
| Front & back | 22 cm × 7 cm (long, thin) | stretcher face |
| Two ends | 11 cm × 7 cm (smallest) | header face |

**Activity:** Dip each face of a brick (or a matchbox — also a cuboid!) in paint and press it on paper. You get **three different rectangles**. The brick always leaves rectangles, never a circle or triangle.

When bricks stand on different faces, a wall looks different: lying flat, standing on the long thin side, or standing on its end.

check.q: How many faces does a brick have?
check.why: A brick is a cuboid with 6 rectangular faces (12 edges and 8 corners).

sections.h: Why walls are built in a pattern
sections.md:
Look closely at any brick wall. The bricks in one row never sit exactly over the bricks in the row below. Each brick **covers the joint** between two bricks underneath. This is called **bonding**.

Why? If the joints were all in one straight line, the wall would have a weak crack running top to bottom and could split. When joints are staggered, the weight is spread out and the wall is strong.

Some bonds you can spot:
- **Stretcher bond** — every brick shows its long side; each row is shifted by half a brick. Common in thin walls.
- **Header bond** — every brick shows its short end.
- **English bond** — one row of stretchers, one row of headers, again and again. Used in thick, strong walls.
- **Flemish bond** — header and stretcher take turns in the same row.

**Try it:** Use matchboxes or erasers to build a small wall in two ways — joints in a line, and joints staggered. Push gently. Which falls apart first?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#f4f4f0'/><g fill='#d0683f' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='3'><rect x='40' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='120' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='200' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='0' y='140' width='80' height='30' x2='0'/><rect x='80' y='140' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='160' y='140' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='240' y='140' width='40' height='30'/><rect x='40' y='110' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='120' y='110' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='200' y='110' width='80' height='30'/></g><g fill='#d0683f' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='3'><rect x='340' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='420' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='500' y='170' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='340' y='140' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='420' y='140' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='500' y='140' width='80' height='30'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 0;6 0;0 0' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><rect x='340' y='110' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='420' y='110' width='80' height='30'/><rect x='500' y='110' width='80' height='30'/></g></g><line x1='420' y1='110' x2='420' y2='200' stroke='#c0392b' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><g font-size='16' font-family='sans-serif'><text x='60' y='60'>Staggered joints: strong</text><text x='350' y='60'>Joints in a line: weak</text></g></svg>

fig.alt: Two walls: one with staggered bricks, one with joints in a line that wobbles.

check.q: Why does each brick cover the joint below it?
check.why: Staggered joints stop a straight crack from forming and spread the weight, so the wall is stronger.

sections.h: Patterns on floors, paths and jaalis
sections.md:
Bricks are also laid flat to make **floors and footpaths**. Workers use patterns:
- **Running pattern** — rows like a wall, lying flat.
- **Basket weave** — pairs of bricks turn by a right angle each time, like a woven basket.
- **Herringbone** — bricks set at a slant in a zig-zag, like the bones of a fish. Very strong for roads.

**Jaali** walls leave neat gaps between bricks. A jaali lets **air and light** come in while still giving shade and privacy. Old havelis and new houses in hot places like Rajasthan and Gujarat use jaalis to stay cool. Laurie Baker, an architect who worked in Kerala, was famous for low-cost brick buildings with jaalis.

**Pattern spotting:** In a pattern, a unit repeats. Look for the smallest piece that repeats and the rule (shift, turn, flip). Draw the next part of a pattern on squared paper by following the rule.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#fffaf2'/><g fill='#c9603a' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='2'><rect x='30' y='40' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='30' y='60' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='70' y='40' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='90' y='40' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='110' y='40' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='110' y='60' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='30' y='80' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='50' y='80' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='70' y='80' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='70' y='100' width='40' height='20'/><rect x='110' y='80' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='130' y='80' width='20' height='40'/></g><g fill='#c9603a' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='2'><rect x='240' y='40' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='320' y='40' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='400' y='40' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='280' y='80' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='360' y='80' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='240' y='120' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='320' y='120' width='60' height='20'/><rect x='400' y='120' width='60' height='20'/></g><g fill='#ffd54a'><circle cx='310' cy='70' r='4'><animate attributeName='cx' values='230;470' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='310' cy='110' r='4'><animate attributeName='cx' values='230;470' dur='3s' begin='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g font-size='15' font-family='sans-serif'><text x='40' y='160'>Basket weave floor</text><text x='280' y='175'>Jaali: air and light pass</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Basket weave pattern and a jaali with breeze flowing through.
fig.alt: A basket weave brick pattern and a jaali wall with moving dots showing air.

check.q: What is the main use of a jaali?
options: To let air and light in
check.why: Gaps in a jaali let air and light pass while still giving shade and privacy.

sections.h: How bricks are made — the kiln
sections.md:
Bricks start as **clay** dug from the ground near a river or field.

1. Clay is mixed with water and kneaded till smooth.
2. Workers press it into a wooden **mould** (a box without top) and turn it out — a raw brick.
3. Raw bricks dry in the sun for several days.
4. They are stacked inside a **bhatta** (kiln) and baked in a fire for many days. The tall chimney carries smoke away.
5. Baked bricks turn hard and red because of iron in the clay.

A skilled moulder can make about a thousand bricks a day. Many bricks have a **hollow (frog)** stamped on one face, often with the maker's name; it saves clay and holds cement better. Kiln workers often work in very hard, hot conditions — an important thing to remember when we see a new building.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#dff0ff'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='40' fill='#b98a52'/><rect x='200' y='120' width='200' height='80' fill='#a0432a'/><rect x='370' y='30' width='24' height='90' fill='#6b2b1a'/><g fill='#999' opacity='0.7'><circle cx='382' cy='25' r='10'><animate attributeName='cy' values='25;-20' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='r' values='8;22' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='390' cy='25' r='8'><animate attributeName='cy' values='25;-20' dur='3s' begin='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g fill='#ff7a00'><path d='M250 200 q10 -30 20 0 z'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0.4;1' dur='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M320 200 q10 -30 20 0 z'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0.4;1;0.4' dur='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><g fill='#d9a06a' stroke='#7a4b25'><rect x='40' y='180' width='30' height='15'/><rect x='75' y='180' width='30' height='15'/><rect x='57' y='165' width='30' height='15'/></g><g font-size='15' font-family='sans-serif'><text x='30' y='155'>drying in sun</text><text x='240' y='110'>bhatta (kiln)</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Clay bricks dry in the sun and are then baked in a kiln.
fig.alt: Drying bricks beside a brick kiln with fire and rising smoke.

check.q: Why do baked bricks turn red?
options: Iron in the clay changes when baked
check.why: Clay contains iron; baking in the kiln changes it and gives the brick its red colour.

sections.md:
At the site, bricks are kept in neat **stacks** so they can be counted quickly. You don't count one by one — you **multiply**.

If a stack has **rows**, **columns** and **layers**:

**Number of bricks = bricks in one layer × number of layers**, and **bricks in one layer = rows × bricks in each row**.

Some stacks are built like steps or a pyramid, with fewer bricks in each higher layer — then **add** the layers.

We can also **estimate**: if one brick is about 7 cm high, a stack 70 cm high has about 70 ÷ 7 = 10 layers.

check.q: A stack has 6 layers, each with 20 bricks. How many bricks?
check.why: 6 layers × 20 bricks = 120 bricks.

workedExamples.q: A stack has 4 rows of 10 bricks in each layer and 5 layers. How many bricks?
A step stack has 6 bricks at the bottom, then 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. How many bricks?
A truck brings 3,000 bricks. One wall needs 750. How many such walls?
Bricks cost ₹8 each. What do 250 bricks cost?

summary: A brick is a cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 corners.
All faces are rectangles; there are three different sizes.
Brick walls stagger joints (bonding) so they are strong.
Stretcher, header, English and Flemish bonds are common patterns.
Floors use running, basket-weave and herringbone patterns.
Jaalis let air and light in while giving shade.
Bricks are made from clay, moulded, sun-dried and baked in a kiln.
The hollow 'frog' saves clay and holds mortar.
Count stacks by multiplying: rows × bricks per row × layers.
Step or pyramid stacks are counted by adding each layer.
Harappan cities were built with baked bricks over 4,000 years ago.
practice: Draw the three different faces of a brick and write their sizes.
Why must bricks in a wall not sit exactly on top of each other?
Draw a basket weave pattern on squared paper and continue it.
Write the steps of making a brick in order.
A stack has 8 bricks in a row, 5 rows and 7 layers. How many bricks?
A pyramid stack has 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 bricks in its layers. Find the total.
Find a jaali near your home or school and draw its pattern.
If one brick weighs about 3 kg, how much do 50 bricks weigh?

rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch2-long-and-short.title: Long and Short
rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch2-long-and-short.subtitle: Hand spans, centimetres, metres and kilometres — measuring the world around you

sections.md:
Riya and her grandfather are measuring the new curtain for the window. Dadaji uses his **hand span**. Riya uses hers. Dadaji says *8 spans*; Riya says *11 spans*! Who is right?

Both are — but their hands are different sizes. That is the problem with body measures like **hand span, foot, arm length (cubit) and steps**. They change from person to person. So people agreed on **standard units** that are the same everywhere: the **centimetre (cm)**, **metre (m)** and **kilometre (km)**. A tailor in Kolkata and a carpenter in Chennai mean exactly the same length when they say *1 metre*.

In this chapter you will:
1. Measure with body units and see why they differ
2. Use a ruler and scale in centimetres and millimetres
3. Measure big things in metres
4. Understand kilometres for long distances
5. Estimate, compare and convert lengths

check.q: Why did Riya and Dadaji get different answers?
options: Their hand spans are of different sizes
check.why: Body measures like hand spans differ from person to person, so answers differ — that is why we need standard units.

sections.md:
Before rulers, people used their body. Try these with a friend:

| Body measure | What it is | About how long (for a 9-year-old) |
|---|---|---|
| Hand span | Tip of thumb to tip of little finger, stretched | 13–16 cm |
| Finger width | Width of one finger | about 1 cm |
| Foot | Heel to toe | 18–22 cm |
| Cubit | Elbow to tip of middle finger | 30–35 cm |
| Step | One walking step | 40–50 cm |

**Activity:** Measure your desk in hand spans. Ask your teacher to do the same. Compare. The bigger the unit, the **smaller** the number you get.

**Guess first, then measure:** Guess the length of your pencil, your book and the classroom. Then measure. Good guessing (**estimating**) is a useful skill — the closer your guess, the better your sense of length.

check.q: If a big hand measures a table as 6 spans, a smaller hand will get…
check.why: A smaller unit fits more times into the same length, so the smaller hand gets a bigger number.

sections.md:
Look at your ruler (scale). The long lines with numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 … mark **centimetres**. Between two numbers are 10 tiny gaps — each is a **millimetre (mm)**.

**1 cm = 10 mm**

**How to measure correctly:**
1. Put the object's one end exactly at **0**, not at the edge of the ruler.
2. Keep the ruler straight along the object.
3. Read where the other end reaches. If it is between lines, count the mm.
4. If your ruler is broken, start at 1 cm and **subtract 1** from the reading.

An eraser might be **4 cm 5 mm** long. A coin's thickness is about 2 mm. Your fingernail is about 1 cm wide.

**Lines of different lengths:** draw a 7 cm line, a 4 cm 3 mm line, and check with a friend's ruler.

check.q: How many millimetres make 1 centimetre?
check.why: Each centimetre on a ruler is split into 10 small gaps, so 1 cm = 10 mm.

sections.md:
Measuring a classroom in centimetres would take forever. For bigger lengths we use the **metre (m)**.

**1 m = 100 cm**

A metre is about the length from your nose to the tip of your outstretched arm for an adult, or a big step for an adult. A door is about 2 m tall; a cricket pitch is about 20 m long (wicket to wicket); a bus is about 10–12 m long.

Tailors use a soft **measuring tape**; builders use a long metal tape; cloth shops use a metre rod.

**Mixed units:** 1 m 35 cm = 100 + 35 = 135 cm. And 250 cm = 2 m 50 cm.

**Heights:** Children in Class 4 are usually about 120–140 cm tall. Make a height chart on the wall and mark everyone in your family — who is tallest, who is shortest, and what is the difference?

check.q: How many centimetres is 2 m 40 cm?

sections.md:
At the school sports day, the long jump is measured in metres and centimetres.

| Name | Long jump |
|---|---|
| Arjun | 2 m 15 cm |
| Sana | 2 m 40 cm |
| Kabir | 1 m 95 cm |
| Priya | 2 m 05 cm |

To compare, change all to cm: Arjun 215, Sana 240, Kabir 195, Priya 205. **Sana jumped farthest**; Kabir the least. Sana beat Kabir by 240 − 195 = **45 cm**.

**Did you know?** In athletics, India's Neeraj Chopra won Olympic gold in 2020 (held in 2021) throwing the javelin about **87.58 m** — longer than most school playgrounds! Long-jump world records are close to 9 m.

check.q: Who jumped farther: 2 m 5 cm or 1 m 98 cm?
check.why: 2 m 5 cm = 205 cm, which is more than 198 cm.

sections.md:
How far is your school? Your grandmother's village? We measure such distances in **kilometres (km)**.

**1 km = 1,000 m**

Walking 1 km takes most people about 12–15 minutes. Around a 400 m running track, 1 km is 2½ rounds.

Milestones on highways show the distance to the next town in km. On a road from Delhi to Agra the distance is roughly 230 km by expressway.

**Choose the right unit:**
- length of an ant → mm
- length of a pencil → cm
- height of a tree → m
- distance between two cities → km

check.q: Which unit suits the distance from Mumbai to Pune?
check.why: Long distances between cities are measured in kilometres.

sections.md:
Remember the ladder: **10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km.** Going to a smaller unit, multiply; going to a bigger unit, divide.

- 3 m = 300 cm
- 5 km = 5,000 m
- 600 cm = 6 m
- 2,500 m = 2 km 500 m
- ½ m = 50 cm; ½ km = 500 m; ¼ km = 250 m

**Before comparing or adding, write lengths in the same unit.** Is 1 km more than 999 m? Yes — 1 km = 1,000 m.

check.q: ½ km equals…
check.why: 1 km = 1,000 m, so half of it is 500 m.

workedExamples.q: Meena's ribbon is 1 m 20 cm. She cuts 45 cm. How much is left?
A school is 2 km 300 m from home. Ravi walks there and back. How far?
A tailor needs 2 m 50 cm cloth for one kurta. How much for 4 kurtas?
Dadaji is 172 cm tall, Riya 128 cm. What is the difference?

summary: Body measures (span, foot, cubit, step) differ between people.
Standard units are the same everywhere.
1 cm = 10 mm.
Always start measuring from 0 on the ruler.
A smaller unit gives a bigger number for the same length.
Estimate first, then measure to check.
Convert to the same unit before comparing or adding.
Choose mm, cm, m or km to suit the size of the thing.
½ m = 50 cm and ½ km = 500 m.
practice: Measure your table using hand span, then a ruler. Write both answers.
Draw lines of 6 cm and 3 cm 4 mm.
Convert: 4 m 5 cm to cm; 3,750 m to km and m.
Arrange from shortest to longest: 1 m 2 cm, 98 cm, 1 m 20 cm, 110 cm.
A rope is 5 m long. How many 50 cm pieces can be cut from it?
Name three things you would measure in m and three in km.
A bus goes 45 km in an hour. How far in 3 hours?
Make a height chart of your family and find the difference between the tallest and shortest.

rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch3-a-trip-to-bhopa.title: A Trip to Bhopal
rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch3-a-trip-to-bhopa.subtitle: Buses, tickets, lunch money and lakes — add, subtract, multiply and divide on a school trip

sections.md:
The bell rings and Ms Fatima walks into Class 4 with a big smile. *"Next month, we are going on a trip to Bhopal!"* The class cheers. The school is in a small town about 150 km from Bhopal, the capital of Madhya Pradesh.

But a trip needs planning — and planning needs **maths**. How many buses? How much money? How much food? What time do we leave? In this chapter you'll solve every question the teachers and children face, using:

1. Addition and subtraction of big numbers
2. Multiplication — many groups of the same size
3. Division — sharing and grouping
4. Money in rupees
5. Time and distance
6. Making sensible estimates

Along the way you'll visit the places Bhopal is famous for: the **Upper Lake (Bada Talab)**, **Bharat Bhavan**, the **Tribal Museum**, and on the way the ancient **stupa at Sanchi** and the **rock shelters of Bhimbetka**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with paintings made thousands of years ago.

check.q: Bhopal is the capital of which state?
check.why: Bhopal is the capital of Madhya Pradesh, often called the City of Lakes.

sections.h: How many are going, and how many buses?
sections.md:
**Who is going:** 45 children from Class 4, 42 from Class 5, and 6 teachers.

Total = 45 + 42 + 6 = **93 people**.

**Buses:** Each bus has 40 seats. How many buses?
- 2 buses = 80 seats — not enough for 93.
- 3 buses = 120 seats — enough! **3 buses** are needed, with 120 − 93 = **27 empty seats**.

When we divide and there is something left over, we must think: *Can the leftover people stay home?* No! So we **round up** to the next whole bus. Real-life division needs common sense.

**Better plan?** Ms Fatima asks a travel agent for a big 52-seat bus and a 45-seat bus: 52 + 45 = 97 seats — only 4 empty seats, and only 2 drivers to pay.

check.q: 93 people, buses of 40 seats. How many buses?
check.why: 2 buses give only 80 seats; 3 buses give 120, enough for 93 — leftover people can't be left behind, so round up.

sections.md:
**Bus hire:** ₹4,500 per bus for the day. 3 buses = 4,500 × 3 = **₹13,500**.

**Entry tickets:** Tribal Museum ₹10 per child, ₹20 per adult (example prices).
- Children: 87 × 10 = ₹870
- Teachers: 6 × 20 = ₹120
- Total = ₹990

**Lunch:** A dhaba gives a thali for ₹45. 93 thalis = 93 × 45.
- 93 × 40 = 3,720
- 93 × 5 = 465
- Total = 3,720 + 465 = **₹4,185**

**Whole trip cost:** 13,500 + 990 + 4,185 = **₹18,675**.

**Per child?** The school pays for teachers; children share the rest. Writing it as an estimate: ₹18,675 ÷ 87 is a little more than ₹200 each (because 87 × 200 = 17,400 and 87 × 215 = 18,705). The school collects ₹215 each and uses the extra ₹30 for water bottles.

head: Item
Working
Cost (₹)
fig.caption: The trip budget, worked step by step

check.q: What is 93 × 45?

sections.md:
The town is **150 km** from Bhopal. The bus goes at about **50 km in one hour**.

150 ÷ 50 = **3 hours**.

If the buses leave at **6:30 a.m.**, they reach at about **9:30 a.m.** On the way they stop at Sanchi for 1 hour, so they actually reach at **10:30 a.m.**

**Return:** They leave Bhopal at 4:00 p.m. and take 3 hours → reach home at 7:00 p.m.

**Time spent away from home:** 6:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. = 12 hours 30 minutes.

**Train idea:** Children also look up a train that covers 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes — faster than the bus! Trains can be faster because they don't stop at traffic lights.

fig.alt: A yellow school bus drives along a road from home to Bhopal.

check.q: A bus goes 50 km in an hour. How long for 150 km?
check.why: 150 ÷ 50 = 3, so it takes 3 hours.

sections.h: Sharing and grouping at the museum
sections.md:
At the museum, the guide can take **12 children at a time**. 87 children ÷ 12:
- 12 × 7 = 84, leaving 3 children.
- So 7 full groups and 1 small group of 3 — **8 groups** in all (or put the 3 into other groups to make 3 groups of 13).

**Bananas:** The school carries 180 bananas for 87 children. Each child gets 2 → 174 used, **6 left** for the teachers.

**Water:** Each person needs 1 litre bottle. A crate holds 12 bottles. 93 ÷ 12 → 7 crates hold 84, so **8 crates** are needed (96 bottles; 3 spare).

Division has two kinds: **sharing** (180 bananas among 87 children) and **grouping** (how many groups of 12 in 87). Both use the same sum.

check.q: 87 children in groups of 12 — how many groups are needed so everyone is included?
check.why: 7 groups of 12 make 84; the remaining 3 need an 8th group.

sections.md:
- **Upper Lake (Bada Talab)** was made about 1,000 years ago, traditionally linked to Raja Bhoj of the Paramara dynasty, after whom the city may be named. It still supplies drinking water to the city.
- **Sanchi Stupa**, about 46 km from Bhopal, was first built in the time of Emperor Ashoka, in the 3rd century BCE — more than 2,200 years ago.
- **Bhimbetka rock shelters**, about 45 km from Bhopal, have paintings of animals, dancers and hunters, some made over 10,000 years ago.
- **Bharat Bhavan** is an arts centre with museums and theatre by the lake.

On the way back, children write in their diaries. Rehana writes: *We travelled 300 km in one day, saw paintings older than the pyramids, and ate 93 thalis!*

check.q: The Sanchi stupa was first built in the time of…
check.why: The great stupa at Sanchi was begun under Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.

workedExamples.q: There are 45 Class 4 and 42 Class 5 children. How many more in Class 4?
A packet of 8 biscuits costs ₹12. The school needs 96 biscuits. Cost?
The school had ₹20,000. The trip cost ₹18,675. How much is left?
Each of 3 buses uses 30 litres of diesel. Diesel costs ₹90 a litre. Total diesel cost?
If 4 children share a boat ride costing ₹120, how much does each pay?

summary: Plan a trip by adding everyone who goes.
When dividing people into buses or groups, round up if some are left over.
Multiply to find the cost of many of the same thing.
Break a hard multiplication into easy parts: 93 × 45 = 93 × 40 + 93 × 5.
Add all costs for the total; divide to find the share per person.
Time = distance ÷ speed when speed is steady.
Count hours from start time to end time to find time taken.
Division can mean sharing or grouping.
Estimates help check whether an answer is sensible.
Bhopal: Upper Lake, Bharat Bhavan; nearby Sanchi and Bhimbetka.

A thali costs ₹55. Find the cost for 64 people.

₹2,400 is shared equally by 8 children. How much does each get?
A museum ticket is ₹15. How much for 38 children?
Plan your own class trip: list people, transport, food and find the total cost.
If a bus goes 45 km in an hour, how far does it go in 4 hours?

rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch4-tick-tick-tick.title: Tick-Tick-Tick
rd-school-c4-maths-a.ch4-tick-tick-tick.subtitle: Seconds, minutes, hours, a.m. and p.m., the 24-hour clock and how long things take

sections.h: What can you do in one minute?
sections.md:
Ready… set… go! Clap as many times as you can in one minute. Some children clap 150 times, some 200! Now: how many times can you write your name in one minute? Hop on one foot? Say the 2-times table?

Time is something we cannot see or touch, but we can **measure** it — with clocks, watches, the sun, even sand. In this chapter:

1. Seconds, minutes and hours
2. Reading a clock with two hands
3. Quarter past, half past, quarter to
4. a.m. and p.m.
5. The 24-hour clock (railway time)
6. Finding how long something takes
7. Long-ago ways of measuring time

check.q: Which is the smallest of these units of time?
check.why: A second is the smallest: 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes an hour.

sections.md:
**60 seconds = 1 minute**
**60 minutes = 1 hour**
**24 hours = 1 day**

A second is about as long as it takes to say *one-thousand-one*. Your heart beats about once a second. In 1 minute a fast runner covers about 400 m.

| Activity | Measure in |
|---|---|
| Blinking | less than a second |
| Brushing teeth | minutes (about 2–3) |
| A cricket T20 innings | minutes (about 85–90) |
| School day | hours (about 6) |
| Train journey Delhi–Mumbai | hours (about 16) |

**Converting:** 2 hours = 120 minutes. 3 minutes = 180 seconds. 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes. ½ hour = 30 minutes; ¼ hour = 15 minutes.

check.q: How many minutes are in 2½ hours?
check.why: 2 hours = 120 minutes, half an hour = 30; total 150 minutes.

sections.md:
A clock face has numbers 1 to 12. The **short hand** shows the **hour**; the **long hand** shows the **minutes**. Some clocks have a thin, fast **seconds hand**.

Between two numbers there are **5 small minute marks**. So when the long hand points to 1, it's 5 minutes past; to 2, 10 minutes; to 3, 15 minutes … to 12, 0 minutes (o'clock).

| Long hand on | Minutes past | We say |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | 0 | o'clock |
| 3 | 15 | quarter past |
| 6 | 30 | half past |
| 9 | 45 | quarter to (next hour) |

**Example:** The short hand is just past 4 and the long hand is on 9 → **4:45**, or **quarter to five**.

When it is half past, the hour hand is **halfway** between two numbers — it moves slowly all the time, not in jumps.

check.q: The long hand is on 6 and the short hand is between 2 and 3. What time is it?
check.why: Long hand on 6 means 30 minutes; the short hand just past 2 means the hour is 2 — so 2:30, half past two.

sections.md:
The hour hand goes round **twice** in a day, so 7 o'clock comes twice — once in the morning and once in the evening! To tell them apart:

- **a.m.** — from 12 midnight to 12 noon (morning)
- **p.m.** — from 12 noon to 12 midnight (afternoon, evening, night)

*School starts at 8:00 a.m. Lunch is at 12:30 p.m. Dinner is at 8:00 p.m.*

**Raju's day** (a timeline):
| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 6:00 a.m. | wake up |
| 7:30 a.m. | leave for school |
| 1:30 p.m. | school ends |
| 4:00 p.m. | play cricket |
| 9:00 p.m. | sleep |

items.what: Wake up
Leave for school
Lunch break
School ends
Play cricket
Sleep

fig.caption: Raju's day from morning to night

check.q: You have breakfast at 7 in the morning. How do you write it?
check.why: Morning times, between midnight and noon, are a.m.

sections.md:
Indian Railways, airports and phones often use the **24-hour clock**. Hours are numbered 0 to 23, so there is no need for a.m. or p.m.

- Morning times stay the same: 7:30 a.m. → **07:30**
- 12 noon → **12:00**
- For p.m. times, **add 12**: 3:15 p.m. → **15:15**; 9:00 p.m. → **21:00**
- Midnight → **00:00**

**Train ticket:** *Departure 16:45, Arrival 22:10.* That is 4:45 p.m. to 10:10 p.m.

To change back from 24-hour time: if the hour is more than 12, subtract 12 and say p.m. — 18:20 → 6:20 p.m.

check.q: What is 20:15 in the 12-hour clock?

sections.md:
To find how much time passed, count **from start to end** — first full hours, then the leftover minutes.

*A film starts at 3:15 p.m. and ends at 5:40 p.m.*
- 3:15 → 5:15 = 2 hours
- 5:15 → 5:40 = 25 minutes
- **Total: 2 hours 25 minutes**

When crossing an hour, jump to the next o'clock first: 9:50 → 10:00 is 10 minutes, 10:00 → 10:35 is 35 minutes, total 45 minutes.

**Find the end time:** A cake must bake for 40 minutes. It goes in at 4:35 p.m. → 4:35 + 25 = 5:00, + 15 more = **5:15 p.m.**

check.q: From 10:45 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. is…
check.why: 10:45 → 11:45 is 1 hour; 11:45 → 12:15 is 30 minutes; total 1 hour 30 minutes.

sections.md:
Before mechanical clocks, people used:
- **Sundials** — a stick's shadow moves round as the sun moves. The **Jantar Mantar** in Jaipur and Delhi, built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1700s, has a giant sundial (the Samrat Yantra) that tells local time to about 2 seconds.
- **Ghati (water clock)** — a bowl with a tiny hole floats in water and sinks in a fixed time; in old India a *ghatika* was 24 minutes.
- **Sand glass (hourglass)** — sand flows from top to bottom in a fixed time.
- **Candle clocks** with marks.

Today atomic clocks are so exact that they lose less than a second in millions of years!

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch2-a-snake-charmers-.title: A Snake Charmer's Story
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch2-a-snake-charmers-.subtitle: Does the cobra really dance to the been? A journey into snakes, music and a changing way of life.

sections.h: A crowd in the village square
sections.md:
Picture a hot afternoon at a village fair in Rajasthan. Drums thump, children push to the front, and an old man sits cross-legged with a round basket in front of him. He lifts the lid, raises a strange instrument to his lips and begins to play. Slowly, a cobra rises, spreads its hood and sways from side to side. The crowd gasps. *Is the snake dancing to the music?*

This chapter is about families who have lived with snakes for hundreds of years. In many parts of India they are called **saperas** or **jogis**, and one well-known community is the **Kalbelia** of Rajasthan. For generations, a father taught his son how to find snakes, how to handle them safely and how to play the **been** — a wind instrument made from a dried gourd (a kind of hollow vegetable shell) with two pipes attached below.

In this read you will learn:

- how snake charmers lived and travelled
- what the been is and how it is played
- how snakes really sense the world
- which Indian snakes are poisonous and which are not
- why the law changed the life of snake charmers
- how this community is now finding new ways to earn a living

> **Did you know?** The been is also called the *pungi* in many places. Its sound is made by blowing steadily while breathing in through the nose — a trick called circular breathing that takes years to learn.

Here is the big secret: **snakes do not have outer ears**, and they cannot enjoy music the way you do. A snake senses sounds mostly as **vibrations** — tiny shakes that travel through the ground and through its jawbone to its inner ear. It can pick up some low sounds in the air, but the tune of the been means little to it.

So why does the cobra sway? Watch the charmer carefully. As he plays, he **moves the been from side to side**. The cobra sees a moving object near its face and treats it as a possible danger. It rises, spreads its hood to look bigger, and follows the been with its head, ready to defend itself. The 'dance' is really the snake keeping its eyes on something it does not trust!

The charmer also taps the ground or the basket. The snake feels these vibrations and becomes alert. A skilled charmer knows exactly how close he can come and when to stop.

| What we think | What really happens |
|---|---|
| The snake loves the music | The snake cannot hear the tune well |
| It dances to the beat | It follows the moving been |
| It is happy | It is on guard |

sections.md:
Snake charmer families often moved from village to village. In each place they would put on a show, and people paid them with grain, flour, clothes or a few coins. Many villagers also called them when a snake entered a house or field, because the charmers knew how to catch it without getting hurt.

Boys grew up with snakes as part of daily life. A child might start by learning about snake behaviour, then helping to feed them, and only much later learn to catch them. Along with this came knowledge of **herbs and jungle medicines** passed down by elders. (Remember: for a real snakebite, today the right thing is always to rush to a hospital.)

The Kalbelia are also famous for music and dance. Kalbelia women dance in flowing black skirts, and their movements look like a gliding snake. The dance is so special that UNESCO has listed Kalbelia folk songs and dances as part of the world's *intangible cultural heritage* (2010). A well-known Kalbelia dancer, **Gulabo Sapera**, has performed this dance in many countries.

> **Think:** Many skills in India pass from parents to children — pottery, weaving, farming, music. Which skill in your family has been passed down?

sections.h: Snakes of India: poisonous or not?
sections.md:
India has around 300 kinds of snakes, but most of them are **not poisonous**. Only a few are dangerous to humans. Four common ones are called the **'Big Four'**:

1. **Indian cobra** (Nag) — has a hood with a spectacle-like mark
2. **Common krait** — shiny black with thin white bands; often comes out at night
3. **Russell's viper** — brown with chains of dark round spots; hisses loudly
4. **Saw-scaled viper** — small, sandy-coloured, rubs its scales to make a rasping sound

Some snakes people often fear but which are **harmless** to us: the **rat snake** (dhaman), the **sand boa**, and the **python** (pythons are not poisonous, though large ones can squeeze prey).

Snakes are very useful. They eat **rats and mice** that would otherwise eat a farmer's grain. Without snakes, rats would multiply and destroy crops.

**Antivenom** — the medicine for snakebite — is actually made from snake venom! Small amounts of venom are collected carefully from snakes, and the medicine is prepared from it. So snakes even help save people from snakebites.

sections.md:
Many stories about snakes are not true. Let us sort them out:

- **'Snakes drink milk.'** — *Myth.* Snakes eat frogs, rats, lizards and birds. A snake kept without water may sip milk out of thirst, but milk can make it sick.
- **'A snake takes revenge.'** — *Myth.* Snakes do not remember faces or plan revenge.
- **'All snakes are poisonous.'** — *Myth.* Most are harmless.
- **'Snakes feel vibrations.'** — *Fact.* This is how they know someone is walking near.
- **'Snakes smell with their tongue.'** — *Fact.* The forked tongue collects smells from the air and passes them to a special organ in the roof of the mouth.

Snakes also **shed their skin** several times a year as they grow. The old skin comes off in one piece, like taking off a sock inside-out.

> **Did you know?** A snake's eyes have no eyelids. That is why snakes always seem to be staring!
keyTerms: Venom — poison made by some snakes
Antivenom — medicine made from venom to treat snakebite
Vibration — a tiny shaking that snakes can feel
Been — a gourd wind instrument played by snake charmers

check.q: How does a snake mostly smell things?
check.why: The forked tongue picks up smells from the air and carries them to a special organ in the mouth.

sections.md:
Keeping snakes in baskets for shows was hard on the snakes. Often their fangs were pulled out, they were not fed properly, and many died. To protect wild animals, India passed the **Wildlife Protection Act in 1972**. Under this law, catching wild animals — including snakes — and keeping them for shows is **not allowed**.

This was good for snakes, but it created a big problem for snake charmer families. Their whole way of earning was suddenly against the law. Many had no land, no other training, and children had to leave the old work.

So what did they do? Different families found different paths:

- **Music and dance:** playing the been and performing Kalbelia dance at festivals, weddings, hotels and on stage.
- **Snake rescue:** some use their knowledge to help forest departments catch snakes that enter homes and release them safely in the wild.
- **Teaching awareness:** explaining to people which snakes are harmless and how to stay safe.
- **New jobs** in farming, crafts and other work.

The skill of understanding snakes is precious. When it is used to **protect** snakes rather than trap them, both people and animals win.

check.why: The Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 protects wild animals, including snakes, from being caught and kept for shows.

sections.md:
You will probably meet a snake one day, especially during the **monsoon**, when water fills their holes and they come out. Here is how to stay safe:

1. **Stay calm and step back slowly.** Most snakes just want to get away.
2. **Never try to catch or kill a snake.** Most bites happen when people try to do this.
3. **Use a torch at night** and wear footwear when walking in fields or gardens.
4. **Shake out shoes and bedding** in rural areas.
5. If someone is bitten: keep them **still and calm**, remove tight rings or bangles, and **go to a hospital at once**. Do not cut the wound, do not suck it, and do not waste time with home remedies. Hospitals have antivenom.

Remember, snakes are not our enemies. They keep the rat population in control and are an important part of nature.

parts.md: Hiran was nine when his grandfather first let him hold the been. It was heavier than it looked, the gourd polished smooth by years of hands. 'Blow from your belly, not your cheeks,' Dada said, and the sound that came out was so squeaky that even the goats looked up. Every evening Hiran practised outside their tent, and slowly the squeak became a song.

Dada kept one old cobra named Sheshu in a basket. Hiran noticed that Sheshu only rose when Dada swayed the been, never when the music played still. 'He is watching me, isn't he, Dada?' Hiran asked. His grandfather laughed. 'Clever boy. Snakes listen with their bellies. They feel the ground, not the song.'

One day a forest officer visited their camp and explained the new rules. Dada was quiet for a long time. The next morning he and Hiran walked Sheshu to the edge of the forest. Dada opened the basket. Sheshu tasted the air with his tongue, then slid into the grass and was gone. 'He belongs there,' Dada said softly.

Years later, Hiran plays the been on stages in Jaipur while his sister dances the Kalbelia dance in a whirl of black and silver. On weekends he helps the forest team rescue snakes from houses. When children ask if snakes dance, Hiran smiles and tells them the secret Dada taught him.

summary: Snake charmers (saperas, jogis, Kalbelia) have lived with snakes for generations.
The been (pungi) is made from a dried gourd with two pipes.
Snakes have no outer ears; they sense vibrations through the ground.
The cobra follows the movement of the been — it is not dancing to music.
Snakes smell using their forked tongue.
India's 'Big Four' poisonous snakes: cobra, krait, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper.
Most Indian snakes are not poisonous; rat snakes and pythons are not venomous.
Snakes help farmers by eating rats.
Antivenom for snakebite is made from snake venom.
The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 banned catching wild animals for shows.
Snake charmer families now earn through music, dance, snake rescue and other work.
For a snakebite, keep the person still and go to a hospital immediately.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch3-from-tasting-to-d.title: From Tasting to Digesting
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch3-from-tasting-to-d.subtitle: How your tongue tastes, why chewing matters, the doctor who peeped into a stomach, and why every child needs good food

sections.md:
Blindfold a friend. Hold their nose. Put a tiny piece of apple on their tongue — then a piece of raw potato. Can they tell which is which? Very often, they can't! Taste and smell work together.

This chapter follows food on its journey:
1. How the tongue senses different tastes
2. Taste and smell together
3. Saliva — the mouth's helper
4. What happens in the stomach (the famous story of Dr Beaumont)
5. Glucose and energy
6. Why some children don't get enough food — and what is being done

**A word of caution:** do the taste activities only with clean, safe food and a clean spoon, with an adult's permission.

check.q: Why is it harder to tell apple from potato when the nose is held?
check.why: Much of what we call flavour comes from smell; blocking the nose makes foods harder to tell apart.

sections.md:
Look at your tongue in a mirror. It is covered with tiny bumps; inside them are **taste buds**. They sense five basic tastes:

| Taste | Example foods |
|---|---|
| Sweet | jaggery, sugar, ripe banana |
| Salty | salt, chips, namkeen |
| Sour | tamarind, lemon, raw mango |
| Bitter | karela (bitter gourd), neem, coffee |
| Umami (savoury) | tomato, mushrooms, cheese |

**Activity (from the chapter idea):** Put a little sugar, then salt, then lemon juice, then a bit of neem or bitter gourd on different parts of your tongue (rinse between each). Note what you feel.

**Old idea, new facts:** Many old books drew a *tongue map* with sweet only at the tip and bitter at the back. Scientists now know that **all parts of the tongue can sense all tastes**; some areas may be a little more sensitive. A dry tongue tastes poorly — wetness (saliva) is needed to dissolve food so taste buds can sense it.

check.why: Karela (bitter gourd) is a common bitter-tasting vegetable.

sections.h: Chew, chew, chew — saliva at work
sections.md:
**Activity:** Take a small piece of roti or bread and chew it slowly for a long time — 30 times or more. What happens? It starts to taste **slightly sweet**!

Why? Your mouth makes **saliva** (spit). Saliva:
- makes food wet and soft so it can be swallowed,
- helps us taste,
- contains a substance that begins breaking down **starch** (in roti, rice, potato) into **sugar**.

We make saliva when we see, smell or even *think* of tasty food — your mouth may be watering right now if you're thinking of hot pakoras on a rainy day!

**Chewing** breaks food into small bits. That's why elders say *chew your food well* — it makes the stomach's work easier.

**After swallowing**, food travels down the **food pipe (oesophagus)** to the stomach. Even if you stand on your head, food goes to the stomach — muscles push it along.

check.q: Why does roti taste sweet after long chewing?
check.why: Saliva starts breaking down starch into sugar, which tastes sweet.

sections.h: A window into the stomach — Dr Beaumont's story
sections.md:
In 1822, in North America, a young man called **Alexis St. Martin** was accidentally shot in the stomach. A doctor, **William Beaumont**, treated him. Alexis survived, but the wound healed in a strange way — it left a small **opening** from the outside of his body into his stomach.

Dr Beaumont realised this was a rare chance to learn how the stomach works. Over several years, with Alexis's help, he:
- tied small pieces of food to a thread and put them into the stomach through the opening, pulling them out after some hours to see how much had been digested;
- took out some of the stomach's juices and saw that they could break down food even outside the body, in a bottle;
- noticed that the stomach **churns** food and that worry or anger affected digestion.

He learned that the stomach makes **digestive juices** (including an acid) that break food into simpler forms. Digestion is a mix of **churning** (physical) and **juices** (chemical).

From the stomach, food moves to the **small intestine**, where digestion finishes and nutrients pass into the blood. Undigested parts go to the **large intestine** and leave the body as waste.

options: It makes juices that break down food and churns it
It sends food to the lungs
check.why: He found the stomach churns food and releases digestive juices that break it down.

sections.md:
Have you seen someone in a hospital with a bottle and tube attached to the arm? That is often a **glucose drip**. When a person is very weak — for example after loose motions (diarrhoea) or when they cannot eat — doctors give glucose straight into the blood.

**Glucose** is a simple sugar. Our body breaks down much of our food into glucose, and our cells use it for **energy**. Because glucose is already simple, the body doesn't need to digest it, so it gives energy quickly.

**Diarrhoea and ORS:** When we lose a lot of water through loose motions, the body becomes **dehydrated**. **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) puts back water, salt and sugar. Packet ORS from a chemist or health centre, mixed exactly as written on the packet, is best. Health workers also teach a home sugar-salt solution (for 1 litre of clean, boiled and cooled water, the commonly taught measure is 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt) — an adult should make it. *Always see a doctor if a child has diarrhoea for long or seems very weak.*

check.q: Why does a glucose drip give quick energy?
options: Glucose is already simple and needs no digestion
check.why: Glucose is a simple sugar the cells can use straight away for energy.

sections.h: Food for all — hunger and the mid-day meal
sections.md:
The chapter also asks: *do all children get enough to eat?* Many children in India and around the world still do not. When children don't get enough good food for a long time they may become **weak**, fall ill often, grow slowly, and find it hard to study. Not having enough **iron** in food can cause **anaemia** — tiredness and pale skin.

To help, many states began serving a free cooked **mid-day meal** in government schools, and in 2001 the Supreme Court ordered it across India. It is now called **PM POSHAN**. A hot meal of dal, rice, vegetables or roti keeps children healthy and helps more children come to school.

**Balanced diet:** Eat a mix of grains (energy), dal, milk, eggs or pulses (body-building), fruit and vegetables (protection), and drink clean water.

> Did you know? Your stomach can stretch to hold more than a litre of food, and the small intestine of an adult is about 6–7 metres long!

check.q: Lack of iron in food can cause…
check.why: Iron is needed to make healthy blood; too little iron leads to anaemia.

summary: Taste buds on the tongue sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
All parts of the tongue can sense all tastes.
Smell and taste work together to give flavour.
Saliva wets food and begins turning starch into sugar.
Chewing well breaks food into small pieces.
Food goes down the food pipe to the stomach, pushed by muscles.
Dr Beaumont studied digestion through Alexis St. Martin's stomach opening (from 1822).
The stomach churns food and adds digestive juices.
Digestion finishes in the small intestine; waste leaves through the large intestine.
Glucose is a simple sugar that gives quick energy.
ORS replaces water and salts lost in diarrhoea; see a doctor.
Hunger and lack of iron harm children's health; the mid-day meal (PM POSHAN) helps.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch4-mangoes-round-the.title: Mangoes Round the Year
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch4-mangoes-round-the.subtitle: Why food spoils, the fuzzy fungus on old bread, and how families keep mangoes for months as aam papad and pickle

sections.md:
Mango season in India is short — roughly April to July. Yet in December your grandmother might open a jar of *aam ka achaar* or hand you a strip of chewy, sweet **aam papad**. How did summer's mangoes survive till winter?

This chapter is about **food spoiling and food saving**:
1. How we know food has gone bad
2. Why food spoils — the fungus-on-bread experiment
3. Which foods spoil fast and which last long
4. Ways of preserving food at home
5. The story of making aam papad
6. Saving food in big ways — and not wasting it

check.q: About when is mango season in most of India?
check.why: Most Indian mangoes ripen in the hot months, roughly April to July.

sections.h: How do we know food has spoiled?
sections.md:
Use your senses — carefully!

- **Smell:** sour or bad smell (spoilt milk, dal left out on a hot day)
- **Look:** changed colour, white/green/black fuzzy patches, slime
- **Taste:** sour or strange (only a tiny bit, and never if it looks or smells bad)
- **Touch:** sticky, slimy or too soft (an over-ripe tomato)

**Never eat spoiled food** — it can cause stomach pain, vomiting and loose motions (food poisoning).

**Which spoil fast?** Cooked rice and dal, milk, paneer, cut fruit — especially in hot, humid weather. **Which last longer?** Dry grains (rice, wheat, dal), whole spices, jaggery, sugar, salt — because they have very little water.

check.q: Why do dry grains last longer than cooked rice?
options: They have very little water, so germs can't grow easily
check.why: Tiny living things that spoil food need water; dry grains have very little, so they keep longer.

sections.h: The bread experiment — meet the fungus
sections.md:
**Activity:** Take a piece of bread or roti. Sprinkle a few drops of water on it and keep it in a closed box in a warm place. Look at it every day for a week (don't touch or smell closely — use a hand lens if you have one). Record what you see:

| Day | What we see |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | no change, a bit soft |
| 3 | tiny white spots |
| 4–5 | spots spread, become fluffy, grey-green or black |
| 6–7 | bread covered with fuzzy patches, bad smell |

The fuzzy growth is a **fungus** (mould). Fungi are tiny living things. Their **spores** float in the air all the time — invisible! When they land on food that is **moist and warm**, they grow and spoil it.

**Try it:** Keep one piece dry, one wet, one in the fridge. Which gets fungus first? Usually the **wet, warm** one. Cold and dryness slow fungus down.

check.q: Fungus grows fastest on bread that is…
check.why: Fungal spores grow best where there is moisture and warmth.

sections.h: Ways to keep food from spoiling
sections.md:
People have found many clever ways to **preserve** food — all work by stopping germs and fungi from growing.

| Method | How it works | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Drying in the sun | removes water | papad, vadi, dried chillies, raw-mango *amchur*, fish |
| Salt | draws out water; germs can't live | pickles, salted fish, lemon in salt |
| Sugar / jaggery | thick sugar stops germs | murabba, jam, aam papad |
| Oil | covers food, keeps air out | mango/lime pickles |
| Vinegar | sour; germs dislike it | onion, chilli pickles |
| Cold | slows germs | refrigerator, matka for water |
| Boiling | kills germs | boiling milk twice a day |
| Airtight cans/packets | no air or germs get in | packed juices, tinned food |

When you buy packaged food, read the **date of manufacture** and **best before/expiry** date on the pack.

check.q: How does salt help preserve pickles?
options: It draws out water so germs can't grow
check.why: Salt pulls water out of food and germs, so they cannot grow and spoil it.

sections.h: Making aam papad — a family story
sections.md:
It is a scorching June morning in a village near Lucknow. Aapa (elder sister) calls the children: *"Come — today we make aam papad!"*

1. **Choose:** ripe, sweet, juicy mangoes are washed.
2. **Pulp:** the mangoes are peeled and squeezed; the pulp is strained through a cloth so no fibres remain.
3. **Sweeten:** jaggery or sugar is mixed in (some add a pinch of salt or cardamom).
4. **Spread:** a thin layer of pulp is spread on a clean, oiled plate, mat or cloth.
5. **Dry:** the plates are kept in hot sun for several days. A net or cloth is put on top to keep away flies, dust and birds; they are taken in at night.
6. **Layer:** when one layer is dry, another is spread on top — again and again until it is thick.
7. **Cut and store:** it is cut into pieces and stored in an airtight jar.

**Why does it last?** The sun dries out the water, and the sugar stops germs. Together they keep mangoes 'round the year'.

**Also:** raw mangoes become *amchur* (dried mango powder), *aam panna* concentrate and many pickles — each region has its own.

check.q: Why is aam papad covered with a net while drying?
options: To keep away flies, dust and birds
check.why: The net keeps it clean and safe from insects and birds while it dries.

sections.h: Food that travels, and food we waste
sections.md:
Today trucks with **cold storage** and big warehouses help fruits and grain travel long distances — mangoes from Ratnagiri reach Delhi, apples from Himachal reach Chennai. Grain is kept in government godowns. But if storage is poor, rain, rats and fungus can spoil huge amounts.

At home and at weddings, a lot of cooked food is thrown away. Ideas to **reduce waste**:
- Cook and serve only what is needed; take small helpings.
- Store leftovers covered and cool; use them soon.
- Share extra food with neighbours or food banks.
- Compost peels and scraps.

> Did you know? Some pickles in Indian homes stay good for over a year because of salt, oil and spices — that's preservation science passed down for generations!

check.q: Which is a good way to reduce food waste at a feast?
options: Take small helpings and go back if needed
check.why: Taking small helpings means less food left on plates and thrown away.

summary: Mango season is short, but preserved mangoes last all year.
Spoiled food shows changes in smell, look, taste and touch.
Never eat spoiled food — it causes food poisoning.
Food with more water (cooked rice, milk) spoils faster than dry grains.
Fungus (mould) grows from tiny spores in the air.
Fungus grows best where it is moist and warm.
Food is preserved by drying, salt, sugar, oil, vinegar, cold, boiling and airtight packing.
Packets show manufacture and expiry dates.
Aam papad: mango pulp + sugar, spread thin and sun-dried layer by layer.
Sun removes water and sugar stops germs.
Cold storage helps food travel; poor storage wastes grain.
We can reduce waste by cooking and serving only what is needed.
practice: Write three signs that milk has gone bad.
Describe the bread-fungus experiment and what you saw.
Why does food spoil faster in summer and the rainy season?
Name two foods preserved with salt, two with sugar and two by drying.
Write the steps of making aam papad.
Why is aam papad dried in many layers?
Look at three food packets at home and note their expiry dates.
Ask an elder how pickles are made in your family and write the method.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds.title: Seeds and Seeds
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds.subtitle: Sprouting moong, what a seed needs, seeds that fly, float, hitch rides and burst — and plants that travelled to India from far away

sections.h: A seed is a baby plant in a lunch box
sections.md:
Soak a few moong beans overnight. In the morning they are fat; in a day or two, tiny white tails pop out. In a week, green leaves! Where was that plant hiding? Inside the seed, all along — a **baby plant (embryo)** packed with its own **food store**, wrapped in a protective **seed coat**, like a lunch box.

In this chapter:
1. Sprouting seeds at home
2. What seeds need to grow — an experiment
3. Looking inside a seed
4. How seeds travel far from the parent plant
5. Plants that came to India from other lands
6. Seeds in our kitchen and farms

check.q: What does the seed coat do?
check.why: The seed coat is a protective cover around the embryo and its food store.

sections.md:
**Activity:**
1. Soak a handful of moong or chana in water overnight.
2. Drain the water and wrap the seeds in a wet cotton cloth.
3. Keep the bundle in a warm place; sprinkle water twice a day.
4. Look every day and draw what you see.

| Day | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | seeds swell, skin wrinkles |
| 2 | a tiny white root (radicle) peeps out |
| 3–4 | root grows longer, hair-like roots appear |
| 5–7 | a shoot with small leaves comes up |

The first part to come out is the **root**, which grows **down**; the shoot grows **up** towards light. Sprouts are also a healthy food — many families eat sprouted moong with lemon, onion and tomato.

fig.alt: A seed in soil sends a root down and a shoot with two leaves up.

check.q: Which part comes out of a sprouting seed first?
check.why: The root (radicle) emerges first and grows downward to anchor the seedling and absorb water.

sections.h: What do seeds need to sprout? — an experiment
sections.md:
Take four small bowls with a few soaked moong in each:

| Bowl | Condition | Result after 3–4 days |
|---|---|---|
| A | dry cotton, no water | no sprouting |
| B | wet cotton, warm room | sprouts well |
| C | seeds completely under boiled-and-cooled water (no air) | little or no sprouting |
| D | wet cotton, in the fridge (cold) | very slow or none |

**Conclusion:** Seeds need **water, air and warmth** to sprout. Interestingly, most seeds **don't need sunlight or soil to sprout**, because they have their own stored food. But once the leaves come out, the young plant needs **sunlight** to make food, and soil for minerals.

**Fair test:** change only *one* thing in each bowl, keep everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.

check.q: Which three things do most seeds need to sprout?
check.why: Bowls without water, without air, or kept cold did not sprout — so seeds need water, air and warmth.

sections.md:
Soak a chana or rajma seed overnight and gently peel the skin. It splits into **two halves** — these are **cotyledons** (seed leaves), full of stored food. Between them you'll see a tiny root and shoot — the **embryo**.

Seeds with two halves (chana, moong, rajma, peanut) are called **dicots**; seeds that don't split (maize, wheat, rice) are **monocots**.

**How many seeds in a fruit?** Count! A mango has 1, a litchi 1, a lady's finger (bhindi) dozens, a papaya or watermelon hundreds, a guava many tiny ones. Some fruits like bananas we grow from cuttings/suckers — their tiny seeds don't grow.

**Seeds of different shapes and sizes:** mustard (tiny, round), rajma (kidney-shaped), coconut (huge — one of the biggest seeds), the double coconut (coco de mer) the largest seed in the world.

check.q: What are the two halves of a chana seed called?
check.why: The two halves are cotyledons, seed leaves that store food for the baby plant.

sections.md:
If every seed fell just below its mother tree, the seedlings would fight for light, water and space. So plants have clever ways to send seeds far away — **seed dispersal**:

| How | Seed feature | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Wind | light, with wings or hairs | madar (aak), cotton, drumstick, maple-like *sal* seeds, dandelion |
| Water | light, waterproof, can float | coconut, lotus |
| Animals (eaten) | tasty fruit; seed passes out unharmed | guava, ber, tomato, mango |
| Animals (hitch-hike) | hooks or spines that stick | *gokhru* (puncture vine), grass burrs, chirchita |
| Bursting | pod dries and pops | balsam, pea, lady's finger, castor |
| People | we carry and sow them | wheat, rice, vegetables |

A coconut can float in the sea for weeks and grow on a faraway beach — that's why coconut palms line coasts.

fig.alt: Hairy seeds drifting from a tree while a coconut bobs on water.

check.q: How does a coconut seed usually travel to new places?
check.why: Coconuts are light and waterproof, so they float on sea water to far-off shores.

sections.h: Plants that came to India from far away
sections.md:
Many foods we think of as completely Indian actually came from other continents, mostly in the last 500 years, brought by traders and travellers (especially the Portuguese, from the 1500s):

| Plant | Came from |
|---|---|
| Chilli (mirch) | South & Central America |
| Tomato | South America |
| Potato | South America (Andes) |
| Maize (makka) | Central America (Mexico) |
| Groundnut (peanut) | South America |
| Cashew | Brazil |
| Papaya | Central America |
| Pineapple | South America |

Before chillies came, Indian food got its heat from **black pepper** and **long pepper** — spices that grew here and were traded across the world.

And India gave the world many plants too — **mango, sugarcane, black pepper, cotton, and many kinds of rice**.

**Saving seeds:** Farmers traditionally saved the best seeds from each harvest. Seed banks today protect thousands of crop varieties so they are not lost.

check.q: Which of these came to India from South America?
check.why: The potato was first grown in the Andes mountains of South America and reached India a few centuries ago.

sections.h: Seeds in the kitchen and the field
sections.md:
Look in your kitchen: **dals and pulses** (moong, masoor, chana, rajma), **grains** (rice, wheat, jowar, bajra, ragi), **spices** (jeera, rai/mustard, methi, saunf, dhaniya, ajwain), **oils** from seeds (mustard, groundnut, sesame, coconut). Seeds feed the whole country!

**On the farm**, seeds are sown by hand broadcasting, in rows with a seed drill, or rice is first grown in a nursery and then transplanted.

> Did you know? Some lotus seeds found in an old lake bed in China sprouted after more than 1,000 years! Seeds can wait a very long time for the right conditions.

check.q: Which of these is a spice made of seeds?
check.why: Jeera is the dried seed of the cumin plant; turmeric and ginger are underground stems.

summary: A seed has a seed coat, stored food and a baby plant (embryo).
Soaked moong and chana sprout in a few days.
The root comes out first and grows down; the shoot grows up.
Seeds need water, air and warmth to sprout.
Most seeds do not need soil or sunlight to sprout, but the young plant needs light to make food.
Change only one thing at a time in a fair test.
Chana and rajma split into two cotyledons (dicots); maize and wheat don't (monocots).
Seeds spread by wind, water, animals, bursting and people.
Spreading seeds avoids crowding under the parent plant.
Chilli, tomato, potato, maize, groundnut and cashew came to India from the Americas.
India gave the world mango, sugarcane, black pepper and cotton.
Our kitchens are full of seeds: dals, grains, spices and oils.
practice: Write the steps for sprouting moong and draw what happens each day.
Design an experiment to show seeds need water to sprout.
Why do most seeds not need sunlight to sprout?
Name two seeds spread by wind, two by water and two by animals.
How does a burr (gokhru) travel? Draw it.
List five plants that came to India from other countries.
Collect ten seeds from your kitchen and group them as dal, grain, spice or oilseed.
Why is it good for a plant that its seeds travel far?

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch6-every-drop-counts.title: Every Drop Counts
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch6-every-drop-counts.subtitle: In a desert that gets little rain, how did people build lakes, wells and stepwells that lasted centuries?

sections.md:
Imagine standing in **Jaisalmer**, a golden city in the Thar desert of Rajasthan, where rain may fall on only a few days a year. And yet, near the city, there is a large lake with stone steps, temples and carved gateways: **Gadisar (Gharsisar) Lake**. It was built in the 14th century by Maharawal Gharsi, so that rainwater flowing from the land around could be **collected and saved**.

The chapter opens with a visitor's description of this lake: wide stone ghats going down to the water, small temples and pavilions around it, and a beautiful gateway. For hundreds of years the people of Jaisalmer drew water from this lake. Everyone, rich or poor, shared in looking after it. When the lake needed cleaning, the whole town came to help, and the king himself is said to have joined.

The chapter asks big questions: **How did people get water in places where it hardly rains? Who looked after the water? Who owned it?** And what can we learn from them today?

> **Did you know?** The Thar desert gets very little rain in a year — far less than Mumbai or Kolkata get in a single monsoon month.

sections.h: Where does it rain how much?
sections.md:
The textbook shows a **rainfall map of India**. Different colours show how much rain each region gets in a year.

- The **north-east** (Meghalaya — Cherrapunji and Mawsynram) and the **west coast** (Konkan, Kerala) get the **most** rain.
- Western **Rajasthan** (Jaisalmer, Barmer, Bikaner) and parts of Ladakh get the **least**.
- Most of the plains get a medium amount, mostly in the **monsoon months** from June to September.

Activity idea: find your own city or village on the map. Does it get a lot of rain or little? Ask the elders at home: Has the rain changed since they were children? Where did their family get water from when they were young — a well, a river, a pond, a hand pump or a tap?

Even places with heavy rain can run short of water if the rain simply runs away into rivers and the sea. So the trick is not only *how much* rain falls, but *how well* we **catch and store** it.

check.q: Which part of India gets the least rain?
check.why: Western Rajasthan, in the Thar desert, receives the least rainfall in India, so people there learnt to save every drop.

sections.md:
The secret of the desert people was simple: **every drop of rain is precious, so catch it where it falls**. This is called **rainwater harvesting**.

- **Kunds / tankas** — round underground tanks built in courtyards or open land. The ground around slopes towards the tank, and rain flows in through small holes. The top is covered (often with a dome) to keep water clean and cool.
- **Rooftop collection** — rain falling on flat roofs is led by pipes into tanks below the house.
- **Johads** — small mud walls (check dams) built across slopes to stop running rainwater so it soaks into the ground and fills wells.
- **Lakes and tanks** — like Gadisar, built where water from a large area would flow.
- **Kuis** — narrow, deep wells that collect water seeping through the sand.

The area from which rain flows into a tank is called its **catchment area**. People kept the catchment clean: no one was allowed to walk on it with shoes or dirty it.
